full_text:
In the ancient kingdom of Sind reigned a tyrannical monarch who extorted heavy taxes from the peasantry, confiscated the estates of merchants, and cast into prison any citizen who spoke of justice.

One afternoon, a young pilgrim dressed in a simple woollen tunic entered the royal audience hall, leaning upon an ebony walking staff. Despite his humble attire, his countenance shone with extraordinary royal dignity and moral authority.

The king frowned: 'Who are you, wandering mendicant, and what brings you to my throne?'

The youth answered: 'I was born Crown Prince of the great kingdom of Balkh. My father possessed armies twice the size of yours and treasuries overflowing with diamonds. Yet he governed with oppression and cruelty.

One day, an earthquake shook our capital; the palace collapsed, my father perished beneath his own golden throne, and our armies were scattered like dust. I walked through the smoking ruins of my ancestral home, and I realized that a throne built on tears is a house built on shifting sand. I renounced worldly power to warn the rulers of the earth:

"He who sows injustice shall reap the whirlwind; the sighs of the oppressed rise higher than the mountain crags, and their tears shall drown the mightiest empire!"'

The words struck the tyrannical king like a thunderbolt. He looked at the youthful prince who had renounced a crown for truth, and looked at his own trembling courtiers.

Profound shame and repentance pierced the king’s soul. He descended from his throne, embraced the pilgrim prince, ordered the immediate release of all prisoners, canceled unjust taxes, and restored confiscated lands, governing for the remainder of his days with justice and mercy.
moral: Earthly power that oppresses the weak is weighed by history and collapses into forgotten dust. [TE]

full_text:
In an ancient grove of walnut trees lived a large flock of crows who had established a peaceful commonwealth. One summer, a fierce hunting hawk took up his perch upon an overhanging granite crag above the grove, sweeping down daily to attack any lone crow that ventured into the open fields.

The elders of the flock called a general assembly. A young, impetuous crow shouted: 'Let our fiercest warrior fly up to the crag and challenge the hawk to single combat!'

An aged, venerable crow shook his head: 'A single crow cannot withstand the hawk's razor talons and hooked beak. But where individual strength fails, united numbers conquer. When the hawk attacks again, let no bird fly alone; let forty of us take wing simultaneously, form a rotating circle around him, and blind his vision with the dust of our wings!'

The next morning, the hawk plunged toward the grove. Instantly, forty crows took flight in coordinated formation!

They surrounded the predator, cawing with deafening unison, darting in and out from every angle, pecking at his wings, and beating the air until the confused hawk could neither focus his attack nor maneuver his broad wings.

Battered, disoriented, and exhausted by the united defense, the hawk broke through the formation and fled across the mountains, never daring to return to the walnut grove.

The crows returned to their boughs in triumph, having learned that collective unity is an impenetrable fortress against tyranny.
moral: United cooperation and collective vigilance protect the community against the fiercest predators. [TE]

full_text:
In a village near Aleppo lived an ambitious snake-charmer named Mansur who caught wild serpents in the rocky hills to perform tricks in the market square. One afternoon, he captured an enormous, venomous black cobra of terrifying power and brought it home in a wicker basket, boasting to his wife:

'Rejoice, wife! With this monstrous serpent, I shall amaze the crowds in the central square and earn fifty silver dirhams every day!'

His prudent wife pleaded with him: 'O husband, be content with harmless grass-snakes! He who harbors a viper beneath his roof invites disaster for a few pieces of silver. Release the beast into the rocky wilderness!'

Mansur laughed scornfully at her fears, placed the wicker basket in the corner of their kitchen, and went to the tavern to celebrate his capture.

While he was absent, the snake rubbed against the wicker lid, worked the latch loose, and crawled onto the floor. When Mansur’s wife entered to prepare the evening meal, she saw the cobra coiled beside the flour-jar, its hood flared and hissing venomously!

Keeping her presence of mind, the courageous woman did not scream. She seized a heavy iron cooking cauldron, dropped it squarely over the serpent, and placed three heavy millstones upon the lid!

When Mansur returned singing and boastful, his wife pointed to the cauldron and handed him his walking staff: 'Pick up your basket and take that monster far into the uninhabited mountains, or seek another hearth! A home is a sanctuary for children, not a cage for venom.'

Mansur blushed with profound shame, released the snake into the distant desert, and resolved never again to risk his family’s safety for reckless gain.
moral: He who brings venomous hazards into his home out of reckless pride endangers those he loves. [TE]

title: The Spider and the Wind (తెలుగు)
summary: Between two branches of a rosebush in a royal garden, a large garden spider spun an intricate, symmetrical web of delicate silk. When the... [TE]
full_text:
Between two branches of a rosebush in a royal garden, a large garden spider spun an intricate, symmetrical web of delicate silk. When the morning dew caught the sunlight, the web sparkled like diamonds strung upon silver cords.

Puffed up with immense pride, the spider strutted to the center of his web, looked down upon the worker ants crawling in the dust, and boasted aloud:

'Look upon my palace! I spin my own architecture out of my own substance, suspended in the air like a celestial bridge! Neither the King of Persia nor the architects of Rome have ever built a palace so geometric, delicate, and radiant!'

A passing honeybee buzzed: 'Your web is beautiful, neighbor, but remember that it hangs upon slender twigs; do not boast until you have tested its strength against the storm.'

The spider scoffed: 'My silk is stronger than iron cables! Let the elements challenge my genius!'

At that moment, the autumn north wind began to blow. A gentle gust of wind swept through the garden; the rose branches swayed, and with a single soft sigh, the delicate spiderweb was torn into shreds and scattered like mist into the grass!

The spider was tumbled into the dirt, bruised and shivering beneath a dry leaf, weeping over his ruined masterpiece.

The humble ant stopped beside him and said: 'He who builds his palace out of pride will find that a passing breeze turns his empire to nothing. Build upon solid ground, and let your works speak without boasting.'
moral: Boastful arrogance in frail works of vanity is swept away in an instant by the breath of nature. [TE]

title: The Two Kings (తెలుగు)

full_text:
Two powerful kings, King Bahram of the East and King Farhad of the West, had mobilized armies of fifty thousand men upon the border plains, ready to plunge their realms into a bloody war over the possession of a fertile border valley.

On the eve of battle, King Bahram, troubled by the prospect of thousands of young men perishing for a strip of earth, rode out alone to the boundary river under a flag of truce, requesting an interview with King Farhad.

The two monarchs met upon an island in the middle of the river, attended only by their chief counselors.

King Bahram said: 'Farhad, our soldiers are sons of honest mothers, our farmers have tilled their fields in hope of harvest, and our merchants have built peaceful commerce. If we fight tomorrow, one of us may win this valley, but both our kingdoms will be filled with widows, orphans, and smoking ruins. Tell me: is a strip of earth worth the blood of ten thousand men?'

King Farhad looked at the peaceful river, and then into the sincere, noble eyes of his rival. His heart was touched with deep reverence.

'You speak truth, Bahram,' replied Farhad. 'Pride blinded my eyes, but your wisdom has restored my sight.'

The two kings drew up a treaty of perpetual alliance: the border valley was declared neutral territory, dedicated to an international market and a shared university of science and agriculture. The revenues were divided equally to build roads, bridges, and hospitals for both nations.

The two armies threw down their weapons, embraced as brothers across the river, and returned home to forty years of unbroken peace and prosperity.
moral: A sovereign’s greatest victory is won through diplomatic wisdom, empathy, and mutual disarmament. [TE]

title: The Blind Man and the Cripple (తెలుగు)

keywords: the blind man and the cripple
full_text:
In a town at the edge of a great forest lived two men afflicted with misfortune: one was strong of limb and fleet of foot, but completely blind from birth; the other possessed sharp, piercing eyesight and keen intellect, but his legs were withered, and he could not walk a single pace without crutches.

One afternoon, a fierce wildfire swept down from the dry pine hills toward the town. The church bells rang in panic, and the citizens fled in all directions across the river.

The blind man stumbled in terror against walls and trees, unable to find the road to safety; the crippled man sat upon his porch, weeping as he watched the flames advance, unable to carry his body across the fields.

As the smoke grew thick, the crippled man shouted through the haze: 'Ho, strong brother! Come toward the sound of my voice!'

The blind man felt his way to the porch. The crippled man proposed a noble partnership: 'You have sturdy legs to walk, and I have sharp eyes to see! Lift me upon your broad shoulders: I shall be your eyes to guide your steps, and you shall be my feet to carry us through the smoke!'

The blind man lifted the cripple onto his back.

With the cripple directing every turn—'Turn right at the well! Step over the ditch! Straight down the willow path!'—the blind man strode swiftly through the burning smoke, avoiding deep crevices and burning branches, until they crossed the river safely onto the green, unburned meadows!

The surviving citizens cheered their miraculous escape. The two men formed a lifelong partnership, establishing an orchard and living in honored fellowship, proving that our limitations are transformed into triumph when we combine our strengths in cooperative love.
moral: When diverse talents unite in selfless cooperation, no obstacle is insurmountable. [TE]

title: The Foolish Fisherman (తెలుగు)
summary: An impoverished fisherman on the Syrian coast cast his net into the sea and drew up five plump, silver sea-bream, each large enough to fe... [TE]
full_text:
An impoverished fisherman on the Syrian coast cast his net into the sea and drew up five plump, silver sea-bream, each large enough to feed his family for supper. As he went to place them into his woven basket, a passing sailor remarked jokingly: 'Those are pleasant little fish, brother; but out in the deep water swims the Great Golden Whale, whose scales are worth a king’s ransom!'

The foolish fisherman’s eyes burned with sudden, reckless greed. Looking at his five silver bream with contempt, he said: 'What are five small fish to a man destined to catch a golden whale?'

He threw all five bream back into the foaming waves, pushed his small rowing boat out into the turbulent deep waters, and cast his net in search of the legendary golden whale.

For three days and three nights, beneath burning sun and cold spray, he rowed across the ocean swells. He cast his net a hundred times, but caught only slimy seaweed, jellyfish, and broken driftwood. His water skin went dry, his strength failed, and a sudden storm smashed his oars.

He drifted back to the coast half-dead with hunger and thirst, his boat battered and his hands blistered, without a single fish to bring to his starving children.

Sitting upon the cold sand, the fisherman wept in bitter remorse: 'Cursed be the greed that made me despise five honest fish in pursuit of a phantom whale! A crust of bread in the hand is worth all the golden fish in the deep ocean.'
moral: Do not discard certain, modest sustenance in the vain pursuit of an impossible phantom. [TE]

title: The Boy and the Thieves (తెలుగు)
summary: A clever twelve-year-old boy named Ali was walking through an isolated lane on the outskirts of Baghdad, carrying a small clay water jug.... [TE]
full_text:
A clever twelve-year-old boy named Ali was walking through an isolated lane on the outskirts of Baghdad, carrying a small clay water jug. He noticed three notorious thieves lurking in the ruins of an ancient cistern, waiting to rob lone travelers.

Realizing that if he ran, the thieves would pursue and rob him, Ali devised a brilliant ruse. He sat upon the stone lip of the deep well, buried his face in his hands, and began wailing with loud, heartbreaking lamentations!

The three thieves crept out from the shadows, curious and greedy. Their leader asked: 'Why are you weeping so bitterly, boy?'

Ali sniffled and sobbed: 'Alas! My master, the wealthiest jeweler of the bazaar, gave me a magnificent golden goblet studded with emeralds to wash at this spring. As I leaned over, my foot slipped, and the golden goblet tumbled to the bottom of the deep well! If I return without it, my master will have me beaten with forty lashes!'

The thieves’ eyes gleamed with avarice: a golden goblet with emeralds at the bottom of a shallow well!

The three cutpurses immediately stripped off their cloaks, boots, and weapons, leaving them upon the grass, and scrambled down the slippery stones into the dark, muddy water of the well, groping frantically in the muck.

The moment the last thief was at the bottom of the pit, young Ali sprang to his feet!

He gathered all three rich cloaks, their boots, their heavy money belts filled with stolen gold, and ran like a deer to the city gates, delivering the loot directly to the Chief of the Watch!

The guards arrived at the well and hauled the three shivering, muddy thieves up by a rope, throwing them into chains amidst the laughter of all Baghdad, praising the boy who had conquered three cutpurses with nothing but his quick wits.
moral: Quick wit and psychological cunning can outsmart the most hardened cutpurses. [TE]

title: The Man and his Wife (తెలుగు)
summary: In the city of Homs lived an affluent merchant named Tariq and his devoted wife, Maryam. A sudden economic catastrophe struck the region:... [TE]
full_text:
In the city of Homs lived an affluent merchant named Tariq and his devoted wife, Maryam. A sudden economic catastrophe struck the region: a caravan bearing their goods was lost in a desert storm, and a fire consumed their city warehouse, leaving them completely ruined.

Their fine carpets and porcelain were sold to satisfy creditors, leaving them only a tiny mud-brick cottage on the edge of the olive groves.

Tariq sat upon the earthen floor with his head between his knees, groaning in despair: 'We are ruined, Maryam! Our youth is gone, our wealth is dust, and our friends avoid us in the street!'

Maryam smiled with serene tenderness, placed a bowl of warm lentil soup and fresh flatbread before him, and took his hands: 'My dear husband, have our hands lost their strength? Has our health failed? Have our minds lost their understanding? Gold is merely a visitor that comes and goes, but the love that binds two faithful hearts cannot be burned by fire or plundered by sandstorms.'

She brought out her spinning wheel and began to spin fine cotton, while Tariq took heart, rented a modest stall in the vegetable market, and traded with cheerful honesty.

Every evening, they shared their simple bread with laughter, encouraging each other through difficult months.

Within five years, their steady industry, spotless reputation, and cheerful resilience restored their fortunes: Tariq rebuilt his business, while Maryam established a weaving school for orphan girls.

Tariq placed a gold bracelet upon her wrist, saying: 'The fire burned our gold, but it revealed that your courage is a treasure that the world cannot equal.'
moral: Mutual love, patience, and cheerfulness in adversity rebuild what misfortune destroys. [TE]

title: The Merchant and the Robbers (తెలుగు)
summary: An honest spice merchant of Damascus was crossing the Syrian desert alone on his camel, carrying three bags of fragrant saffron and a lea... [TE]
full_text:
An honest spice merchant of Damascus was crossing the Syrian desert alone on his camel, carrying three bags of fragrant saffron and a leather pouch of two hundred gold dinars sewn inside four loaves of dry flatbread.

In a rocky ravine, twelve armed desert brigands rode down from the hills, surrounded his camel with leveled lances, and ordered him to dismount.

The merchant did not tremble or plead for mercy. He dismounted with calm dignity, unrolled his prayer mat upon the sand, and bowed respectfully to the robber chief:

'Welcome, travelers of the desert! The sun is sinking, and it is unseemly that men of the desert should meet without breaking bread. I have traveled far, and my only food is this water and four fresh loaves of bread. Sit with me by the rocks, and let us share my meal before you take my goods.'

The robber chief, surprised by his fearless courtesy, sat cross-legged with his men.

The merchant broke the four loaves of bread to distribute the pieces. As he did so, the seam opened, and the two hundred gold dinars spilled out onto the sand before the eyes of all twelve brigands!

The merchant looked at the gold, and then at the chief with an open smile: 'Take the gold if you will, brothers; it was earned by sweat, but hospitality is sacred. Eat the bread first, for food shared between men is a covenant of peace.'

The robber chief looked at the bread, and then at the merchant’s noble countenance. He was struck with profound shame.

'By heavens!' cried the chief, standing up. 'Shall we rob a man who invites his robbers to break bread, and whose hands are pure as spring water? Keep your gold, merchant, and keep your saffron!'

The twelve brigands not only refused to take a single coin, but escorted the merchant safely across the dangerous desert passes to Damascus, proving that sacred hospitality disarms the fiercest blades.
moral: Generous hospitality and courageous honesty disarm the fiercest outlaws. [TE]

title: The Jackals and the Wolf (తెలుగు)
summary: In a rocky wilderness, a pack of jackals lived peacefully by foraging for wild berries and fallen fruit. A fierce, tyrannical wolf entere... [TE]
full_text:
In a rocky wilderness, a pack of jackals lived peacefully by foraging for wild berries and fallen fruit. A fierce, tyrannical wolf entered their territory, driving them from their dens, snarling with bared fangs, and demanding that the jackals deliver to him a share of whatever game they found, while he lay in the cool shade.

The young jackals were terrified, but an elderly, experienced jackal gathered the pack in secret:

'Brute force cannot defeat the wolf’s jaws; but his greed is a trap that he will walk into with his own feet. Follow my counsel, and we shall liberate our valley without shedding our blood.'

The elder jackal trotted up to the wolf, bowed with obsequious deference, and whispered: 'O mighty sovereign! In the deep pit beneath the rocky ledge, the farmers have left a fat sheep that has fallen into the ravine. It is too heavy for us to lift, and we have guarded it exclusively for your royal appetite!'

The greedy wolf sprang up, saliva dripping from his jowls. Without pausing to examine the ground, he galloped to the ledge and looked down into the deep, sheer pit.

At that moment, the entire pack of jackals, emerging quietly from the rocks behind him, gave a united, sudden push!

title: The Shepherd and the Rogue (తెలుగు)
summary: An affluent landowner in Egypt entrusted a flock of five hundred sheep to an honest young shepherd named Mansur. The landowner praised th... [TE]
full_text:
An affluent landowner in Egypt entrusted a flock of five hundred sheep to an honest young shepherd named Mansur. The landowner praised the shepherd’s integrity so highly at the coffee-houses of Cairo that a cynical sharper wagered fifty gold dinars that he could induce the shepherd to sell him a lamb without his master's knowledge.

The sharper traveled to the pasture, dressed as an affluent traveler, approached Mansur, and pointed to a fat, prime lamb: 'Young shepherd, sell me that lamb for three gold dinars—which is thrice its market value! You can tell your master that a wolf snatched it in the rocky hills; no man will ever know!'

Mansur looked at the gold, and then at the stranger with calm, piercing eyes: 'You say that no man will know. But tell me, traveler: when my master asks where the lamb is, and I say "A wolf took it," where shall my conscience hide? The Creator sees the deed, my soul records the lie, and my honor will be forfeit for three pieces of gold. Take your money away; my master’s trust is not for sale.'

The sharper increased the offer to ten dinars, then twenty, and finally fifty gold dinars!

Mansur raised his shepherd’s crook and said sternly: 'If you offered me fifty thousand dinars, I would not betray the duty placed upon my shoulders! Begone before I summon my sheep-dogs!'

The sharper bowed his head in humble admiration. He returned to Cairo, paid his wager, and testified before all the merchants that in the pastures of Egypt lived a shepherd whose integrity was an unyielding rock against all the gold of the world.
moral: Unshakeable integrity and commitment to duty cannot be seduced by any wager. [TE]

title: The Francolin and the Tortoises (తెలుగు)

full_text:
Beside a marshy lake in the Mesopotamian delta lived a proud francolin—a swift game-bird with mottled brown feathers—and a colony of ancient tortoises who dwelt among the reeds.

Whenever the francolin darted swiftly across the mud, he would mock the slow-moving tortoises: 'Look at you, miserable creatures! You crawl half a pace an hour, carrying an absurd stone shield upon your backs, while I run like the desert wind and fly across the rushes!'

An elderly tortoise looked out from her shell and replied gently: 'Speed is a gift, neighbor; but steady patience and a strong shelter preserve life when the hunter enters the marsh.'

The francolin laughed scornfully and continued his proud displays.

One afternoon, a company of royal fowlers entered the delta with trained hunting falcons, nets, and archery bows.

The tortoises immediately drew their heads, legs, and tails inside their hard, thick shells, resting peacefully upon the muddy bottom of the reeds, resembling smooth river stones. The arrows glanced off their shells harmlessly, and the falcons saw only rocks.

The francolin, by contrast, panicked! He darted back and forth across the mud, fluttered his noisy wings, and took flight into the air, screaming with fear.

The fowlers spotted him immediately, released a swift falcon, and trapped the bird in their nets.

As the captured francolin was carried away in a wicker cage, he looked down at the peaceful tortoises resting safely in the reeds, lamenting: 'Alas! I despised their slow patience, but their modest armor saved them, while my boastful wings became my snare.'
moral: Patience and steady endurance achieve lasting safety, while hasty pride rushes into danger. [TE]

full_text:
In Alexandria lived two neighbors: Abu Kir, a cunning, deceitful dyer who cheated his customers, and Abu Sir, an honest, gentle barber who served the poor with patient skill. Both were reduced to poverty and agreed to travel together to foreign lands, sharing their earnings as brothers.

They sailed to an uncharted island capital where the art of dyeing was unknown—the inhabitants wore only uncolored white wool. Abu Kir opened a dyeing shop, colored cloth with brilliant indigo, saffron, and madder, and was showered with gold by the King. Intoxicated by wealth, he abandoned his sick friend Abu Sir in a wretched caravanserai.

When Abu Sir recovered through his own resilience, he discovered that the city possessed no public bathhouses. Using his skills, Abu Sir constructed the first magnificent hammam in the kingdom, with marble basins, scented vapors, and massage halls.

The King and the entire court visited the bathhouse, rewarding Abu Sir with palaces and honors.

Abu Kir, seeing his former partner’s prosperity, was consumed by toxic envy. He crept to the King, whispering that Abu Sir was a foreign spy who intended to poison the royal bath!

The deceived King condemned Abu Sir to be sewn into a sack and cast into the sea.

However, the honest captain of the execution barge, whose sick son Abu Sir had previously healed with soothing remedies, rescued the barber and substituted an empty sack of stones!

While fishing in the bay, Abu Sir’s net caught a fish containing the King’s lost signet ring!

Abu Sir returned the ring to the monarch, the foul conspiracy was exposed, and Abu Kir fell into the very pit of execution he had dug for his innocent friend. The King made Abu Sir his Grand Vizier, proving that honest virtue outlasts the darkest malice.
moral: Treacherous malice and envy will ultimately destroy the schemer, while gentle virtue is vindicated. [TE]

full_text:
Abdullah was an impoverished fisherman of Alexandria who struggled to support his wife and nine children. One morning, casting his net into the deep surf, he drew up an extraordinary creature: a merman, half human and half fish, with scales of shimmering turquoise!

The merman spoke with human speech: 'Do not slay me, brother! I am Abdullah of the Sea, even as you are Abdullah of the Land. Release me, and let us form a sacred friendship: whenever you cast your net, I shall fill it with rare oceanic pearls and rubies, and in return, you shall bring me the sweet fruits of the land—grapes, pomegranates, and figs—which grow not in the ocean depths.'

Abdullah the Fisherman released him joyfully.

For years, the extraordinary friendship flourished: every week, the fisherman brought baskets of melons, peaches, and dates to the rocky reef, and the merman emerged from the waves, presenting heavy baskets filled with pearls of peerless luster.

Abdullah the Fisherman became the wealthiest man in Egypt, yet remained humble, using his wealth to feed the poor and build schools.

One day, the merman invited Abdullah to visit the undersea cities, rubbing his eyes with magical ointment that allowed him to breathe underwater.

Exploring the palaces of coral and pearl, the fisherman was astonished to see that the mermen used diamonds and rubies merely as common pebbles to pave their garden walks, valuing them as nothing, while cherishing the sweet memory of ripe fruit!

Abdullah returned to land, enlightened by the realization that value is an illusion of scarcity: what one realm despises as common gravel, another worships as treasure, while true wealth is found only in love, friendship, and clean hands.
moral: True friendship respects the different natures of others, recognizing that gold is nothing compared to wisdom. [TE]

Abu Hasan, a noble merchant of Oman, possessed a great fleet of trading ships that sailed the Indian Ocean. A catastrophic series of typhoons sank his vessels, and dishonest agents plundered his warehouses, reducing him from prince-like wealth to absolute poverty.

Refusing to default on his commercial obligations, Abu Hasan sold his palaces, his gardens, and his family heirlooms to pay every single dirham owed to his creditors, departing his native city with clean hands and a clear conscience.

Arriving in Baghdad, he took service as an assistant clerk in the imperial docks.

One evening, Caliph Harun al-Rashid, walking disguised through the harbor, observed Abu Hasan settling an intricate dispute between foreign sea captains with remarkable legal acumen, multilingual fluency, and unshakeable fairness.

The Caliph summoned the clerk to the imperial palace the next morning: 'Who are you, stranger, whose manners belong to a prince though your coat is frayed?'

Abu Hasan recounted the loss of his merchant fleet and his sacrifice to preserve his commercial honor without cheating a single creditor.

Harun al-Rashid stood from his throne, embraced the merchant, and declared before his ministers: 'A man who preserves his integrity when his empire collapses is richer than a king!'

The Caliph restored Abu Hasan’s fleet with twelve newly built merchant vessels from the royal shipyards of Basra, appointed him Admiral of the Commercial Fleets of the Caliphate, and granted him an estate in Baghdad, proving that honor tested by adversity receives the highest crown of restoration.
moral: Patient endurance under misfortune and fidelity to commercial honor receive imperial restoration. [TE]

full_text:
Ibrahim, a handsome and virtuous young gentleman of Cairo, saw an exquisitely painted portrait of Jamilah, daughter of the Grand Vizier of Basra, and his heart was stirred by her noble countenance.

Traveling across the deserts to Basra, he opened an art and book emporium near the city gardens. Jamilah, who was celebrated for her poetic learning, visited the shop to examine illuminated manuscripts.

Instead of declaring his passion with intrusive haste, Ibrahim presented her with an exquisite leather-bound volume of his own poetry, in which he had inscribed verses celebrating the beauty of virtue, the harmony of minds, and the sanctity of honorable companionship.

Jamilah read the poems with enraptured delight, recognizing a soul of equal refinement and moral elevation.

However, her father, intending to form a political alliance, had betrothed her to an arrogant general of the army.

With the assistance of a kind, venerable physician who recognized their pure devotion, Ibrahim and Jamilah presented their petition directly before the Sultan of Basra. Ibrahim recited a defense of sincere affection and family honor with such brilliant eloquence and poetic majesty that the Sultan was moved to tears.

The Sultan annulled the forced betrothal, compensated the general with an honorable military post, and celebrated the marriage of Ibrahim and Jamilah amidst thirty days of public festivities, proving that true eloquence and chivalry conquer the proudest barriers.
moral: Pure love, sustained by artistic eloquence and courteous chivalry, overcomes the widest distances. [TE]

His doors were never locked, and an illuminated lantern burned upon his terrace every night, welcoming travelers, scholars, and pilgrims to enjoy free lodging, savory banquets, and fresh horses without charge.

A political upheaval in Khorasan caused an oppressive governor to confiscate Abu al-Hasan’s estates on false charges, forcing the generous host to flee in disguise to Baghdad.

Penniless and wandering the bustling streets of the capital, Abu al-Hasan stopped before the grand emporium of a wealthy jewel merchant.

The jewel merchant looked out, recognized Abu al-Hasan, and rushed into the street with open arms! 'Welcome, master of Khorasan! Ten years ago, when I was an impoverished student freezing in the snow, your roof sheltered me for two months, and your purse paid for my journey!'

The jeweler brought Abu al-Hasan into his home, clothed him in silk robes, and introduced him to twenty other prominent merchants of Baghdad—all of whom had received his legendary hospitality in past years!

The merchants gathered together, raised thirty thousand gold dinars, and petitioned Caliph Harun al-Rashid.

The Caliph investigated the case, dismissed the corrupt governor of Khorasan, restored all Abu al-Hasan’s palaces and lands, and appointed him Governor of the province, demonstrating that bread cast upon the waters of hospitality returns as a fortress of protection in the hour of need.
moral: Boundless generosity toward travelers creates a network of friendship that shields a man in his hour of trial. [TE]

Kamar al-Zaman, a handsome young gem merchant of Baghdad, was celebrated for his impeccable honesty in evaluating precious stones. His workshop stood adjacent to that of an elderly master jeweler named Ubayd.

During Ubayd’s absence on a purchasing journey to the mines of Golconda, an unscrupulous courtier attempted to extort a valuable diamond necklace from Ubayd’s wife through forged letters and legal intimidation.

Kamar al-Zaman intervened with fearless courage: he examined the forged letters, proved before the city magistrate that the seal was counterfeit, and used his own funds to pay the municipal taxes, guarding his neighbor’s home and honor with the protective care of a brother.

When master Ubayd returned from India and discovered how the young merchant had shielded his household from ruin, he wept with profound gratitude.

His brothers, reckless and envious, squandered their ships and twice returned to him destitute. Twice Abdullah embraced them, opened his coffers, and purchased new ships for them without a word of reproach.

During a trade voyage to the uncharted City of Stone—where an ancient population had been petrified for their idolatry—Abdullah discovered the surviving princess, who had been preserved for her piety. They fell in love and agreed to wed.

Consuming jealousy seized the two brothers: one night on the high seas, they threw Abdullah and his bride into the dark waves and sailed away with the ship!

Abdullah and the maiden were washed ashore on an enchanted island. Through divine providence and his unshakeable faith, Abdullah befriended a gentle sea-spirit who carried them back to Basra.

When Abdullah arrived at his home, he found his two brothers arrested by the city magistrate for piracy and facing the scaffold.

Abdullah ran to the tribunal, threw his arms around his weeping brothers, and pleaded for their lives! He gave them a share of his recovered wealth and forgave them completely before all the people.

Overwhelmed by such saintly, superhuman mercy, the brothers repented with genuine tears, renounced their envy, and lived in peaceful brotherhood for the rest of their days, proving that true love overcomes the darkest malice.
moral: Pious patience and endless forgiveness towards ungrateful kin break the hardest curse of envy. [TE]

In Cairo lived an impoverished, gentle cobbler named Ma'aruf, who was tormented daily by his quarrelsome wife, Fatimah, who demanded dishes of honey pastries which he could not afford. Fleeing her wrath in tears, Ma'aruf took refuge in an ancient ruined mosque and prayed for peace.

A benevolent Ifrit appeared, took pity on the gentle cobbler, lifted him through the air, and set him down outside the distant, magnificent city of Ikhtiyan al-Khatan in China.

There, an old childhood friend advised Ma'aruf to present himself as a wealthy merchant whose colossal caravan had been delayed on the road.

Ma'aruf’s open-handed generosity astonished the city: whenever he borrowed gold, he immediately gave it to the beggars in the street! The King, believing he was the wealthiest merchant on earth, gave him his daughter Princess Dunya in marriage.

When Ma'aruf confessed the truth to Princess Dunya—that he was only a poor cobbler without a single dirham—the noble princess loved him even more for his honesty and pure heart, and helped him escape the wrath of the suspicious vizier.

Fleeing into the desert, Ma'aruf discovered an ancient subterranean vault containing the magical ring of the Jinni Abu al-Sa'adat!

Ma'aruf used the ring not for selfish tyranny, but to summon a colossal, real caravan of a thousand camels laden with gold, silks, and jewels to fulfill his promise to the city!

He distributed the wealth to the poor, overthrew the corrupt vizier, was crowned King, and governed in peace, proving that gentle humility is rewarded by the highest blessings.
moral: Gentle patience in poverty, generosity in abundance, and honest humility triumph over adversity. [TE]

title: Conclusion of Shahrazad and Shahryar (తెలుగు)
summary: When the thousand and first night had drawn to its close, Shahrazad concluded her final tale, fell silent, and bowed her head before King... [TE]
full_text:
When the thousand and first night had drawn to its close, Shahrazad concluded her final tale, fell silent, and bowed her head before King Shahryar.

The king looked upon her with luminous eyes overflowing with tears of deep tenderness, respect, and profound gratitude.

Shahrazad called for her attendants, who brought forth three young princes whom she had borne to the king during those three years of storytelling: the first was walking, the second crawled upon the carpet, and the third was a babe in arms.

Shahrazad wept and said: 'O King of the Age! These are your sons. For a thousand and one nights I have unfolded before you the chronicles of ancient kings, the wonders of the seas, the wit of the humble, and the justice of the wise, seeking only to heal your heart from sorrow. If your soul is still troubled by suspicion, I submit to your royal decree; but if my tales have brought light to your mind, grant me life for the sake of these innocent children!'

King Shahryar sprang from his golden throne, lifted Shahrazad in his arms, and wept with heartfelt joy:

'By the Creator of all the heavens, O Shahrazad! My heart was healed long before these children appeared! Your wisdom, patience, and pure virtue have delivered my soul from the darkness of melancholy and saved the daughters of my empire! You are my Queen, my teacher, and the light of my life forever.'

The king summoned his grand vizier—Shahrazad’s father—and embraced him with royal honors. He sent for his brother Shahzaman, who wed Shahrazad’s sister Dunyazad in a magnificent double celebration.

The city of Baghdad was illuminated for thirty days with lanterns and fountains of rosewater; the prisons were opened, debts were canceled, and granaries distributed to the poor. The scribes transcribed all the thousand and one tales in golden letters, preserving them for all generations as an eternal monument to the triumph of wisdom, love, and narrative truth.
moral: The healing power of wisdom, literature, and patience cures the wounded heart and restores peace to an empire. [TE]

title: The Sleeper and the Waker (తెలుగు)
summary: Abu al-Hasan was a merry bachelor of Baghdad who inherited a modest fortune, dividing his life with eccentric order: he lived frugally by... [TE]
full_text:
Abu al-Hasan was a merry bachelor of Baghdad who inherited a modest fortune, dividing his life with eccentric order: he lived frugally by day, and every evening invited one stranger to dine with him in his garden pavilion, under the rule that they should never meet again.

One evening, his guest was none other than Caliph Harun al-Rashid in merchant disguise!

Over dinner, Abu al-Hasan confessed his whimsical dream: 'If I were Caliph for just one single day, I would dismiss the corrupt magistrate of our quarter, reward the honest baker, and distribute a thousand dinars to the poor!'

The Caliph slipped a harmless sleeping draught into Abu al-Hasan’s cup. When the host fell into a deep slumber, the Caliph had him carried to the imperial palace, dressed in the royal robes, and laid upon the imperial bed.

At dawn, Abu al-Hasan awoke to the sound of silver flutes! Ministers bowed to the carpet, the Grand Vizier Ja'afar knelt for orders, and courtiers addressed him as Commander of the Faithful!

After pinching his ears and marveling at the miracle, Abu al-Hasan acted with admirable wisdom: he held council, dismissed the corrupt magistrate, rewarded the poor baker, and ordered a thousand dinars sent to Abu al-Hasan’s mother!

That evening, another sleeping potion was administered, and he awoke in his own modest bed in patched sheets.

The resulting confusion of identity delighted all Baghdad. Harun al-Rashid revealed the jest, made Abu al-Hasan his permanent companion at court, and gave him an annual pension, proving that a man who uses power for justice—even in a dream—is worthy of real honor.
moral: Royal power is a heavy mantle of responsibility; true happiness is found in good deeds and contentment. [TE]

title: Story of the Larrikin and the Cook (తెలుగు)

full_text:
In the crowded food bazaar of Cairo, a hungry, ragged street youth named Salim spent his days lounging near the cooking stalls, begging for scraps and occasionally snatching a piece of fried pastry when the vendors turned their backs.

One afternoon, Salim approached the grand stall of Master Mahmud, the most celebrated cook in the quarter, famed for his roasted mutton and almond-crusted savory pies. Salim stood staring at the smoking grill with ravenous eyes, his stomach groaning.

Instead of driving the ragged boy away with a stick, Master Mahmud smiled warmly, wiped his hands upon his apron, and called out: 'Step forward, young man! Food is meant for the hungry, not for the display of greed.'

He seated Salim upon a bench, placed before him a steaming platter of spiced roast meat, fluffy saffron rice, and a bowl of chilled mint yogurt.

When Salim had finished every grain, he lowered his head, expecting the cook to demand payment or threaten him with the magistrate.

Master Mahmud placed a gentle hand upon his shoulder: 'Salim, you have sharp eyes and strong hands. Shall you spend your youth begging like a stray dog, or will you learn to build fires, knead dough, and master the spices? An honest trade is an armor that protects a man from hunger and shame forever.'

Tears of gratitude rolled down the boy’s cheeks. He knelt, kissed the master’s apron, and became his apprentice.

For ten years, Salim labored with devoted industry, mastering the craft until he became the chief pastry chef of the Sultan’s palace, never forgetting the generous cook who had offered him an apron instead of a blow.
moral: Kindness and practical mentorship transform an idle youth into an honest master craftsman. [TE]

title: The Caliph Omar Bin Abd al-Aziz and the Poets (తెలుగు)

full_text:
When the saintly Umayyad Caliph Omar bin Abd al-Aziz ascended the throne in Damascus, a delegation of famous court poets arrived from across the empire, expecting to receive rich gifts of gold and estates in exchange for reciting elaborate panegyrics of royal praise.

The poets waited outside the audience hall for three days. Finally, the renowned poet Jarir gained entrance, reciting an eloquent ode praising the new Caliph’s imperial majesty.

Omar bin Abd al-Aziz listened with grave, sorrowful composure. When the verse ended, the Caliph looked at the poet with clear, compassionate eyes:

'Jarir, your verses are beautifully crafted and your meter is flawless. But tell me: from what fund do you expect me to reward you? Shall I take from the bread of the widows of Mesopotamia? Shall I take from the clothing of the orphans of Egypt? Or shall I take from the grain stores of the laborers of Medina? The treasury of the empire belongs to the needy, not to the vanity of the sovereign!'

The poet stood dumbfounded, his heart pierced by the absolute moral integrity of the ruler.

Omar reached into his own personal purse, pulled out fifty silver dirhams of his own private earnings from weaving palm baskets, and placed them in Jarir’s hand: 'This is my own bread, earned by my own labor; take it as a gift from a brother, but do not ask a shepherd to rob his flock to purchase praise.'

Jarir departed with tears in his eyes, proclaiming across all the markets: 'I have met a monarch who fears the heavens more than all the armies of the earth; his justice is the truest poem ever written.'
moral: Public funds belong to the needy; true leaders refuse to spend the people's treasury on flattering verses. [TE]

The night watch of Basra arrested three young men walking through the streets after the strict curfew imposed by the fierce governor Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf. Brought before the governor’s tribunal at dawn, Al-Hajjaj glared at them with fury: 'Who are you, and what gives you the arrogance to defy my curfew? Identify your lineage before the executioner strikes!'

The first youth stepped forward and recited with bold poetic elegance:
'My father is one whose command the people obey,
Before his sharp blade their banners give way;
He holds up the world in the storm and the fight,
And nations submit to his courage and might!'
Al-Hajjaj thought: 'Surely, his father is a mighty general!' and held back his sword.

The second youth declaimed with equal majesty:
'My father is one who turns charcoal to gold,
Whose wisdom and skill through the cities are told;
The mighty bow down as he shapes the hot glow,
And kings seek the treasures his craft can bestow!'
Al-Hajjaj thought: 'His father must be the chief alchemist and jeweler of the realm!'

The third youth spoke with quiet, fearless dignity:
'My father is one whose high deeds are his own,
Who walks without fear and who stands all alone;
I boast of no lineage, I lean on no name,
For virtue and honor are my only claim!'

Al-Hajjaj investigated their parentage: the first youth’s father was a humble village barber; the second youth’s father was a common charcoal-burner; and the third youth was an orphan scholar!

Al-Hajjaj laughed aloud, his wrath completely conquered by their brilliant wit, poetic eloquence, and courageous presence of mind.

He declared: 'Learn from these youths! A man’s true lineage is the sharpness of his mind and the integrity of his character, not the dust of his ancestors!' The governor rewarded each with a hundred dinars and appointed them to the municipal academy.
moral: True nobility is earned through personal virtue, intellect, and courage, not mere ancestral pride. [TE]

Following the tragic fall of the illustrious Barmecide family in Baghdad, when their palaces were sealed and their estates confiscated, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid prohibited any citizen from reciting elegies in praise of their former generosity.

One morning, as the Caliph was walking through the garden quarter, an elderly lady wrapped in a frayed, clean woollen mantle stepped before him. Though dressed in poverty, her bearing was that of a queen, and her eyes shone with unyielding dignity.

She recited aloud in a ringing, melodious voice:
'May heaven grant you, O Caliph, the exact measure of justice that you have meted out to the house of Barmak!'

Harun al-Rashid frowned, his hand resting upon his scimitar: 'Do you pray for me, woman, or do you curse me?'

The lady replied with fearless composure: 'I prayed that justice may be your reward, O Commander of the Faithful. If you dealt with them in truth and equity, my prayer is a blessing; but if you broke the vessels of generosity, exiled your truest friends, and left their widows to beg for bread, then my prayer is the judgment of history upon your throne.'

The words struck the Caliph like an iron mace! He recognized her: she was the noble widow of Yahya bin Khalid.

Tears of profound remorse welled in Harun al-Rashid’s eyes. He bowed before her, ordered an annual pension of ten thousand dinars to be settled upon her household, and restored her ancestral home, having learned that true nobility speaks truth to power without fear of death.
moral: Poetic eloquence and moral dignity disarm the wrath of monarchs, commanding respect and justice. [TE]

full_text:
In the ancient kingdom of Sistan reigned King Azadbakht, a monarch of great renown who was blessed with ten ministers of state, each presiding over a department of government. When a mysterious, brilliant young traveler named Bakhtiyar arrived at court, displaying peerless wisdom in statecraft, the king appointed him Chief Counselor.

The Ten Wazirs, consumed by jealousy at being eclipsed by a newcomer, conspired to bring about Bakhtiyar’s downfall.

They whispered false accusations of treason into the king’s ear, demanding that Bakhtiyar be led to the scaffold.

King Azadbakht, remembering that hasty anger is the ruin of monarchs, resolved to test both the accusers and the accused through ten days of public philosophical inquiry.

Each day, one of the Ten Wazirs stepped forward to argue for immediate execution, presenting a parable on the necessity of stern punishment. In reply, Bakhtiyar took the floor, presenting an answer of sublime moral elevation, illustrating his defense with histories of patience, providence, clemency, and justice.

For ten days, the court was transformed into a grand academy of statecraft, where the principles of governance, the nature of human character, and the duties of kings were analyzed with classical brilliance.

On the tenth day, Bakhtiyar produced documented proof that unmasked the conspiracy of the Ten Wazirs!

King Azadbakht embraced Bakhtiyar as his worthy son, dismissed the envious ministers, and appointed Bakhtiyar sovereign of his realm, proving that wisdom and patience triumph over the darkest intrigues.
moral: A wise monarch tests the counsel of his advisers with philosophical inquiry, refusing to act on hasty impulse. [TE]

Before the tribunal of King Azadbakht, the First Wazir presented an argument on the stubborn nature of misfortune: 'Sire, when destiny decrees that a man shall experience adversity, all his clever schemes become nets to trap his feet; he who struggles against the current with frantic pride only drowns.'

Bakhtiyar stood before the throne, bowed with courtly respect, and answered with philosophical clarity:

'It is true, O King, that when the storm rages, human schemes are like leaves before the gale. But adversity is not an eternal decree; it is a season of testing designed to burn away the dross of arrogance and forge the pure gold of character.

He who surrenders to despair when misfortune strikes is like a sailor who throws away his rudder because the waves are high. The wise man does not curse the tempest; he trims his sails, anchors his soul in patient endurance, and continues his honest labor.

For every midnight has its appointed dawn, and every winter dissolves into the blossoms of spring. He who preserves his integrity through the darkest hour will find that fortune returns to crown his steadfastness with double glory, even as the history of the Merchant Who Lost His Luck demonstrates before all men.'
moral: When adversity blows like a tempest, patient endurance and honest labor outlast the storm. [TE]

To illustrate his defense, Bakhtiyar recounted the history of an affluent merchant of Shiraz named Abu al-Majd:

'Abu al-Majd had inherited a great fleet of trading ships, but within three years, misfortune struck his household with unceasing blows: three of his vessels were sunk by typhoons, his warehouses in Basra burned to the ground, and dishonest foreign agents absconded with his ledgers. He was reduced to absolute poverty, having to sell his furniture to purchase barley bread.

His companions mocked him, saying: "Your luck has died, Abu al-Majd; sit in the dust and beg!"

Abu al-Majd shook his head: "My gold has departed, but my hands can labor, my mind can calculate, and my honor is unbroken."

He took a job as a simple porter in the vegetable bazaar, carrying heavy baskets of onions and turnips for two copper coins a day. He performed his labor with such cheerful dignity, measuring his steps with care and never complaining, that the vegetable vendors entrusted him with the management of their collective scales.

Observing that much fresh produce spoiled during the summer heat, Abu al-Majd designed underground ventilated cooling chambers packed with mountain snow.

The merchants adopted his invention, and within five years, Abu al-Majd had revolutionized the storage of food across Shiraz!

The King of Persia appointed him Grand Controller of the Granaries, and his fortunes were restored threefold. He sat once more in his ancestral gardens, proving that misfortune is merely a shadow that vanishes before the steady light of honest labor.'
moral: Resilient labor and unyielding honesty turn repeated disasters into enduring prosperity. [TE]

title: Of Looking To the Ends of Affairs (తెలుగు)
summary: On the second day, the Second Wazir argued before King Azadbakht on the necessity of calculating the distant consequences of every deed: ... [TE]
keywords: of looking to the ends of affairs

On the second day, the Second Wazir argued before King Azadbakht on the necessity of calculating the distant consequences of every deed: 'Sire, he who looks only at the immediate profit before his feet is like a child who reaches for a ripe fig, unmindful that a viper sleeps upon the branch.'

Bakhtiyar smiled in agreement, elaborating upon the principle of foresight:

'Your minister speaks a pearl of wisdom, O King! True intelligence is not measured by the cleverness with which one acts in the moment, but by the clarity with which one anticipates the end of affairs.

A deed begun in passionate haste without calculating its conclusion is like an arrow shot into the fog: it may strike an innocent friend or shatter upon stone.

The wise statesman plants seeds today whose fruit he may never eat, and avoids taking a path whose exit he has not examined. He weighs every decree upon the balance of time: "What will this word bring tomorrow? What will it bring in seven years? And how will history record it when our bones are dust?"

He who cultivates foresight builds stone aqueducts that endure for centuries, while the impulsive ruler builds houses of straw that collapse with the first autumn wind, as the chronicle of the Merchant and His Sons illustrates for all who have ears to hear.'
moral: Prudent foresight that considers the long-term consequences of actions protects a household from sudden ruin. [TE]

title: Tale of the Merchant and His Sons (తెలుగు)
summary: Bakhtiyar recounted the story of an affluent merchant of Isfahan who had three sons: [TE]
keywords: tale of the merchant and his sons
full_text:
Bakhtiyar recounted the story of an affluent merchant of Isfahan who had three sons:

'Feeling his strength failing, the merchant called his three sons to his bedchamber, divided his fortune into three equal parts of ten thousand dinars, and said: "Go forth into the world, and in three years, return to show me how you have employed your inheritance."

The eldest son went to the capital, bought a magnificent palace, filled it with sixty servants, and gave sumptuous banquets every evening, boasting: "I am enjoying the fruits of my father’s labor!" Within two years, his gold was spent, his flattering friends vanished, and he was reduced to begging in rags.

The second son, fearing to lose his gold, dug a deep pit beneath his cellar floor, buried his ten thousand dinars, and sat above it with a cudgel, starving himself on stale crusts in perpetual anxiety. His gold neither grew nor fed a hungry soul.

The youngest son, Farhad, took his portion and invested it in knowledge and production: he purchased barren hillside land, dug irrigation canals from the mountain river, planted ten thousand olive trees and almond saplings, and established an agricultural craft school for poor youths of the district.

At the end of three years, the three sons returned to their father.

The eldest stood in rags; the second produced his rusted, useless gold; but Farhad led his father to the mountain slope, showing him thriving green orchards laden with fruit, water flowing in clean canals, and a hundred young artisans singing at their work!

The father embraced Farhad with tears of joy, saying: "You alone understood the true end of affairs! Gold buried in stone is dead, and gold spent on vanity is poison; but wealth invested in knowledge, labor, and the welfare of others lives forever."'
moral: True wealth is not gold to be spent, but knowledge and productive skills that sustain future generations. [TE]

title: Of the Advantages of Patience (తెలుగు)
summary: On the third day, the Third Wazir argued that persistent patience is often mistaken for weakness: 'Sire, he who waits too long allows his... [TE]
full_text:
On the third day, the Third Wazir argued that persistent patience is often mistaken for weakness: 'Sire, he who waits too long allows his enemies to build fortresses around him; action must be swift and uncompromising!'

Bakhtiyar stepped forward and delivered his counter-discourse on the majesty of patience:

'O King, let not the hasty confuse patience with sluggish weakness! Impatience is the fire of the straw, which blazes furiously for a second and leaves only cold black ash; but patience is the deep, steady heat of the furnace that tempers the finest Damascus steel.

Patience is the virtue by which the tiny acorn becomes the mighty oak that defies the storms of a century; it is the quality by which the silkworm weaves its cocoon, and the diamond crystal is forged in the darkness of the earth.

He who possesses patience can smile at insults, knowing that truth requires no loud shout to defend itself; he can endure the winter of misfortune, knowing that spring is already walking across the hills.

The impatient man breaks his bow by bending it with violent haste; but the patient archer waits until the breath is still and the aim is true, hitting the mark of honor, even as the history of Abu Sabir demonstrates across all generations.'
moral: Patience under trial is an unshakeable shield; it disarms wrath and turns the bitterest cup into sweet nectar. [TE]

title: Story of Abu Sabir (తెలుగు)
summary: Bakhtiyar related the celebrated saga of Abu Sabir: [TE]
full_text:
Bakhtiyar related the celebrated saga of Abu Sabir:

'In a border village of Persia lived an honest farmer named Abu Sabir—whose name meant "Father of Patience." A tyrannical local governor plundered his cattle, burned his farmhouse, and drove him with his wife and children into exile. While his companions urged him to rebel or curse his fate, Abu Sabir replied calmly: "Patience is the key to deliverance; the wheel of time turns, and truth shall prevail."

In a foreign city, he took service as a laborer in a royal quarry. When an unjust overseer struck him falsely, Abu Sabir did not retaliate, but worked with quiet diligence, winning the love of all the workers.

A sudden revolution broke out in the capital: the old tyrannical dynasty collapsed, and the citizens, seeking a ruler whose character was untainted by cruelty, greed, or factional hatred, looked for the most just man in the realm.

The quarrymen, the merchants, and the elders came forward unanimously, pointing to Abu Sabir: "Here is a man who suffered every injustice without losing his gentleness, and who possesses the patience to govern an empire!"

Abu Sabir was crowned King amidst the cheers of the nation.

When the former oppressive governor was captured and brought before his throne in chains, expecting execution, King Abu Sabir descended from his dais, struck off his chains, and said:

"I conquered your oppression through thirty years of patient virtue; shall I now imitate your cruelty? Go in peace, and learn that patience is a stronger fortress than all your iron spears."'
moral: Unshakeable patience and refusal to seek vengeance transform a persecuted exile into a beloved king. [TE]

title: Of the Ill Effects of Impatience (తెలుగు)

On the fourth day, the Fourth Wazir addressed King Azadbakht on the dangers of hasty execution. Bakhtiyar stood before the throne and deepened the counsel:

'Sire, impatience is a fever of the blood that makes a man leap into the well to escape the rain. It is born of childish pride that demands the harvest before the seed has taken root in the soil.

The impatient general attacks before his scouts have returned, and leads his army into a mountain ambush; the impatient merchant sells his cargo before the market opens, and forfeits his profit; the impatient judge strikes with the sword before hearing the witness, and sheds innocent blood.

How many friendships of thirty years have been shattered in thirty seconds by an impatient tongue? And how many kingdoms have been overthrown because a monarch could not wait until tomorrow to verify a rumor?

He who masters his temper masters his kingdom; but he who is mastered by impatience is a slave to every passing breeze, as the history of Prince Bihzad illustrates with tragic clarity.'
moral: Hasty impatience blinds reason, breaks alliances, and plunges the rash into sudden destruction. [TE]

title: Story of Prince Bihzad (తెలుగు)
summary: Bakhtiyar recounted the history of Prince Bihzad of Azerbaijan: [TE]
full_text:
Bakhtiyar recounted the history of Prince Bihzad of Azerbaijan:

'Prince Bihzad was a youth of fiery valor, peerless skill with the scimitar, and boundless impatience. When an invading army of nomads crossed the northern frontier, the venerable commander of the royal forces counseled: "Prince, the nomads are swift in the open plain, but their supplies are meager; let us hold the mountain passes for seven days, and hunger will force them to retreat without a battle."

Bihzad scoffed at the veteran’s advice: "Shall we cower behind rocks like frightened foxes? A true champion charges the enemy without waiting for the sun to rise!"

Deaf to all counsel, Bihzad sounded the charge, galloped into the narrow defile at the head of five thousand horsemen, and fell squarely into a disguised pit-trap prepared by the invaders!

His army was scattered, four thousand brave soldiers fell in the ambush, and Bihzad was dragged from his horse, wounded and captured.

For three years, the proud prince labored as a captive in the northern steppes, herding shaggy horses in the snow, reflecting every bitter day upon his reckless impatience that had destroyed five thousand innocent companions.

When he was finally ransomed by his father, Bihzad was a transformed man: his fiery pride had been burned away, replaced by profound humility, strategic patience, and reverence for wise counsel.

When he ascended the throne, he never issued a military order without consulting his council of elders, ruling in peace for forty years as one of the wisest monarchs of the Caucasus.'
moral: Youthful impatience that ignores experienced counsel leads to defeat; humility rebuilds the kingdom. [TE]

'Sire, the universe is governed by an unbending law of moral balance that no emperor can decree away. As a man sows, so shall he reap: he who plants sweet pomegranate seeds will gather sweet fruit, and he who scatters thorns will harvest only briars that tear his own flesh.

An evil deed may seem to triumph for an hour, cloaked in gold and protected by armies; but its root is rotten, and it carries the seed of its own downfall within its chest. Injustice creates an army of invisible adversaries in the hearts of the oppressed.

A good deed, by contrast, even if performed in secret by a humble water-carrier, radiates like a candle in the dark. It wins the allegiance of souls, disarms malice, and calls down the blessings of the heavens.

The tyrant imagines that his sword makes him safe, but history records that the throne built on cruelty collapses into dust, while the king who rules with justice and mercy lives forever in the grateful memory of his people, as shown in the chronicle of King Dadbin.'
moral: Every deed bears fruit according to its seed; benevolence returns as a blessing, and malice as ruin. [TE]

title: Story of King Dadbin and His Wazirs (తెలుగు)
summary: Bakhtiyar related the story of King Dadbin of ancient Persia: [TE]
keywords: story of king dadbin and his wazirs
full_text:
Bakhtiyar related the story of King Dadbin of ancient Persia:

'King Dadbin had two ministers: the first was Kardan, an unprincipled courtier who used his office to amass gold, sell justice to the wealthy, and flatter the king’s vanity; the second was Rast-Rushan, an upright statesman whose name meant "Righteous Light," who spent his energy building public granaries, protecting the peasantry, and refusing all bribes.

Kardan, envious of Rast-Rushan’s spotless reputation, forged letters to convince the king that Rast-Rushan was secretly plotting with foreign enemies.

King Dadbin, desiring to discover the truth himself, donned the disguise of a common dervish and spent a month wandering through the provinces of his empire.

Wherever he went, the farmers, merchants, and scholars cursed the name of Kardan, recounting his extortions and cruelties; while everywhere, the people blessed Rast-Rushan with tears of gratitude, showing the schools, irrigation canals, and fair markets he had established!

The king returned to his capital, cast off his disguise, and held a public tribunal.

He confronted Kardan with the evidence of his extortions, stripped him of his robes, and banished him to the salt mines; while Rast-Rushan was appointed Grand Vizier with supreme authority over the empire.

King Dadbin proclaimed: "The flatterer brought me letters of false praise, but the people’s bread testified to the truth! Righteousness is the only foundation that sustains the state."'
moral: Integrity that serves the public good outlasts the deceitful conspiracies of corrupt ministers. [TE]

'O King! Human intellect and honest endeavor are necessary duties; we must till the soil, build the ship, and steer with the oar. But he who relies entirely upon his own frail cunning, imagining that his intellect alone commands the universe, is like an ant that thinks it moves the mountain!

True trust in providence is not passive sloth; it is the courage to do what is right, just, and honorable, and then leave the outcome peacefully in the hands of the Creator of all things.

When the storm is fierce and all earthly instruments fail, the soul that trusts in providence remains serene, knowing that behind the darkest cloud shines the sun of divine wisdom.

This unshakeable trust removes fear from the heart, delivers a man from the temptation to compromise his honor for temporary gain, and opens doors of deliverance where human eyes see only sheer stone walls, as the chronicle of King Bakhtzaman illustrates.'
moral: Trust in divine guidance provides peace of soul and delivers the righteous in the hour of trial. [TE]

summary: Bakhtiyar recounted the history of King Bakhtzaman of Yemen: [TE]
full_text:
Bakhtiyar recounted the history of King Bakhtzaman of Yemen:

'A military rebellion led by an ambitious general overthrew King Bakhtzaman, driving the righteous monarch into the desert with his queen and young infant. Wandering across trackless dunes, the king lost his camel, his water, and was captured by desert brigands who separated him from his family.

In his darkest hour, chained in a foreign port, Bakhtzaman did not curse heaven or surrender to despair. He said: "The heavens that gave me a crown can take it away, and the providence that sustains the sparrow in the storm can restore the wanderer. I place my soul in the hands of the Merciful."

He worked as an honest porter in the docks for seven years, conducting himself with such integrity that the city merchants appointed him guardian of the harbor storehouses.

When the tyrannical usurper in Yemen died, leaving the kingdom in civil strife, the people rose in revolt, demanding the return of their beloved King Bakhtzaman.

Envoys were dispatched to search the ports of the East. They discovered their former monarch working in the harbor, his hands calloused by labor and his spirit purified by faith!

Bakhtzaman was escorted back to Yemen, joyfully reunited with his queen and son who had been preserved in safety, and restored to his throne amidst national celebrations, proving that trust in providence outlasts the darkest exile.'
moral: Unwavering faith and adherence to justice restore the rightful ruler to his throne. [TE]

'Sire! Any barbarian can draw a sword and take the life of a fallen enemy; brute force requires neither wisdom nor greatness of soul. But to stay the hand when the sword is raised, to forgive when you have the absolute power to destroy, is the divine attribute of true kingship!

Vengeance only perpetuates the cycle of bitterness: the son of the slain man will harbor hatred, and his grandson will sharpen a dagger. Blood cannot wash away blood; only the sweet water of mercy cleanses the stain of enmity.

Clemency turns an enemy into a devoted defender, softens the hardest heart, and wins a victory that steel can never achieve.

The conqueror who slays his captives rules over corpses and slaves; but the monarch who pardons with magnanimity rules over the grateful hearts of free men, as shown in the history of King Bihkard.'
moral: Pardoning an adversary when you have the power to destroy him is the highest victory of a monarch. [TE]

title: Story of King Bihkard (తెలుగు)
summary: Bakhtiyar related the story of King Bihkard of ancient Persia: [TE]
full_text:
Bakhtiyar related the story of King Bihkard of ancient Persia:

'King Bihkard defeated a formidable rebel chieftain named Ardashir, who had led an insurrection in the northern mountains for ten years. Captured in the final battle, Ardashir was brought into the royal palace in chains, bruised, defiant, and expecting the scaffold.

The king’s viziers shouted unanimously: "Off with his head! Strike him down, sire, as a warning to all rebels!"

King Bihkard looked upon the captive chieftain, stepped down from his golden throne, and with his own hands struck the iron chains from Ardashir’s wrists!

The king said with noble serenity: "Ardashir, you are a valiant warrior of ancient blood. We fought for ten years because we misunderstood each other’s hearts. Today, victory is mine; and my victory is to grant you life, honor, and complete pardon. Return to your mountains in peace, or remain as my brother."

Ardashir stood dumbfounded, tears streaming down his scarred cheeks. He fell at the king’s feet, kissed his sandals, and wept:

"O King! For ten years I hated your crown, but today your clemency has conquered my soul! By the heavens, the blade that sought your throne shall henceforth be your truest shield."

Ardashir became King Bihkard’s most faithful general, defending the frontiers of the empire against all invaders for thirty years, proving that mercy builds fortresses that no army can overthrow.'
moral: Magnanimous clemency transforms a mortal enemy into the most faithful defender of the realm. [TE]

title: Story of Aylan Shah and Abu Tammam (తెలుగు)
summary: Bakhtiyar recounted the story of King Aylan Shah of Khwarazm: [TE]
keywords: story of aylan shah and abu tammam
full_text:
Bakhtiyar recounted the story of King Aylan Shah of Khwarazm:

'King Aylan Shah had a wise and virtuous counselor named Abu Tammam, whose learning, honesty, and charity won the love of the entire nation. A jealous courtier named Qasim, burning with envy at Abu Tammam’s favor, resolved to destroy him.

Qasim approached the king and whispered falsely: "Sire, Abu Tammam boasts in private that your breath is foul and offensive; observe tomorrow when he approaches your throne: he will cover his mouth with his sleeve!"

Qasim then invited Abu Tammam to his home for dinner and served him a dish heavily seasoned with raw garlic.

The next morning, when Abu Tammam approached the throne to deliver state papers, he discreetly placed his sleeve before his mouth so that the smell of garlic would not offend the monarch.

The king, believing the slanderer’s accusation, wrote a royal order to the captain of the city fortress: "Strike off the head of the bearer of this letter immediately!" The king handed the sealed parchment to Abu Tammam, saying: "Deliver this to the captain."

title: Story of King Ibrahim and His Son (తెలుగు)
summary: Bakhtiyar related the story of King Ibrahim of Balkh: [TE]

full_text:
Bakhtiyar related the story of King Ibrahim of Balkh:

'King Ibrahim had an only son, Prince Ismail, whom he wished to train in the highest virtues of statecraft. When the prince reached eighteen years of age, the king sent him disguised as a common student to live in the provincial cities for two years.

Prince Ismail lived in student hostels, ate barley bread with poor weavers, helped farmers harvest wheat, and sat among the litigating peasants in the courts of justice.

He saw how corrupt magistrates favored the wealthy, how oppressive tax-collectors seized the milk-goats of widows, and how the honest poor suffered in silence.

When he returned to the palace, his father seated him upon the throne and asked: "What did you learn of your royal destiny, my son?"

Prince Ismail answered with tears in his eyes: "Father, I learned that a king is not a master to be served, but the chief servant of the realm! His palace exists to shelter the helpless, his army to defend the peaceful, and his treasury to feed the hungry. If a single orphan cries in the night from injustice, the king’s crown is stained with blood."

King Ibrahim embraced his son, weeping with joyful pride, and crowned him king before the assembled nation, and Prince Ismail governed for fifty years as the most beloved monarch of the East.'
moral: A prince’s true destiny is to serve his people with justice, empathy, and humble dedication. [TE]

title: Of the Appointed Term (తెలుగు)

full_text:
On the tenth and final day, the Tenth Wazir demanded that the execution proceed without delay. Bakhtiyar stepped forward and delivered his final, crowning discourse before King Azadbakht:

'O King! Every mortal creature has an appointed term upon this earth. The mightiest conqueror whose armies shook the continents, and the humble beggar who slept upon the doorstep, both step down into the same narrow earthen bed.

Neither gold, nor ivory palaces, nor armies of iron can delay the hour by a single heartbeat.

What then remains of a king when his body is laid beneath the marble?

His gold is plundered by strangers, his palaces crumble into dust, and his armies are scattered by time. Only one treasure outlasts the grave: the memory of the tears he wiped away, the justice he established, the schools he built, and the mercy he showed to the weak!

He who lives for his own selfish vanity dies completely; but he who lives for the welfare of his fellow men achieves an immortality that shines brighter than the stars, as the chronicle of King Sulayman Shah demonstrates.'
moral: Earthly life is a passing journey; only the enduring memory of justice and charity outlives the grave. [TE]

'King Sulayman Shah was on the brink of waging a devastating war against the King of Khorasan over a disputed border province. His generals urged immediate invasion, sharpening their swords and mobilizing sixty thousand horsemen.

The king’s niece, Princess Shahzanan, an educated statesman who had mastered jurisprudence, philosophy, and history, stepped boldly into the royal council.

She presented an economic and diplomatic audit demonstrating that the war would cost twenty times the value of the disputed province, exhaust the treasury, and invite barbarian invasions from the north.

With her uncle’s permission, Shahzanan rode as the imperial ambassador to the court of the King of Khorasan.

Before the foreign monarch, she delivered an oration of sublime diplomatic eloquence, presenting a compromise: the disputed province was established as a shared commercial emporium, with a joint court of arbitration to govern fair trade.

The King of Khorasan was so impressed by her brilliant intellect, dignity, and statesmanship that he ratified the treaty on the spot, celebrating thirty years of peace.

King Sulayman Shah proclaimed before his council: "A wise woman’s word has saved sixty thousand lives and preserved two empires from ruin!"'
moral: Feminine wisdom, diplomatic skill, and moral courage save an entire nation from catastrophic war. [TE]

The treasurer sat in the darkness, praying with calm serenity: "O Creator, You know that my hands are clean; into Your care I commit my breath."

That very night, an earthquake shook the citadel! A heavy stone fell from the dungeon ceiling, striking the iron chains and shattering the master link, freeing the prisoner’s hands!

At that same hour, the chief conspirator, stricken with terror by the earthquake, believed that celestial judgment had arrived. He ran into the palace square, confessed his forgery before the king, and produced the stolen gold!

The king rushed to the dungeon with torches, embraced the innocent treasurer, and appointed him Grand Vizier of the empire!'

Knowing the legendary chivalry of the Barmecide family, Abd al-Malik visited Ja'afar the Barmecide late at night, recounting his unjust humiliation.

Ja'afar spoke with magnificent eloquence on Abd al-Malik’s forty years of unblemished service, his honesty in managing the Nile granaries, and the malice of the slanderers who had engineered his fall.

Harun al-Rashid, enlightened by his vizier's courageous defense of an innocent elder, ordered the full restitution of Abd al-Malik’s estates, granted him an imperial pension, and appointed him Counselor of the realm.

Abd al-Malik embraced Ja'afar with tears of gratitude, saying: 'You did not merely save my livelihood, O Barmecide; you restored my honor, which is dearer to me than life itself.'

title: Al-Rashid and the Barmecides (తెలుగు)
summary: Following the downfall of the Barmecide viziers in Baghdad, Caliph Harun al-Rashid rode through the provinces of Iraq, accompanied by his... [TE]
full_text:
Following the downfall of the Barmecide viziers in Baghdad, Caliph Harun al-Rashid rode through the provinces of Iraq, accompanied by his courtiers.

Passing through the agricultural district of Nahrawan, the Caliph stopped to admire a colossal stone bridge spanning the river, surrounded by clean irrigation canals and thriving date orchards.

The Caliph asked an elderly farmer: 'Who constructed this magnificent bridge and these canals that bring such fertility to your fields?'

The old farmer lifted his hands with tears of gratitude: 'May heaven shower blessings upon the noble house of Barmak! It was Yahya and his sons Ja'afar and Al-Fadl who built this bridge, dug these canals, and distributed seeds to the poor without demanding taxes.'

A courtier frowned and whispered sternly: 'Old man, do you not know that the Caliph has forbidden the praise of the Barmecides?'

The old farmer looked at the courtier with fearless dignity: 'You can forbid the tongues of flatterers in the palace, but can you forbid the river to flow beneath this bridge? Can you forbid the date palms to yield their sweet fruit? Every drop of water that irrigates these fields is a tongue that praises their generosity!'

Harun al-Rashid covered his eyes, wept with deep remorse, and said to his escort: 'Leave the old man in peace. He speaks truth. We had the power to destroy their palaces, but their good deeds have built a monument in the hearts of the people that will outlive our dynasty.'
moral: True statesmen who serve with benevolence leave a fragrance that royal edicts cannot erase. [TE]
