full_text:
Prince Khudadad of Harran was a youth of peerless martial prowess, raised in seclusion by his noble mother. Arriving at his father the King’s court, his forty-nine half-brothers grew envious of his valor and departed on a reckless adventure into the mountains, where they were all captured and imprisoned in the Black Castle of an immense, cannibalistic giant.

Khudadad tracked them to the mountains, challenged the giant to single combat, and through agile horsemanship and heroic valor, slew the monster, breaking the chains of his forty-nine brothers and liberating the captive Princess of Daryabar!

Instead of thanking him, consuming envy seized the brothers: while Khudadad slept by a stream, they stabbed him and left him for dead, carrying the princess back to court, claiming they had slain the giant themselves!

Recovering from his wounds through the nursing of a friendly hermit, Khudadad returned to Harran just as an invading army of nomads besieged the capital.

Khudadad charged into the fray, routed the enemy, and saved his father’s crown!

Revealing his identity, Khudadad forgave his treacherous brothers before the full council, pleading for their pardon. The King embraced Khudadad, crowned him heir to the throne, and celebrated his union with the heroic Princess of Daryabar.
moral: Chivalric valor, filial loyalty, and boundless fraternal forgiveness conquer the fiercest monsters. [TE]

full_text:
The Princess of Daryabar recounted her extraordinary life before the court of Harran:

'I was the daughter of the King of the Isle of Daryabar. A military rebellion overthrew my father’s throne, and I escaped aboard a merchant vessel. A violent storm wrecked the ship, and I was washed ashore on a desolate rocky coast.

Surviving alone on wild shellfish and spring water, I was captured by a band of desert corsairs. Rather than weeping or surrendering to despair, I maintained my regal dignity, learned their language, and seized an opportunity to escape during a night thunderstorm.

Wandering into the mountains, I fell into the hands of the monstrous giant of the Black Castle, where I was imprisoned alongside forty-nine foreign princes, facing daily peril.

Yet my spirit remained unbroken; I encouraged the weeping prisoners with hope and faith until Prince Khudadad arrived like an angel of valor, slew the giant, and shattered our iron gates!

In Khudadad, I recognized not only an invincible warrior, but a soul of supreme mercy, chivalry, and forgiveness.'

The Princess of Daryabar ruled beside Khudadad, celebrated as a queen whose courage and resilience had matched the greatest heroes of the East.
moral: Courage, independence, and resilience sustain a noble soul through shipwreck and adversity. [TE]

title: The Caliph's Night Adventure (తెలుగు)
summary: Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his golden diwan beside Vizier Ja'afar the Barmecide. The night was sultry, and sleep had fled from the mon... [TE]
full_text:
Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his golden diwan beside Vizier Ja'afar the Barmecide. The night was sultry, and sleep had fled from the monarch's eyes.

'O Ja'afar,' said the Caliph, 'my heart feels heavy within my breast, and no music or council eases my spirit. Let us disguise ourselves in the rough woolen robes of foreign merchants from Mosul. We shall wander through the moonlit alleys of Baghdad, inspect the bridges across the Tigris, and observe how our subjects fare when they believe no sovereign watches them.'

Ja'afar bowed low and summoned Masrur, the sword-bearer, who joined them disguised as a caravan servant. Slipping through a private postern gate in the palace gardens, the trio emerged into the bustling night quarter near the Great Mosque.

Baghdad hummed with life: bakers drew fragrant sesame loaves from glowing ovens, storytellers enchanted gatherings around copper tea urns, and night watchmen tapped their oak staves upon cobblestones.

As they reached the Bridge of Boats spanning the calm Tigris, the Caliph stopped. In the center of the bridge stood a blind mendicant who, whenever a passerby placed a copper coin in his hand, would grasp the giver's wrist and plead:
'I pray thee, good benefactor, give me also a gentle buffet on the cheek, or I cannot accept thy charity!'

Harun al-Rashid was astonished. 'By Allah,' whispered the Caliph, 'here is a riddle that demands understanding. A beggar who demands a blow alongside an alms must bear a strange secret.'

Further on, at an inn courtyard, they beheld an elegant young rider who fiercely scolded his spirited mare yet wept as he groomed her with tender affection. In another quarter, they saw an opulent mansion belonging to a rope-maker whose doorway bore inscriptions of praise to providence.

Returning to the palace at dawn, the Caliph commanded:
'Ja'afar, bring before me tomorrow the blind beggar of the bridge, the tearful horseman, and the wealthy rope-maker. For tonight's wanderings have shown us that beneath every strange habit lies a tale of divine chastisement, repentant virtue, or sudden fortune.'

Thus began the renowned cycle of the Caliph's Night Inquiries, where justice was delivered not through cold decrees, but through the patient understanding of human hearts.
moral: A ruler who walks among his citizens without pomp discovers both the hidden wisdom and quiet sorrows of his people. [TE]

title: The Story of the Blind Man Baba Abdullah (తెలుగు)
summary: The blind beggar of the bridge was brought before Caliph Harun al-Rashid, kneeling humbly upon the carpet of audience. [TE]
keywords: the story of the blind man baba abdullah
full_text:
The blind beggar of the bridge was brought before Caliph Harun al-Rashid, kneeling humbly upon the carpet of audience.

'O Commander of the Faithful,' Baba Abdullah began, 'my sightlessness was not born of disease, but carved out by the poisonous thorn of boundless greed.

In my youth, I was an enterprising camel merchant, owning eighty sturdy beasts. One day, returning from Basra with empty pack-saddles, I encountered an ascetic dervish resting near an oasis. In conversation, he told me of a hidden valley among the desolate mountains containing treasure beyond the dreams of kings. He offered to lead me there on condition that we split the gold evenly, forty camel-loads for him and forty for me.

I gladly swore solemn oaths. We rode into a narrow canyon where the dervish kindled a fragrant fire and threw herbs into the smoke. The earth cleft asunder, revealing a subterranean vault filled with gold chalices, pearls, and diamonds.

We loaded all eighty camels until they knelt under the glorious weight. As we parted at the crossroads, jealousy ignited within my soul. I thought: "He is a monk with no family; what need has he of forty camels?" I rode after him, pleading that handling forty beasts would distract his devotions. He smilingly surrendered ten, then twenty, until at last, through shameless badgering, I coaxed all eighty back into my possession!

Still unsatisfied, I noticed a tiny golden box in his sash. "What is that?" I asked.
"It holds a magical salve," replied the dervish. "If anointed upon the left eye, it reveals all hidden treasures buried in the earth. But beware: if applied to the right eye, blindness follows instantly."

I begged him to test it on my left eye. He did so, and immediately the soil beneath my feet appeared like transparent crystal, showing veins of gold, forgotten vaults, and sunken emeralds!

A demonic covetousness seized my reason. I reasoned: "If the left eye sees treasures beneath the earth, surely the right eye will reveal the treasures of heaven and jinn!" Despite his solemn warnings, I demanded he anoint my right eye.

He touched my right eyelid. Instantly, an impenetrable pitch-black darkness enveloped me forever! The golden visions vanished. When I cried out in terror and groveled for help, the dervish mounted the lead camel and rode away, saying:
"Thou hadst wealth enough for twenty lifetimes, Baba Abdullah, but thy greed could not endure a single empty corner in thy heart."

I was left alone in the wilderness until wandering shepherds rescued me. In bitter penitence, I vowed that every coin given to me must be accompanied by a stroke upon my cheek, to remind my soul of the foolish greed that traded eternal sight for dirt.'

Harun al-Rashid sighed with profound sadness and decreed:
'Thy punishment was severe, Baba Abdullah, but thy repentance is sincere. Henceforth, receive a daily pension from our treasury, and cease asking blows from strangers, for thou hast borne thy lesson to the core.'
moral: Greed blinds the spiritual eye long before it takes away physical sight; contentment is the true cure for desire. [TE]

title: History of Sidi Nu'uman (తెలుగు)
summary: The young gentleman who had been seen grooming his mare with mingled tears and reprimands bowed before the Caliph and introduced himself ... [TE]
full_text:
The young gentleman who had been seen grooming his mare with mingled tears and reprimands bowed before the Caliph and introduced himself as Sidi Nu'uman.

'Commander of the Faithful,' he said, 'the mare in my stable is no ordinary beast; she was once Aminah, my treacherous wife, who practiced forbidden sorcery.

When I married her, she was reputed to be a woman of modesty and noble lineage. Yet at our dining table, she behaved most unnaturally: instead of eating our meals, she would pick up grains of rice one by one with a tiny ivory bodkin. Suspecting an eerie mystery, I pretended to fall asleep one night, only to follow her stealthily out of the city gates.

To my horror, I tracked her to a desolate graveyard, where she communed with ghouls under the pale crescent. When I confronted her the following dawn and demanded she repent her profane ways, her face contorted with wicked fury. She dipped a cup of water, threw the spray into my face, and pronounced a terrible curse:
"Quit the shape of man and take the form of an outcast dog!"

Instantly my bones cracked, my posture dropped upon four paws, and I barked in agony. Driven out of my own home, I wandered the alleys, hunted by butcher boys and starved near gutters. Yet my human intellect remained trapped within the canine shell.

One day, I sought refuge inside the bakery of a kind-hearted man. Seeing my gentle eyes, he tossed me a loaf of bread, which I ate with clean, orderly manners. Astonished, the baker adopted me as his watchman. Soon after, a woman came into the shop and tried to pay with counterfeit silver coins. Recognizing the deception, I leaped up, pinned the woman's robe with my paws, and overturned the bad money!

A learned lady passing by observed my discernment. She was a practitioner of white magic and lawful wisdom. She whispered to the baker:
"This is no dog, but an honorable man ensorcelled by a malevolent sorceress!"

She brought me to her home, prepared a bowl of consecrated spring water, and cast the counter-spell upon my head. My limbs straightened, my voice returned, and I knelt in tearful thanksgiving. She then gave me a flask of magical dew and said:
"Go back to thy house. Cast this upon thy treacherous wife and pronounce her punishment."

I strode into my home, took Aminah by surprise, and threw the water upon her, commanding: "Leave the form of woman and become a mare, bearing burdens as a beast of toil!"

Thus she became the mare. Every morning I tend her with good grain and clean straw out of humane duty, but I reprove her sternly to remind her spirit of the wickedness that stripped her of humanity.'

Caliph Harun al-Rashid marveled at the divine balance of justice, granting Sidi Nu'uman honors and protection throughout the empire.
moral: Deceit and sorcery unravel before courage and righteousness, restoring dignity to those who uphold honor. [TE]

title: History of Khwajah Hasan al-Habbal (తెలుగు)
summary: Next stood Khwajah Hasan al-Habbal, the former rope-maker who now resided in an imperial palace. [TE]
full_text:
Next stood Khwajah Hasan al-Habbal, the former rope-maker who now resided in an imperial palace.

'O Caliph,' began Hasan, 'two lifelong friends of mine, Sa'ad and Sa'adi, held a perpetual debate. Sa'adi argued that a man becomes wealthy only if given a large sum of gold to trade with. Sa'ad insisted that without divine blessing and industrious labor, gold would slip away like water through fingers, and that modest gifts often build lasting empires.

To test their philosophy, Sa'adi approached me at my modest rope-spinning shed. He pressed two hundred gold dinars into my hands, saying: "Go, buy hemp in bulk and become rich!"

I was overwhelmed. Having never seen such treasure, I tucked ten dinars into my pocket for daily bread and sewed the remaining one hundred and ninety inside the linen fold of my turban. Walking to the market, I stopped at a butcher's stall to buy meat for my hungry children. While negotiating, a ravenous kite smelled the meat, swooped down from the sky, missed the beef, and snatched my turban by its protruding fold! The bird flew across the city walls with all my fortune!

I returned home weeping, poorer and more sorrowful than before.

Six months later, the two friends visited again. Sa'adi, believing I had squandered the gold on follies, shook his head, but gave me another two hundred dinars out of pity.

This time, determined to keep it safe from birds, I hid the gold at the bottom of an earthenware jar filled with wheat bran in my pantry. Days later, while I was out buying hemp, an itinerant merchant came selling washing clay. My wife, knowing nothing of the hidden coins and needing soap clay, traded the old jar of bran for two blocks of soap!

When I returned and found the jar gone, I collapsed in utter despair.

A year passed before Sa'ad and Sa'adi returned. Seeing me still weaving coarse twine in rags, Sa'adi gave up in frustration. But Sa'ad smiled gently. He reached into his robe and handed me a small, worthless piece of lead he had picked up in the street.
"Take this, friend Hasan," said Sa'ad. "It has no market value, but may providence bless it."

I put the scrap of lead on my shelf. That evening, a neighboring fisherman knocked frantically, saying his lead weights had torn away and he needed a sinker immediately to cast his nets before sunset. I gave him my lead scrap. Grateful, he promised: "Whatever comes up in my first net shall be thine!"

The next dawn, the fisherman brought me a large, fine fish. When my wife cleaned it for dinner, she found inside its stomach a brilliant, clear glass pebble. The children played with it as a toy, and at night, it lit the entire room like a lamp!

A Jewish jeweler passing our window noticed the luminescence and offered ten dinars, then a hundred, then ten thousand! It was the celebrated lost diamond of the grand treasury! I sold it for one hundred thousand dinars!

With that fortune, I did not waste or revel; I established great rope manufactories, employed hundreds of honest artisans, and built caravanserais for travelers.

Months later, my workmen discovered a kite's nest in an ancient hollow tree—and inside it was my old turban, the original one hundred and ninety dinars completely intact! Shortly after, a grain merchant returned my old bran jar, having bought it unopened from the soap seller!

Thus did Sa'ad prove his truth: gold given before its appointed season flies away on the wings of kites, but the smallest gift, blessed by honest diligence and heaven's decree, blossoms into enduring abundance.'
moral: Wealth does not come from unearned hoards or careless chance, but from patient industry blessed by providence. [TE]

keywords: ali baba and the forty thieves
full_text:
In a bustling town of Persia lived two brothers: Kasim, who married a wealthy heiress and operated a grand shop, and Ali Baba, a humble woodcutter who earned a frugal livelihood gathering fuel in the forest with three donkeys.

One day deep in the woods, Ali Baba heard the thundering gallop of horsemen. Fearing bandits, he tied his donkeys in a thicket and climbed a tall tree leafy enough to conceal him. Forty fierce brigands drew rein before a towering rock face. Their captain dismounted, faced the stone wall, and proclaimed with a ringing voice:
'Open, Sesame!'

A hidden door swung open in the solid rock. The thieves carried heavy saddlebags inside, emerged empty-handed, and the captain commanded:
'Shut, Sesame!' The stone door sealed seamlessly.

When the troop rode away, Ali Baba descended, approached the rock, and repeated: 'Open, Sesame!' To his amazement, the portal opened into a luminous cavern filled with stacks of silk, spices, and mounds of silver and gold coin—the accumulated plunder of generations.

Ali Baba took only what his three donkeys could carry, covered the gold bags with firewood, sealed the cave with 'Shut, Sesame!', and returned home. He revealed the secret to his wife, urging secrecy. Needing to measure the gold coins, his wife borrowed a measuring bowl from Kasim's wealthy wife. Suspicious, Kasim's wife smeared beeswax at the bottom of the vessel. When returned, a gold dinar stuck to the wax!

Kasim confronted his brother, demanding the secret of the hoard under threat of denunciation. Gentle Ali Baba generously shared the secret words and the cave's location.

Greedy Kasim rushed to the cave with ten mules and iron chests. Entering with 'Open, Sesame!', he became intoxicated by the mountain of jewels. But when he turned to leave, his mind, blinded by avarice, forgot the magic word!
'Open, Barley!' he shouted. 'Open, Wheat!'
The rock remained unyielding. Trapped, Kasim trembled until the forty thieves returned. Finding him inside, they slew him without mercy.

When Kasim did not return, Ali Baba searched the cavern, discovered his brother's remains, and brought them home with heavy sorrow.

Now in Ali Baba's household lived Morgiana, an enslaved maiden of extraordinary intelligence, agility, and courage. To preserve the secret and grant Kasim an honorable burial without suspicion, Morgiana devised a clever plan: she engaged Baba Mustafa, an elderly blind cobbler, blindfolded him, and led him through winding lanes to Kasim's house, where he stitched the remains together so a traditional shroud could be fitted.

The captain of the thieves soon discovered that the body had been removed. Realizing someone else possessed the secret, he sent a scout to town. The scout met Baba Mustafa, who boasted that he had sewn together a corpse in a mysterious house. Bribing the cobbler to retrace his steps blindfolded, the scout located Ali Baba's house and marked the door with white chalk.

Alert Morgiana noticed the white chalk mark. Guessing danger, she marked every house in the neighborhood with identical chalk, confounding the bandits. A second spy marked the door with red chalk, but Morgiana again foiled the plot by marking all neighboring doors in red.

Enraged by his scouts' failure, the captain surveyed the house himself, memorizing its shape. He disguised himself as an oil merchant traveling with nineteen mules bearing thirty-eight large leather jars: one filled with olive oil, and thirty-seven concealing his armed men!

Arriving at Ali Baba's gate at dusk, the disguised captain requested hospitality, which hospitable Ali Baba gladly granted, having the jars stacked in the courtyard.

During the night, Morgiana's oil lamp went out. Seeking a cup of oil from the courtyard jars, she approached one and heard a whisper from within:
'Is it time, Captain?'
Morgiana, never losing her presence of mind, replied in a deep whisper: 'Not yet, but soon.'

Discovering thirty-seven armed killers hidden inside the jars, Morgiana acted decisively. She heated a massive caldron of boiling oil and poured enough into each occupied vessel to instantly incapacitate the assassins, saving her master's entire family.

When the captain gave the signal to strike and received no answer, he found his gang destroyed and fled into the night.

Months later, the captain returned disguised as a merchant of fine silks named Kogias Hassan, befriending Ali Baba's son and becoming a guest at dinner. But sharp-eyed Morgiana recognized his face beneath the false beard and noticed a concealed dagger in his belt.

During the banquet, Morgiana dressed as a traditional dancer, performing an intricate, swirling dance with a silver dagger to the sound of the tambourine. Whirling closer to the false guest, she plunged the dagger into his black heart before he could draw his weapon!

Ali Baba cried out in horror, but Morgiana revealed the hidden dagger and unmasked the bandit captain.
Weeping with gratitude, Ali Baba embraced Morgiana, gave her her freedom, married her to his beloved son, and endowed her with half the mountain treasure. For generations, the family used the secret cave with moderation, using the gold to feed orphans, heal the sick, and bless the poor of Persia.
moral: Greed and arrogance dig an early grave, but loyalty, sharp wit, and discretion overcome the deadliest perils. [TE]

title: Ali Khwajah and the Merchant of Baghdad (తెలుగు)
summary: In the days of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, there lived in Baghdad a devout merchant named Ali Khwajah. Having decided to undertake the holy p... [TE]
keywords: ali khwajah and the merchant of baghdad
full_text:
In the days of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, there lived in Baghdad a devout merchant named Ali Khwajah. Having decided to undertake the holy pilgrimage to Mecca, he sold his household goods and closed his shop.

After paying all debts, he possessed one thousand gold dinars. Not wishing to carry such wealth on perilous desert roads, he placed the gold at the bottom of a large earthen jar, covering it completely with fresh, plump olives.

He carried the jar to an old friend, a reputable olive merchant, saying:
'Brother, I embark upon the pilgrimage tomorrow. Keep this jar of olives safely in your warehouse until my return.'
The friend gave him the keys, pointing to a corner: 'Place it there with your own hands, Ali Khwajah; it shall remain untouched until thou claimest it.'

Ali Khwajah completed the pilgrimage, but finding great trading opportunities, traveled onward to Cairo, Damascus, and Persia, remaining abroad for seven full years.

During the seventh year, the Baghdad merchant's wife expressed a sudden craving for fresh olives. Her husband remembered Ali Khwajah's jar: 'It has stood in my cellar for seven years; the man is surely dead. Let us taste them.'
Opening the jar, he found the top olives moldy and rotten. Pouring them into a basin to check the lower layers, a cascade of golden dinars clattered onto the stone floor!

Temptation overcame the merchant's soul. He scooped the thousand dinars into his private coffer, threw away the spoiled olives, bought fresh green olives from the morning market, filled the jar to the brim, and sealed it with wax.

A month later, Ali Khwajah returned safely to Baghdad. He visited his friend, who returned the jar with warm embraces. But when Ali Khwajah opened it in his lodgings, he found only green olives—the thousand pieces of gold were gone!

He returned to the merchant, pleading quietly: 'Friend, perhaps thou hadst need of the gold? Repay it as a loan when able, and I shall speak no word of it.'
The merchant became indignant: 'Art thou mad? Thou didst place the jar with thine own hands and didst retrieve it sealed! Accuse me not of theft!'

Ali Khwajah took the matter before the Kazi, but having no witnesses and only a sealed jar, the court dismissed the case. Desperate, Ali Khwajah wrote a petition to Caliph Harun al-Rashid.

That evening, the Caliph walked disguised through the streets with Vizier Ja'afar. Passing a courtyard, he saw children playing a courtroom game. A bright boy sat upon a bench as the 'Caliph', another played 'Ali Khwajah', and a third played the 'Dishonest Merchant'.

The child-judge listened carefully, then commanded: 'Bring the jar of olives before me!'
He tasted an olive and said: 'These olives are crisp and fresh! Olive merchants know that olives spoil within three years! How can olives stored for seven years taste fresh from the tree? The jar has been tampered with!'

Harun al-Rashid was struck by the child's brilliant deduction. The next morning, he summoned the boy to the imperial diwan, along with Ali Khwajah, the accused merchant, and two master olive tasters of Baghdad.

The expert tasters sampled the fruit and affirmed: 'Commander of the Faithful, these olives are of this year's harvest; no olive can preserve flavor beyond two seasons.'

Confronted with undeniable proof, the dishonest merchant confessed, wept, and restored the thousand dinars with damages. The Caliph rewarded the clever boy with a purse of gold and an appointment to royal tutorship, establishing the principle that forensic truth cuts through the craftiest perjuries.
moral: Truth has a quiet fragrance that deceit cannot extinguish; youth and clear eyes often perceive justice when adults are blinded by form. [TE]

title: Prince Ahmad and the Fairy Peri-Banu (తెలుగు)
summary: In India ruled a mighty Sultan who had three sons: Prince Husayn, Prince Ali, and Prince Ahmad, alongside a beautiful orphaned niece, Pri... [TE]
keywords: prince ahmad and the fairy peri-banu
full_text:
In India ruled a mighty Sultan who had three sons: Prince Husayn, Prince Ali, and Prince Ahmad, alongside a beautiful orphaned niece, Princess Nur al-Nahar. All three brothers loved their cousin deeply.

To resolve their rivalry without bloodshed, the Sultan proclaimed:
'Travel to distant corners of the world. Whosoever brings back the most extraordinary curiosity shall have Nur al-Nahar as his bride.'

Prince Husayn traveled to the markets of Bishangar, where he purchased an enchanted tapestry: whoever sat upon it was transported instantaneously across mountains and seas to any destination desired.

Prince Ali traveled to Shiraz, where he acquired an ivory viewing-glass through which one could see any person or place in the world simply by wishing it.

Prince Ahmad journeyed to Samarkand, where he bought a magical artificial apple: inhaling its fragrance cured any mortal sickness instantly.

Meeting at an appointed caravanserai to compare their treasures, Prince Ali looked through his viewing-glass and cried in horror: 'Princess Nur al-Nahar lies dying in our father's palace!'
Prince Husayn spread his tapestry, all three leaped upon it, and arrived in the Princess's chamber in the twinkling of an eye! Prince Ahmad held the enchanted apple to her lips; she inhaled its healing fragrance and arose in perfect health!

The Sultan was in a dilemma: Ali's glass discovered the danger, Husayn's tapestry brought them in time, and Ahmad's apple cured her life. None was superior. He declared an archery contest: whoever shot his arrow farthest should win her hand.

Husayn shot far; Ali shot farther; but Ahmad's arrow flew so high and distant that none could find where it landed. Ali married Nur al-Nahar, while broken-hearted Husayn became a solitary hermit.

Ahmad, determined to find his arrow, wandered for days across rocky hills until he found the arrow lying far beyond possible human reach, near the foot of an iron cliff. Approaching, he found an iron door set in the mountain.

Entering, he was welcomed into a subterranean palace of crystal and jade by Peri-Banu, a powerful fairy princess. She revealed:
'Prince Ahmad, it was I who drew thy arrow across the sky. I have loved thee for thy gentleness and courage. If thou wilt accept my hand, my kingdom and devotion are thine.'

Ahmad gladly wed Peri-Banu, living in sublime happiness. Yet, missing his father, he obtained her permission to visit the Sultan with royal gifts, promising to return.

However, a wicked enchantress whispered poison into the Sultan's ear, suggesting Ahmad was amassing fairy armies to seize the throne. The Sultan, gripped by suspicion, demanded impossible tributes from Ahmad: first, a tent so vast it could shelter an entire army yet so light it could be held in the palm of a hand; then, water from the Fountain of Lions that cured all fevers; and finally, a man one foot tall with a beard thirty feet long who carried an iron club weighing five hundredweight!

Peri-Banu smiled at each demand. With fairy power, she provided the magical pocket tent, sent her enchanted lion-taming perfume to fetch the miraculous water, and summoned her brother Schaibar, a tiny dwarf of colossal strength.

When the Sultan and his wicked councilors drew their scimitars upon Schaibar, the dwarf whirled his iron club, routing the plotters and ending the reign of deceit. Ahmad was crowned Sultan, ruling with benevolence, accompanied by Peri-Banu whose wisdom brought peace and prosperity to the empire for decades.
moral: True worth is proven through devotion and integrity, while magical wonders pale before sincere affection and civic duty. [TE]

title: The Two Sisters Who Envied Their Cadette (తెలుగు)
summary: Khosrou Shah, Emperor of Persia, walking in disguise through the city one evening, overheard three poor sisters conversing in a cottage. ... [TE]
keywords: the two sisters who envied their cadette
full_text:
Khosrou Shah, Emperor of Persia, walking in disguise through the city one evening, overheard three poor sisters conversing in a cottage.
The eldest said: 'If I married the Sultan's chief baker, I would eat the finest sweetmeats every day.'
The second said: 'If I married the Sultan's chief cook, I would feast on royal dishes.'
The youngest, sweet Parizadah, blushed and said: 'If I married the Sultan himself, I would bear him three children whose hair would be gold and silver, who would weep pearls and smile with sunlight.'

The Sultan, charmed by her innocence, married Parizadah the next day, appointing her elder sisters to the royal household. Consumed by bitter jealousy, the two older sisters plotted revenge.

When Parizadah gave birth to a handsome prince, the wicked sisters replaced the infant with a dead puppy and threw the child into the palace canal inside a floating basket. The next year, when a second prince was born, they replaced him with a kitten. In the third year, when a radiant princess was born, they substituted a block of wood!

The heartbroken Sultan, believing his Empress was cursed, demoted her and confined her to a solitary stone pavilion near the mosque, where worshippers threw dust upon her head.

Meanwhile, the palace superintendent, an honorable man with no children, found the three baskets floating in his water-gardens. He rescued the infants, named them Prince Bahman, Prince Perviz, and Princess Parizadah, and raised them with exquisite care in a country estate.

Years later, after their foster father passed away, an elderly devout pilgrim visited the estate. She praised its gardens, but remarked:
'This paradise lacks three wonders: the Speaking Bird that sings harmonies like an angel, the Singing Tree whose leaves sound like flutes, and the Golden Water that fills any basin with eternal glittering fountain spray.'

Princess Parizadah yearned for these wonders. Her elder brother Bahman rode forth to find them, leaving her a magic knife that would turn rusty if he perished. When the knife blade darkened with rust, the second brother, Perviz, rode forth with a string of pearls that would stop moving if misfortune befell him. Soon, the pearls became motionless.

Undeterred, courageous Princess Parizadah dressed as an armor-clad youth, rode to Mount Zagros, and reached the dervish at the crossroads. He gave her cotton wool to plug her ears, warning:
'As thou climbest the mountain, thousands of phantom voices will mock, insult, and threaten thee. Turn not thy head, or thou wilt turn to black stone like the hundreds of statues lining the ridge!'

With ears securely stopped, Parizadah climbed courageously, ignoring howling specters, reached the mountain crest, and captured the Speaking Bird in a golden cage!

Following the Bird's guidance, she gathered a branch of the Singing Tree, drew a vial of Golden Water, and sprinkled the water over the black stones. Instantly, Bahman, Perviz, and hundreds of enchanted knights returned to life!

Returning home, they planted the Singing Tree, let the Golden Water cascade in their courtyard, and hung the Speaking Bird in their pavilion.

Soon after, the Sultan visited their estate while hunting. During the banquet, the Speaking Bird spoke in human speech:
'O King, thou marvelest at cucumbers stuffed with pearls, yet believed that thy virtuous Empress bore dogs and wood? Behold thy true children, Bahman, Perviz, and Parizadah!'

The Sultan embraced his children with tears of boundless joy. The wicked sisters were condemned to exile, Empress Parizadah was restored with imperial honors, and the palace flourished in divine justice and enduring peace.
moral: Envy breeds cruel plots against innocence, but purity of heart and perseverance reveal truth and reunite divided families. [TE]

title: Story of the Sultan of Al-Yaman and His Three Sons (తెలుగు)
summary: In ancient Yemen reigned a wise Sultan who, on his deathbed, left his vast kingdom to his three sons, commanding: 'Go to the Chief Judge ... [TE]
keywords: story of the sultan of al-yaman and his three sons
full_text:
In ancient Yemen reigned a wise Sultan who, on his deathbed, left his vast kingdom to his three sons, commanding:
'Go to the Chief Judge of the Desert, Sage Al-Mustansir, whenever a dispute arises, for his discernment will guide your steps.'

After their father's burial, the three princes rode across the sand dunes toward the judge's oasis. As they traveled, they noticed camel tracks in the sand.

The eldest prince observed: 'The camel that passed here was blind in one eye.'
The second prince remarked: 'It was missing one front tooth.'
The youngest prince added: 'It was lame in its left hind leg, carried a load of sweet honey on one flank, and a load of oil on the other!'

Further along the path, an agitated camel merchant stopped them, shouting: 'Noble youths, have you seen my lost camel?'
The eldest asked: 'Was it blind in one eye?'
'Yes!' cried the merchant.
The second asked: 'Was it missing a tooth?'
'Yes, exactly!'
The youngest asked: 'Was it lame, carrying honey on the right and oil on the left?'
'By heaven, you have seen it! Where is it?'
The princes replied: 'We swear we have never seen your camel with our eyes.'

The merchant, convinced they had stolen his beast and goods, seized their reins and dragged them before Judge Al-Mustansir, accusing them of theft.

The Judge turned to the princes: 'You described the camel with absolute precision. How can you claim innocence?'

The eldest explained: 'My lord, the grass was cropped only on the right side of the path, while lush grass on the left remained untouched. A beast with two eyes feeds equally on both sides; therefore, it was blind in its left eye.'

The second said: 'Where it bit the grass, small tufts were left unbroken in the middle of each bite mark, indicating a missing front tooth.'

The youngest said: 'The prints of three hooves were deep and clear, while the left hind hoof dragged lightly in the sand, proving lameness. Furthermore, swarms of flies clustered on the right side of the trail where honey had dripped, while ants swarmed on the left where oil had fallen!'

The Judge laughed with admiration, dismissed the merchant's charge, and soon after, shepherds found the wandering camel unharmed in a canyon.

Impressed by their extraordinary acumen, Al-Mustansir mediated the succession of the kingdom equitably among the three brothers, who ruled Yemen with balanced judgment and legendary wisdom.
moral: Wisdom and keen observation reveal what hidden secrets conceal, proving that intellect surpasses brute force. [TE]

title: Story of the Three Sharpers (తెలుగు)
summary: Three notorious tricksters met outside the city gates of Damascus: Haydar the Pickpocket, Mansur the Counterfeiter, and Qasim the Conjuro... [TE]
full_text:
Three notorious tricksters met outside the city gates of Damascus: Haydar the Pickpocket, Mansur the Counterfeiter, and Qasim the Conjuror.
'Brothers,' boasted Haydar, 'let each of us perform his masterpiece today; whoever pulls off the most audacious trick without using weapons shall be declared Master of the Guild.'

First went Haydar. He watched a wealthy farmer walking into the market leading a fat, prize ram by a hemp halter, with a little brass bell tied to the ram's tail so the farmer could hear it following.
Haydar sneaked behind, gently untied the bell from the ram, attached it to the farmer's belt loop, and led the prize ram away. The farmer walked half a mile, hearing the bell clinking behind him, until a neighbor laughed: 'Uncle, why art thou leading thine own coat tail?'

Next went Mansur. Finding the farmer weeping beside an open well, Mansur sat on the stone coping, crying loudly.
'Why weepest thou, friend?' asked the farmer.
'Woe is me!' sobbed Mansur. 'I dropped a casket containing two hundred gold dinars into this deep well. If an expert swimmer would dive and fetch it, I would gladly reward him with fifty dinars!'
The farmer thought: 'Here is my chance to recover my loss!' He stripped off his fine silk robes and boots, dove into the cold well water, and searched the muddy bottom for an hour. Meanwhile, Mansur scooped up the farmer's expensive clothes and boots and vanished!

Finally went Qasim. He observed the chief of police riding out with his patrol to apprehend the two tricksters. Qasim bought a pot of honey, covered himself in white sheepskins, climbed an ancient tombstone in the cemetery, and howled: 'I am the Guardian Spirit of the Tomb!'
When the captain approached, Qasim threw flour into his eyes, declared that whoever touched him would be transformed into a marble column, and took the captain's jeweled saddle while the patrol scattered in superstitious panic.

The three sharpers met at an inn to celebrate their spoils. But while they argued over whose trick was greatest, the clever baker's apprentice who overheard them locked their tavern door from the outside and alerted the municipal guard!

All three were marched before the governor. Their loot was returned to the poor farmer and the captain, while the three tricksters were sentenced to sweeping the public bazaar for three years, proving that those who spin webs of deceit eventually entangle their own feet.
moral: Trickery may succeed against the gullible for a day, but cleverness devoid of virtue ends in disgrace. [TE]

title: The Sultan Who Fared Forth in the Habit of a Darwaysh (తెలుగు)
summary: Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna, feeling that his courtiers shielded him from the realities of his realm, laid aside his embroidered robes, dress... [TE]
keywords: the sultan who fared forth in the habit of a darwaysh
full_text:
Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna, feeling that his courtiers shielded him from the realities of his realm, laid aside his embroidered robes, dressed in the patched wool cloak of a wandering dervish, and took up a beggar's bowl.

He walked out into the countryside, sleeping in modest caravanserais, sharing dry crusts with camel drivers, and listening to weavers and field workers.

In a remote village, he encountered an elderly farmer working late into the evening by candlelight. Mahmud asked: 'Venerable uncle, why dost thou toil when other men rest?'
The old man sighed: 'The local tax collector charges double taxes, threatening to confiscate my small olive grove. I must work day and night to pay his unlawful exactions, for our Sultan sits far away in his palace, unaware of our plight.'

Mahmud made careful notes in his memory. Moving to another town, he met a widow whose house had been seized by an unjust magistrate who altered the property deeds. She wept: 'If only Sultan Mahmud could hear my voice, he would restore my roof!'

For three weeks, Mahmud traveled as a dervish, gathering evidence of extortion, injustice, and hidden virtue.

Returning to Ghazna, the Sultan summoned a grand public audience. He ordered the corrupt tax collector and the dishonest magistrate to stand before the throne.
Stepping down from the dais, Mahmud cast aside his royal mantle to reveal the patched dervish cloak underneath!

The oppressors turned white as linen.
'Did you believe,' declared Mahmud, 'that because the Sultan was absent from his throne, heaven had closed its ears? I was the dervish who asked for water at your door; I saw the tears of the widow and the toil of the farmer.'

The Sultan immediately dismissed the corrupt officials, returned the confiscated lands, compensated the victims threefold from the royal treasury, and established a traveling court of justice. He proved that a king who walks with the humble rules with the eternal strength of truth.
moral: True majesty is found not in diadems and thrones, but in listening to the heartfelt sorrows of the humble. [TE]

title: History of Mohammed Sultan of Cairo (తెలుగు)
summary: Mohammed, Sultan of Cairo, was a brave warrior but cursed with a fiery, impulsive temper. Whenever angered, he issued hasty decrees of ex... [TE]
keywords: history of mohammed sultan of cairo
full_text:
Mohammed, Sultan of Cairo, was a brave warrior but cursed with a fiery, impulsive temper. Whenever angered, he issued hasty decrees of execution that he later regretted in bitter remorse.

Realizing his dangerous weakness, he summoned his venerable Grand Vizier, Burhan al-Din, and said:
'O wise counselor, my temper is like a desert whirlwind. I appoint thee the guardian of my soul. Whenever thou seest me inflamed with wrath and ready to order a man's death, thou hast my royal permission to delay the decree three days, presenting me three questions before the blade is drawn.'

Weeks later, a foreign ambassador brought a rare gift: a luminous crystal vase of ancient Persian manufacture, translucent as morning air and engraved with floral traceries. The Sultan prized it above all treasures in his citadel.

One afternoon, a young cupbearer accidentally tripped on the edge of the royal carpet. The crystal vase slipped from his hands and shattered into a thousand glittering shards upon the marble floor.

Furious, the Sultan leaped to his feet, drew his scimitar, and shouted: 'Behead him this instant!'

Vizier Burhan al-Din stepped forward, bowed low, and placed his hand gently upon the executioner's scimitar:
'Remember thy covenant, O King. Grant the three days.'

The Sultan, trembling with rage, consented.

On the third morning, when the Sultan's anger had subsided into calm reflection, Burhan al-Din brought the cupbearer before the throne and asked the three questions:
'First: Can the execution of this youth reassemble the shattered crystal?'
The Sultan answered softly: 'No.'
'Second: Does the loss of an earthen, fragile object equal the destruction of a living human soul created by Allah?'
The Sultan replied with bowed head: 'No.'
'Third: Which memory will bring greater peace to thy heart when thou facest the Eternal Judge—the memory of a broken vase avenged with blood, or the memory of royal mercy extended to a trembling servant?'

Tears filled Sultan Mohammed's eyes. He sheathed his sword, embraced his wise Vizier, and rewarded the cupbearer with freedom and gold. From that day forward, the Sultan became celebrated throughout Egypt as Mohammed the Just, proving that true sovereignty lies in the mastery of oneself.
moral: A ruler's greatest victory is overcoming his own wrath and governing through mercy and steadfast counsel. [TE]

title: Story of the First Lunatic (తెలుగు)
summary: Sultan Mohammed of Cairo, continuing his inspection of the city, visited the Moristan—the great hospital and sanctuary for the mentally a... [TE]
full_text:
Sultan Mohammed of Cairo, continuing his inspection of the city, visited the Moristan—the great hospital and sanctuary for the mentally afflicted.

In one tranquil garden courtyard, he observed a dignified man with silver hair and luminous eyes, sitting beneath an orange tree and reading an ancient parchment.
Surprised by his composed demeanor, the Sultan approached and asked: 'Peace be upon thee, venerable sir. Why art thou confined in this house of the distracted?'

The man smiled with serene courtesy:
'O visitor, I am confined here because I suffer from an incurable illness called Truth-Telling.

In the bazaar and the imperial court, men flatter one another with false praise. They call cowards heroes, greedy thieves noble patrons, and fools sages, all to gain coppers and favor.
When I was a chief accountant in the treasury, I declared publicly that the grand chamberlain was pocketing public wheat. The chamberlain laughed, declared that only a raving lunatic would speak such inconvenient truths against powerful men, and had me placed in this peaceful hospital.

Here, within these quiet walls, no one lies to me. The madmen are honest about their delusions: one claims he is the moon, another that he is an earthenware pot. Neither pretends to love virtue while stealing from orphans.
Tell me, my noble guest: who is truly insane—the man who speaks truth and enjoys contentment under an orange tree, or the men in silk robes who betray their conscience every hour for fleeting dust?'

The Sultan stood transfixed by the philosopher's penetrating insight. He realized that society often labels those who refuse to participate in deceit as madmen.
He ordered the sage released with highest honors and appointed him Royal Censor of Truth, learning that genuine wisdom is often banished where falsehood reigns.
moral: Apparent eccentricity often conceals profound philosophical clarity; judge no man by outward appearances. [TE]

title: Story of the Second Lunatic (తెలుగు)
summary: Moving through the corridors of the hospital, Sultan Mohammed encountered a second inmate sitting upon a stone bench, holding a dry twig ... [TE]
full_text:
Moving through the corridors of the hospital, Sultan Mohammed encountered a second inmate sitting upon a stone bench, holding a dry twig and drawing geometric circles in the sand.

'Peace be upon thee, friend,' said the Sultan. 'What kingdom art thou measuring in the sand?'

The inmate looked up with eyes sparkling with unburdened joy:
'I am measuring the kingdom of complete tranquility, which has no walls, no guards, and no rivals.

Before they brought me here, I was a wealthy merchant owning seven ships in the Red Sea. Every night I tossed in bed, tormented by anxieties: Will the monsoon sink my spices? Will pirates raid my silk? Will the harbor master double his bribes? Will my competitors ruin my prices? I had bags of gold, yet I could not eat bread without stomach spasms or sleep two hours without nightmares.

Then one storm wrecked five ships, and fire consumed my warehouses. I lost everything.
When I sat on the beach with nothing left but my wool tunic, a sudden miraculous breeze touched my face. For the first time in thirty years, I took a deep breath without fear! I realized I had nothing left to lose!

I sang with joy, gave away my remaining shoes, and began contemplating the stars. My relatives, seeing me dancing without money, concluded I had lost my wits and sent me here.
Yet look at me now: I eat fresh lentil porridge, drink pure well water, sleep like an innocent child, and have no fear of thieves, storms, or kings.
Tell me, sovereign visitor: who has the greater kingdom—he who trembles over gold, or he who rejoices in an empty hand?'

The Sultan sighed with profound humility, recognizing that true liberation is not the accumulation of possessions, but freedom from the fear of losing them.
moral: Freedom from material desire brings tranquility that kings and conquerors can never purchase. [TE]

title: Story of the Sage and the Scholar (తెలుగు)
summary: A proud young scholar from Al-Azhar University, puffed up with arrogance from memorizing ten thousand verses of poetry and theological te... [TE]
keywords: story of the sage and the scholar
full_text:
A proud young scholar from Al-Azhar University, puffed up with arrogance from memorizing ten thousand verses of poetry and theological texts, sought out the famous desert ascetic Sage Abu Ishaq.

Finding the sage watering a neglected pomegranate bush outside his mud-brick cell, the young scholar bowed perfunctorily and began to lecture:
'O Master, I have mastered the seven schools of grammar, the intricacies of inheritance law, the disputes of logic, and the commentaries of philosophy. I have come that thou mayest examine me and declare me the leading scholar of Cairo.'

Abu Ishaq continued watering the thirsty plant, then said gently:
'Fetch me a bowl of fresh milk from the peasant woman in yonder hut.'

The scholar went and brought back a shallow wooden bowl filled to the brim with goat's milk.
'Now,' said the sage, 'carry this bowl three times around the entire perimeter of our village without spilling a single drop. If thou spillest even one bead, thy learning is void.'

The scholar lifted the bowl carefully, walking with tense, rigid steps. He focused his eyes solely on the white surface, sweating under the afternoon sun, balancing the liquid with intense concentration.
He returned triumphant: 'Behold, Master! I walked the entire circuit, and not a single drop was spilled!'

Abu Ishaq looked at him calmly:
'While walking through the village, didst thou notice the blind orphan crying by the ditch?'
'No,' replied the scholar. 'I looked only at the milk.'
'Didst thou see the poor laborer struggling under a fallen timber?'
'No, I was guarding the bowl!'
'Didst thou hear the greetings of peace offered by the village elders?'
'I could hear nothing, for fear of losing a drop!'

Abu Ishaq shook his head with sorrowful smile:
'Thou hast carried a bowl of milk, but missed the entire world.
Thy books have taught thee to balance words, but have blinded thee to the suffering, joy, and reality of thy fellow men. Go, throw away thy arrogance. Learn to see the orphan, help the laborer, and return the elder's greeting. For learning that does not blossom into kindness is nothing more than vanity.'

The young scholar lowered his head in shame, kissed the sage's rough hand, and began his true education in humility and service.
moral: Book knowledge without compassionate practice is like a donkey laden with books; true learning lives in conduct. [TE]

title: The Night-Adventure of Sultan Mohammed of Cairo (తెలుగు)
summary: One moonless night, Sultan Mohammed of Cairo slipped out of the Citadel disguised as an ordinary municipal guard, carrying a sturdy oak c... [TE]
keywords: the night-adventure of sultan mohammed of cairo
full_text:
One moonless night, Sultan Mohammed of Cairo slipped out of the Citadel disguised as an ordinary municipal guard, carrying a sturdy oak cudgel and a hooded lantern.

As he traversed the quiet alleys near the Bab Zuweila gate, he heard muffled cries of distress coming from a deserted courtyard. Peering through a broken wooden lattice, he saw four armed ruffians surrounding a lone traveling merchant and his young daughter, demanding their baggage of silks.

Without hesitating, the Sultan kicked open the decayed gate, raised his lantern high, and shouted with thunderous authority:
'Stand fast in the name of Justice!'

The bandits, seeing only a single guard, mocked him and drew their scimitars. But Sultan Mohammed was a master swordsman. With swift, powerful strokes of his cudgel, he disarmed the first two, tripped the third, and pinned the fourth against the stone wall.

The city patrol, alerted by the clamor, rushed into the courtyard and bound the brigands. The captain of the patrol, not recognizing the disguised Sultan in the shadows, praised him:
'Well fought, comrade! Who art thou that handlest a cudgel like an imperial general?'

The Sultan smiled: 'I am a humble servant of Cairo who believes that the night belongs to peaceful citizens, not to jackals.'

The grateful merchant fell to his knees, offering a purse of gold coins: 'Noble guardian, take this reward, for thou hast saved my life and my daughter's honor!'

The Sultan gently raised the old man:
'Keep thy gold, merchant, to trade fairly in our markets. The protection of honest travelers is not bought with coins; it is the sacred debt every strong arm owes to the defenseless.'

The next morning, the Sultan summoned the merchant and his daughter to the palace. When the merchant saw the Sultan seated on the throne, he gasped, recognizing the heroic guardian of the night!
The Sultan restored all their goods, punished the bandits with labor on the city ramparts, and established night lanterns along every alley in Cairo, demonstrating that true kings watch while their people sleep in peace.
moral: Courage in the dark and vigilance in defense of the innocent are the sacred duties of righteous leadership. [TE]

title: Story of the Broke-Back Schoolmaster (తెలుగు)
summary: In a bustling ward of Cairo lived a schoolmaster named Master Mansur, who walked with a severe hunch in his back yet possessed the most c... [TE]
full_text:
In a bustling ward of Cairo lived a schoolmaster named Master Mansur, who walked with a severe hunch in his back yet possessed the most cheerful disposition in the neighborhood.
The local youths, curious about his curvature, gathered around him one holiday afternoon and asked: 'Master, how came thy back to be bent like a crescent bow?'

Master Mansur chuckled, adjusted his spectacles, and replied:
'Listen, boys, and learn how hasty vanity bows a man's spine!

In my youth, I was tall, vain, and excessively proud of my erect stature. I walked through the markets with my chin held high, looking at the clouds and admiring my own shadow.
One day, the Grand Kazi announced that the chief clerk of his registry had retired, and that the position would be awarded to the candidate of most commanding presence and dignified carriage.

Determined to impress the Kazi, I dressed in a high, stiff turban that added two cubits to my height and walked toward the court building with majestic, haughty strides, refusing to look down at the cobblestones.

As I approached the courthouse entrance, an elderly porter was carrying a massive crate of imported damask fabrics out of a low cellar door. Because my head was held so high in self-admiration, I failed to see the heavy oak beam above the cellar lintel, nor did I see the porter's crate!

I crashed headlong into the oak beam! The impact buckled my knees, and the crate of damask fabrics tumbled from the porter's shoulder directly onto my spine!
When the physicians finally set my bones, my back remained permanently curved in this humble arch.

At first, I wept in bitter despair. But then I realized: before the accident, I was a foolish peacock looking down upon everyone; now, my bowed posture keeps my eyes fixed upon the humble earth where blossoms grow and children play.
My hunch reminds me every day that pride goeth before a fall, and that a bent back that carries knowledge to children is a thousand times better than a straight spine full of arrogance!'

The students laughed, gained deep respect for their teacher, and learned that true dignity lies in the spirit, not the silhouette.
moral: Physical afflictions endured with cheerfulness and patience reflect greater nobility than unblemished folly. [TE]

title: Story of the Split-Mouthed Schoolmaster (తెలుగు)
summary: Beside Master Mansur sat another tutor, Master Faraj, who possessed a wide scar across his upper lip that gave him a permanent, crooked g... [TE]
full_text:
Beside Master Mansur sat another tutor, Master Faraj, who possessed a wide scar across his upper lip that gave him a permanent, crooked grin.
When the students inquired how he gained his mark, Master Faraj smiled wryly:

'Ah, my young scholars, my scar was earned by the incurable disease of poking my nose into another man's kettle!

Thirty years ago, I was not a teacher, but an inquisitive apprentice tailor who could never mind his own stitching. Whenever an argument broke out in the street, I would abandon my needle and thrust myself into the fray, giving unsolicited opinions.

One afternoon, a fiery blacksmith and an equally stubborn coppersmith stood in the lane arguing fiercely over who owned an iron horseshoe found in the dirt.
Instead of letting them resolve their minor squabble, I pushed between them, puffed up my chest, and cried:
"Halt! As an impartial observer of human law, I shall examine the horseshoe and deliver a binding verdict!"

I seized the horseshoe. But alas! The blacksmith had only moments before pulled it straight from the glowing charcoal forge to cool it, and it was still scorching red beneath its black soot crust!

The burning iron seared through my fingers! In agonizing pain, I threw the horseshoe backward over my head without looking.
The flying horseshoe struck the coppersmith's prized brass samovar, which fell and shattered the blacksmith's clay water jug!
Both craftsmen, enraged by my clumsy interference, turned upon me together. The blacksmith swung a leather bellows, and the brass nozzle caught me squarely across the mouth, splitting my lip!

As the apothecary stitched my lip, he said: "Let this stitch remind thee that he who enters a fight uninvited always receives the hardest blow."

From that painful day, I gave up interfering in strangers' affairs. I became a schoolmaster, teaching children to guard their tongues and keep their hands upon their own work, for quiet discretion is the best guard of peace.'
moral: Unchecked meddling in matters that do not concern one leads to pain; discretion preserves the tongue and the jaw. [TE]

title: Story of the Limping Schoolmaster (తెలుగు)
summary: The third teacher of the academy, Master Kamil, walked with a noticeable limp, leaning upon a polished pearwood cane. He smiled at the ga... [TE]
full_text:
The third teacher of the academy, Master Kamil, walked with a noticeable limp, leaning upon a polished pearwood cane.
He smiled at the gathered youths: 'Since my brothers have confessed their follies, let me complete the trio with the tale of my stubborn foot!

In my youth, I was an impatient copyist who hated copying long manuscripts line by line. I was constantly seeking shortcuts to wealth.
One day, an eccentric alchemist told me that on the highest ledge of the Citadel cliffs, there grew a rare wild herb whose juice, when mixed with ink, would write letters of pure gold.

Instead of taking the winding, paved road that climbed safely to the summit, I reasoned: "Why walk three miles around the mountain when I can climb the sheer rock face in twenty minutes?"

I began scaling the crumbling limestone precipice. Halfway up, with the city roofs spread far below, I reached for a tuft of green weeds growing out of a rock fissure.
The moment my fingers closed around the weed, the rock ledge crumbled beneath my sandals!

I tumbled down twenty cubits, bouncing off thorny brambles, until I landed hard in an olive orchard, snapping my ankle bone into splinters!

When the bone-setter finished binding my leg, he looked at the crushed weeds still clutched in my bruised hand. He laughed and said:
"Young fool! This is not an alchemical herb; it is ordinary bitter spurge, which even goats refuse to eat!"

My ankle healed crookedly, leaving me with this eternal limp. But that stumble was the greatest blessing of my life. It taught me that there are no magic shortcuts in life—neither to knowledge, nor to wealth, nor to virtue.
Since then, I walk slowly upon the paved road of patient study, teaching you boys that slow, steady steps upon the right path always outstrip the reckless leaps of vanity.'
moral: Greed for shortcuts brings a heavy stumble; the straight path of honest patience leads safely home. [TE]

title: Story of the Three Sisters and Their Mother the Sultanah (తెలుగు)
summary: In a distant maritime kingdom of Andalusia lived a widowed Sultanah and her three devoted daughters: Princess Yasmin, Princess Soraya, an... [TE]
keywords: story of the three sisters and their mother the sultanah
full_text:
In a distant maritime kingdom of Andalusia lived a widowed Sultanah and her three devoted daughters: Princess Yasmin, Princess Soraya, and Princess Layla.
When an usurping uncle seized the throne through treachery, he banished the Sultanah and her daughters to an abandoned watchtower on a desolate, rocky coast.

Instead of weeping in helpless despair, the three sisters united their talents to sustain their mother.
Yasmin, skilled in embroidery, spun fine threads from sea-grass and silk remnants, creating tapestries of coastal dawns that fishermen sold in the capital.
Soraya, knowledgeable in herbal medicine, gathered sea-lichens, rock-fennel, and wild sage, concocting remedies that healed the fishing villagers of winter fevers.
Layla, the youngest, had a voice of crystalline purity; she befriended the dolphins and sea-birds, learning the signs of tides and coming storms, warning the fishing fleets before tempests struck.

The humble coastal folk came to love the three sisters and their noble mother, bringing them fresh fish, barley flour, and firewood.

One stormy night, a magnificent royal vessel belonging to the Sultan of Cordoba was driven upon the treacherous reefs near their watchtower.
Princess Layla heard the distress bells above the howling wind. Guided by her knowledge of the shoals, Yasmin and Soraya kindled a massive beacon atop the tower, while the fishing boats, directed by the sisters, launched into the surf and rescued the entire crew, including the young Sultan himself!

The Sultan of Cordoba was amazed to find four women of royal bearing and exquisite virtue living in a lonely tower, beloved by an entire coastal province.
When he learned of their royal lineage and the uncle's usurpation, he was moved by their dignity and resilience.

Calling upon his fleet and allies, the Sultan of Cordoba escorted the Sultanah and her daughters back to the capital. The citizens, already disgusted by the tyrant uncle's cruelty, opened the city gates and welcomed the rightful heirs with joyous acclamation!

The usurper was banished, the Sultanah was restored as Queen Regent, and the Sultan of Cordoba asked for the hand of Princess Yasmin, while his two noble brothers married Soraya and Layla.
Their united kingdom flourished in peace, proving that love, industrious labor, and mutual loyalty overcome the darkest seasons of exile.
moral: Filial devotion, unity among siblings, and courage under adversity turn sorrow into triumph and vindicate honor. [TE]

title: History of the Kazi Who Bare a Babe (తెలుగు)
summary: In the city of Aleppo presided a Chief Kazi who was so conceited that he believed himself immune to human weakness. He levied severe fine... [TE]
keywords: history of the kazi who bare a babe
full_text:
In the city of Aleppo presided a Chief Kazi who was so conceited that he believed himself immune to human weakness. He levied severe fines upon citizens for the smallest errors, lecturing them from his velvet bench with unbearable self-righteousness.

A witty young scholar named Dalil, who had been unfairly fined by the Kazi for singing a joyful song in his own garden, resolved to teach the pompous judge an unforgettable lesson in humility.

Knowing that the Kazi was excessively superstitious and obsessed with bodily health, Dalil disguised himself as a foreign physician from Bukhara. He visited the Kazi, examined his pulse with exaggerated solemnity, and gasped in horror:
'Alas, your Excellency! A monstrous malady has seized your abdomen! The humors have congested into an extraordinary internal growth!'

The Kazi, trembling with panic, cried: 'Is it fatal, O Hakim? What can be done?'
Dalil replied: 'I shall prepare a marvelous herbal poultice to be bound across your waist with a silk sash under your outer robes. But beware! You must breathe gently, walk softly, and speak no harsh words for seven days, or the growth will rupture!'

Dalil placed a cleverly stuffed leather air-bladder beneath the Kazi's silk robe. Every day, the disguised physician visited to adjust the sash, secretly inflating the bladder further with a small hand bellows!
Within three days, the Kazi appeared so round and protruding beneath his gown that he could barely waddle!

Convinced he had contracted a bizarre swelling, the Kazi called his fellow judges to his bedside, weeping: 'Brothers, pray for me! An unnatural affliction has transformed my body!'

At that moment, Dalil entered with the Governor of Aleppo and several respected scholars.
'Fear not, your Excellency!' said Dalil. 'Let us perform the grand extraction!'
With a swift stroke of a lancet, Dalil punctured the concealed leather bladder! A long, loud whistling hiss escaped from the cushion as it deflated, filling the room with the scent of rosewater!

The Kazi looked down to find his belly completely flat, and the deflated leather cushion falling onto the carpet!
The Governor and the assembly roared with uncontrollable laughter.
Dalil bowed: 'Your Excellency, you see how easily a man can imagine himself carrying an impossible affliction when vanity and gullibility blind his reason. Henceforth, be gentle in judging the simple follies of citizens, for even a Chief Kazi can be tricked by a cushion of air!'

Cured of his pomposity, the Kazi returned the unjust fines and governed his courtroom with newfound modesty and genuine fairness.
moral: Pompous hypocrisy is easily punctured by sharp satire; those who judge others without self-awareness become laughingstocks. [TE]

title: Tale of the Kazi and the Bhang-Eater (తెలుగు)
summary: In Damascus lived an idle dreamer named Bakr, who spent his days consuming intoxicating herbal pastes and dreaming extravagant daydreams ... [TE]
keywords: tale of the kazi and the bhang-eater
full_text:
In Damascus lived an idle dreamer named Bakr, who spent his days consuming intoxicating herbal pastes and dreaming extravagant daydreams in sunny courtyards instead of working.

One sunny afternoon, under the influence of his delusions, Bakr imagined he was the Grand Emperor of China, seated upon a throne of solid sapphire, distributing sacks of emeralds to kneeling ambassadors.
He began commanding imaginary armies at the top of his voice: 'Bring forth the golden elephants! Let the dancing peacocks assemble!'

A crowd gathered, laughing at his antics, until the municipal guards arrested him for disturbing the peace and hauled him before the austere City Kazi.

The Kazi glared at Bakr and demanded: 'Why dost thou cause public disorder and shout senseless commands in the marketplace?'

Bakr, still half-entangled in his reverie, blinked and replied:
'Your Honor, in my dream I was an all-powerful emperor who could grant wishes and heal poverty with a wave of my hand. If a man may be a glorious king in his sleep for free, why should he wake up to be a hungry porter in Damascus?'

The Kazi stroked his beard, saw through the poor man's delusion, and ordered:
'Place this Emperor of China in a cool bath, feed him warm chicken broth with lime juice, and bring him back when his head is clear.'

The next morning, with the fog of herbs gone, Bakr returned to court shivering in an ordinary woolen tunic.
The Kazi asked: 'Where are thy sapphire thrones and golden elephants today, O Emperor?'
Bakr hung his head: 'They vanished into thin air, your Honor, leaving me with a pounding headache and an empty stomach.'

The Kazi smiled gently:
'Dreaming of glory while neglecting the work before thee is like pouring perfume into a broken jug. Imaginary riches cannot buy a loaf of bread, and a clouded mind loses the true sweetness of life. Take this silver coin, buy a basket and pruning shears, and earn thy bread in the fig orchards. For an honest copper earned by the sweat of thy brow is worth ten thousand imaginary empires.'

Bakr took the counsel to heart, threw away his intoxicating herbs, and became an industrious gardener, enjoying the clear sunshine of reality.
moral: Illusions born of indolence vanish like smoke; genuine peace is found in clear minds and honest reality. [TE]

title: History of the Bhang-Eater and His Wife (తెలుగు)
summary: In the town of Homs lived an amiable but foolish man named Salim, who wasted his meager earnings on sweet herbal confections that filled ... [TE]
keywords: history of the bhang-eater and his wife
full_text:
In the town of Homs lived an amiable but foolish man named Salim, who wasted his meager earnings on sweet herbal confections that filled his head with absurd fantasies.
His prudent and devoted wife, Zubayda, despaired of his indolence, for their cupboards were often bare while Salim sat on the roof smiling at invisible angels.

One evening, Salim returned home with a glaze in his eyes, sat upon the floor, and declared:
'Zubayda, rejoice! I have just been appointed Supreme Admiral of the Red Sea Fleet! Tomorrow morning, thirty war galleys with purple sails will dock in our garden pond to await my commands!'

Zubayda looked at the tiny stone pond in their courtyard, which barely held three ducks, and decided it was time to cure her husband once and for all.

She set an empty clay bowl before him and an empty wooden spoon, saying:
'O Great Admiral, feast upon this royal banquet of roasted pheasants stuffed with almonds and saffron rice!'

Salim stared at the empty bowl: 'Wife, the bowl is completely empty!'
Zubayda feigned astonishment: 'What? Can an Admiral who sees thirty war galleys in a duck pond not see roasted pheasants in a porcelain bowl? Eat, my lord, eat of the feast thy imagination has prepared!'

Salim blinked, realizing the biting absurdity of his pretensions.
Next, Zubayda brought him an empty pottery jug: 'Drink, my Admiral, this goblet of cooled pomegranate sherbet!'
Salim tilted the dry jug to his lips, but nothing came out.

He sat back, his stomach growling loudly in the quiet room.
'Zubayda,' he admitted softly, 'I am terribly hungry, and empty air cannot fill my belly.'

Zubayda then brought from the kitchen a warm, fragrant dish of real lentil stew, freshly baked flatbread, and a wedge of white cheese.
'Here is real food, Salim, purchased with real coins earned by real spinning. If thou wilt be an honest weaver instead of an imaginary admiral, thy home will never lack bread, warmth, or honor.'

Salim wept, embraced his wise wife, and swore to touch foolish stimulants no more. He returned to his loom the next dawn, worked with diligence, and within a year owned a thriving textile shop, blessed by the love and wisdom of his faithful wife.
moral: Patience and clever household management can guide a straying spouse back to reason and domestic harmony. [TE]

title: How Drummer Abu Kasim Became a Kazi (తెలుగు)
summary: Abu Kasim was a cheerful festival drummer in the city of Mosul, renowned for his rhythmic precision and his unwavering honesty. While oth... [TE]
keywords: how drummer abu kasim became a kazi
full_text:
Abu Kasim was a cheerful festival drummer in the city of Mosul, renowned for his rhythmic precision and his unwavering honesty. While other men flattered wealthy patrons, Abu Kasim played his drum for weddings, harvest fairs, and children's processions, asking only fair wages.

One year, the Sultan of Mosul dismissed his entire judiciary after discovering that the magistrates were accepting golden platters from wealthy litigants.
Frustrated by corruption, the Sultan declared:
'I will appoint no more professional jurists who twist words for profit. I shall find a man whose rhythm in life is pure and incorruptible!'

The Sultan walked disguised through the bazaar and observed a dispute between a wealthy goldsmith and a poor water-carrier. The goldsmith claimed the water-carrier had splashed water on his fine silk coat and demanded ten dinars damages.
Abu Kasim, who was sitting nearby tightening the goatskin of his drum, intervened:
'Wait, neighbor! The coat was splashed by two drops of clean water, which have already dried without leaving a mark. Why charge ten dinars for water that dried into cool air? But since the goldsmith was startled, let the water-carrier give him a cool drink of water, and let the goldsmith give the carrier a copper for his labor!'

The crowd cheered, and both parties departed satisfied.

The Sultan, stepping forward, summoned Abu Kasim to the palace that evening and appointed him Chief Magistrate of the Civil Court!

Abu Kasim protested: 'O King, I know nothing of dusty law volumes; I am only a drummer!'
The Sultan replied: 'A good drummer knows balance, timing, and how to keep every beat true. Apply that rhythm to human affairs.'

On his first day on the bench, a wealthy landholder tried to slip a purse of fifty gold pieces onto Abu Kasim's table to sway a boundary dispute.
Abu Kasim picked up the purse, laid it upon his drum, and beat a furious, deafening rhythm upon the skin!
The coins bounced and jangled loudly across the courtroom floor!
'Listen, citizens!' cried Abu Kasim. 'The gold of corruption makes a hollow, ugly sound! Let the boundaries be measured with honest ropes, not with the jingle of bribes!'

The people cheered Abu Kasim's unbending integrity. For twenty years he served as Kazi, settling disputes with good humor, common sense, and absolute fairness, proving that an upright heart makes the finest magistrate.
moral: Honesty, rhythmic composure, and refusal to accept bribes can elevate the humblest citizen to seats of honor. [TE]

keywords: story of the kazi and his slipper
full_text:
In Baghdad lived a wealthy but notorious miser named Abu Kasim, who possessed a pair of ancient, wretched slippers. For twenty years he had patched them with bits of old leather, copper rivets, and coarse twine, until they weighed as much as stone blocks and were known to every resident as the ugliest shoes in Islam.

One day, Abu Kasim visited the public baths. While he was bathing, an honorable Kazi came to bathe as well, leaving his brand-new yellow morocco leather slippers by the dressing benches.
When Abu Kasim finished, he looked for his footwear, but someone had moved his wretched slippers. Seeing the elegant yellow slippers, the miser chuckled: 'Ah! Some friend has left me a gift!' He slipped them on and walked home.

When the Kazi emerged and found only Abu Kasim's infamous patched clogs, he flew into a rage, had the miser arrested, and fined him a heavy sum of thirty dinars.

Humiliated, Abu Kasim returned home and angrily threw his old slippers out of the window into the Tigris river.
Three days later, a fisherman casting his net dragged up the heavy slippers. The sharp iron rivets tore the net to shreds. Enraged, the fisherman ran to Abu Kasim's house and hurled the wet slippers through the window!
The heavy shoes struck a row of expensive crystal rosewater flasks that Abu Kasim had purchased for resale, shattering them all!

Abu Kasim wept: 'Accursed slippers!'
He took a spade, carried the shoes into his garden in the dead of night, and began digging a deep pit to bury them.
A neighbor, seeing him dig in the dark, reported to the watch that Abu Kasim had found a buried treasure without declaring it to the treasury!
The police arrested him, and the Governor fined him another hundred dinars before releasing him!

Desperate, Abu Kasim carried the slippers far outside the city and threw them into a mountain aqueduct.
The bulky shoes lodged in the sluice gate, blocking the water supply to the royal gardens and drowning the Sultan's prize tulip beds!
Once again, Abu Kasim was identified by his famous slippers and fined five hundred dinars!

Exasperated to the brink of madness, Abu Kasim picked up the soaked, mud-caked slippers, walked straight into the Grand Kazi's hall, slammed them onto the judge's table, and shouted:
'My Lord! Behold the cause of all my ruin! I beg thee, draw up a solemn legal decree declaring that these slippers are divorced from me, that I am no longer their owner, and that whatever disaster they commit henceforth—be it flood, fire, or earthquake—Abu Kasim is not responsible!'

The entire court erupted in laughter. The Kazi pardoned him on condition that he cast the accursed shoes into the public furnace and buy a clean, modest pair of shoes, teaching the old miser that false economy and stubborn clinging to old junk cost far more than honest generosity.
moral: Clinging stubbornly to worn-out possessions out of avarice brings endless trouble; let go of what is past. [TE]

title: Tale of Mahmud the Persian and the Kurd Sharper (తెలుగు)
summary: Mahmud, an affluent merchant of Isfahan, was traveling through the rugged mountains of Kurdistan with a caravan of fine saffron and silks... [TE]

full_text:
Mahmud, an affluent merchant of Isfahan, was traveling through the rugged mountains of Kurdistan with a caravan of fine saffron and silks. As dusk descended over the snowy passes, he pitched his tent near a mountain spring.

A wandering traveler wrapped in a coarse sheepskin cloak approached the campfire, begging for warmth. Mahmud welcomed him warmly, offered him a seat upon a woolen rug, and served him roasted lamb, dried figs, and steaming tea.

The traveler was a notorious mountain sharper who had intended to scout the camp and signal his comrades to plunder the pack-mules. Yet, as he watched Mahmud serving him with genuine courtesy and respectful affection, the sharper felt a sudden pang of shame.

'Noble merchant,' said the guest, 'thou treatest me like a brother, yet thou knowest not my name or business. What if I were a thief sent to betray thee?'
Mahmud smiled with tranquil faith:
'Our holy traditions teach that every guest is sent by heaven, and hospitality is a debt we pay to our shared humanity. If thou comest as a friend, my bread is thine; if thou comest with evil intent, may the bread we share be an oath between our souls.'

The sharper lowered his eyes. He stood up, cast aside a concealed dagger, and confessed:
'Master Mahmud, I came to rob thee. My band waits in the ravine above to ambush thy caravan at midnight. But thy kindness has disarmed my heart. No man can eat salt at another's table and then shed his blood.'

The sharper led Mahmud and his caravan along a secret, safe highland trail that bypassed the bandit ambush completely, guiding them safely to the plains of Hamadan.
Mahmud rewarded the man with three bags of saffron and seed money to open an honest mountain inn. The former sharper became a faithful guide and protector of travelers, proving that generous charity possesses a power greater than steel.
moral: Generous hospitality offered in good faith conquers malice, turning even a cheat into an honorable ally. [TE]
