title: Tale of the Sultan and His Sons and the Enchanting Bird (తెలుగు)
summary: In Khorasan ruled a benevolent Sultan who fell victim to a deep melancholia that no physician could heal. An ancient traveler told him: '... [TE]
keywords: tale of the sultan and his sons and the enchanting bird
full_text:
In Khorasan ruled a benevolent Sultan who fell victim to a deep melancholia that no physician could heal. An ancient traveler told him:
'O King, in the enchanted valley of Mount Qaf perches the Bird of Dawn, whose song restores youth and drives away all sorrows of the soul.'

The Sultan had three sons. The two elder princes, proud and selfish, volunteered to fetch the bird, demanding chests of gold and royal escorts. They rode forth, but upon reaching the pleasure city of Rey, squandered their gold on revelry and forgot their ailing father.

The youngest prince, Prince Yusuf, loved his father sincerely. He took only a sturdy horse and a loaf of barley bread, setting out alone into the wilderness.

Along the mountain path, Yusuf found a starving desert fox trapped beneath a fallen boulder. With great effort, Yusuf freed the animal and shared his bread.
The grateful fox spoke with human speech:
'Prince Yusuf, thy gentle heart preserves life. I shall be thy guide to Mount Qaf. When thou reachest the enchanted garden, thou wilt find the Bird of Dawn sleeping in an ebony cage. Beside it hangs a cage of solid gold. Beware! Place the bird only in the plain ebony cage; do not touch the golden one, or the palace guards will awaken!'

Yusuf reached the fairy palace, found the bird, but seeing its magnificent iridescent feathers, thought: 'Such a divine bird deserves a golden cage!'
The moment his fingers touched the golden wires, magical bells rang out, awakening the palace guards, who captured him!

The King of the castle spared Yusuf on one condition: that he bring him the Golden Steed of Baghdad.
Again the fox assisted Yusuf, warning him not to use the jeweled bridle. Once more, Yusuf's human frailty tempted him to touch the bridle, leading to a second trial: to bring the radiant Princess Shirin of Oman.

With the fox's counsel, Yusuf won Princess Shirin's heart by his honesty, obtained the Golden Steed, and secured the Bird of Dawn in the humble ebony cage.

Returning toward Khorasan, Yusuf encountered his two elder brothers, now destitute beggars. Overjoyed to see them alive, Yusuf embraced them, clothed them, and shared his provisions.
Yet envy consumed the elder brothers. At a remote well, they cast Yusuf into the abyss, seized Princess Shirin, the steed, and the bird, and presented them to the Sultan, claiming they had conquered Mount Qaf!

However, the Bird of Dawn remained silent, the steed refused oats, and Princess Shirin wept day and night.

Meanwhile, the faithful fox lowered a rope of vines into the deep well, rescuing Prince Yusuf.
Yusuf returned to his father's court in a humble shepherd's tunic. The moment he crossed the threshold, the Golden Steed whinnied with delight, Princess Shirin's face shone with radiance, and the Bird of Dawn burst into a celestial melody that instantly restored the Sultan's vitality!

Princess Shirin revealed the elder brothers' treachery. The Sultan banished the plotters, crowned Prince Yusuf as his heir, and celebrated his marriage with forty days of feasts, showing that pure virtue outshines the darkest betrayals.
moral: True loyalty and filial love are proven through selfless bravery, overcoming jealousy and deceit. [TE]

title: Story of the King of Al-Yaman and His Three Sons and the Enchanting Bird (తెలుగు)
summary: The King of Yemen possessed an exquisite botanical palace, yet his heart longed for the legendary Night-Blooming Rose of Mount Arafat, wh... [TE]
keywords: story of the king of al-yaman and his three sons and the enchanting bird
full_text:
The King of Yemen possessed an exquisite botanical palace, yet his heart longed for the legendary Night-Blooming Rose of Mount Arafat, whose single blossom was said to confer the wisdom of Solomon and perpetual vigor upon whoever smelled it.

He called his three sons and announced:
'Whosoever brings me the Night-Blooming Rose shall receive the royal signet ring and succeed to my crown.'

The two eldest sons set out with fanfare, boasting loudly of their courage. On their way, they encountered a withered hermit sitting beside a dry stone brook, asking for a drop of water.
The elder princes pushed the hermit aside, saying: 'Out of our path, beggar! We ride on a royal quest!'

The youngest prince, Prince Zayd, followed hours later. When he saw the thirsty hermit, he immediately dismounted, offered his leather canteen, and poured water for the old man with gentle hands.
The hermit smiled:
'Prince Zayd, thy courtesy opens the gates that pride locks tight. Mount Arafat is guarded by the Valley of Mirages, where roaring phantom waters drown the arrogant. Take this branch of mountain myrtle. When the mirages rise, cast the branch before thee, and follow the narrow trail of real moss.'

Zayd thanked the hermit and continued into the desert. He soon found the horses of his two elder brothers wandering riderless; both princes had chased the deceptive mirages into quicksand bogs and were trapped up to their chests!
Zayd threw them ropes, pulled them from the mire, and gave them dry cloaks. But instead of showing gratitude, the brothers sulked with bitter shame.

Following the trail of green moss revealed by the myrtle branch, Zayd reached the hidden cliff garden where the Night-Blooming Rose glowed beneath the silver stars like a ruby lamp. He plucked the blossom with reverence and carried it back to Yemen.

When the King inhaled the rose's sweet fragrance, his eyes cleared, his strength returned, and he saw the true character of his sons.
He crowned Zayd King of Yemen, while the elder brothers were appointed to tend the royal orchards, learning that humility and compassionate service are the true roots of noble authority.
moral: Humility and obedience to wise counsel triumph where boastful self-confidence meets ruin. [TE]

title: History of the First Larrikin (తెలుగు)
summary: In the outskirts of Cairo lived an avaricious miller named Shakir, who took an unlawful half-measure of flour from every peasant's sack a... [TE]
full_text:
In the outskirts of Cairo lived an avaricious miller named Shakir, who took an unlawful half-measure of flour from every peasant's sack as his 'milling toll'. When the poor complained that their children were starving, Shakir laughed: 'My waterwheel turns for those who pay my price!'

A quick-witted youth named Hasan resolved to end the miller's extortion.
He dressed in the fine wool mantle of a traveling merchant, bought two sacks of fine river gravel from the Nile shore, covered the top layer with white wheat grains, and arrived at the mill on a spirited mule.

'Peace be upon thee, Master Miller,' said Hasan. 'I have brought two sacks of rare imperial grain imported from Antioch. It is dry and fragile. Let us weigh it carefully, and take thy lawful half as toll, but grind the remainder with utmost delicacy.'

The greedy miller, eager to claim half of this supposedly valuable Antiochian grain, eagerly hoisted the sacks onto his stone mill without opening them fully.
He threw the lever, the heavy grindstones whirled, and immediately a horrific grinding screech shattered the air! The hard river pebbles chipped the millstones into jagged fragments, smoking with friction and ruining the expensive granite gears!

Shakir screamed in horror: 'Woe is me! My millstones are broken! What devil's seed didst thou bring?'
Hasan replied with calm innocence:
'Master Shakir, my Antiochian grain is simply firm! But since thou tookest half the sacks before inspecting them, thou art an equal partner in the grinding! Now, pay me the value of my lost grain, or we go before the Kazi!'

Terrified of the Kazi discovering his unlawful toll-taking, the miller pleaded for mercy.
Hasan agreed to settle on one condition: that the miller sign a binding covenant before the village elders to reduce his milling toll to a single fair cup per bushel, and provide free flour to widows for three years.

Shakir signed the covenant. The waterwheel turned once more, but now it ground bread for the poor with honest measures, proving that wit in defense of justice can shatter the stones of greed.
moral: Greedy monopolists who exploit the needs of the poor find their own cunning turned against them by quick-witted justice. [TE]

title: History of the Second Larrikin (తెలుగు)
summary: In the gold souk of Aleppo operated a sly moneychanger named Bahram, who used two sets of brass weights: a slightly heavier set when he b... [TE]
full_text:
In the gold souk of Aleppo operated a sly moneychanger named Bahram, who used two sets of brass weights: a slightly heavier set when he bought silver and gold coins from travelers, and a lighter set when he sold them back, cheating both ways.

A clever student named Tariq observed this fraud. He took a hollowed-out brass inkpot, filled it with molten lead until it weighed precisely twelve ounces, and polished it until it gleamed like pure gold bullion.

Tariq walked into Bahram's booth:
'Peace, master of the scale. I have an ingotted ornament of heavy mountain gold. Weigh it for me, and give me silver dirhams in exchange, for I must pay my tuition at the college.'

Bahram's eyes gleamed with greed. He placed Tariq's brass inkpot upon the scale, secretly using his heavy buying weights.
'Aha!' said Bahram, intending to cheat the student. 'My scale shows it weighs only ten ounces. I can pay thee only ten ounces of silver.'

Tariq feigned sorrow: 'Ah, my scale must be mistaken. Very well, give me ten ounces of silver.'
Bahram counted out ten ounces of silver coins using his light selling weights—which in reality weighed only eight ounces!

Tariq took the silver, then turned and shouted to the Market Overseer passing by:
'O Inspector of Weights! Come witness the miracle of Aleppo!'
The Overseer entered the booth with his certified imperial balances.
Tariq declared: 'I offered this merchant a piece of metal which he certified upon his scales as weighing ten ounces of pure gold. Here is the silver he gave me. Let us test his scales and certified weights before your eyes!'

The Overseer weighed both: Bahram's weights were tested against the imperial standards and found blatantly falsified! The Overseer confiscated Bahram's scales, smashed his falsified weights in the public square, and fined him five hundred dinars to be distributed to cheated customers!

Bahram was banned from the moneychanger's guild, while Tariq demonstrated that those who construct traps of false measures inevitably step into their own snares.
moral: Deceitful weights and dishonest balances bring public exposure and ruin to the covetous. [TE]

title: History of the Third Larrikin (తెలుగు)
summary: During a dry summer in Damascus when wheat was scarce, a wealthy baker named Kasim locked three large storage bins of flour in his cellar... [TE]
full_text:
During a dry summer in Damascus when wheat was scarce, a wealthy baker named Kasim locked three large storage bins of flour in his cellar, refusing to bake until bread prices doubled in the bazaar. Poor mothers stood weeping outside his shuttered shop while he claimed he had no flour left.

A resourceful young apprentice named Bilal resolved to break the artificial famine.
He knew that Kasim was pathologically fearful of rats eating his hoarded grain. Bilal bought a large clay pot containing twenty fat, noisy crickets, walked to Kasim's back cellar window at night, and emptied the crickets through the iron grate into the dark flour bins.

The crickets began chirping loudly, scratching frantically against the wooden partitions and dry wheat husks.
Inside his house, Kasim heard the rhythmic scratching and rustling. He panicked:
'Heavens! Thousands of giant granary rats have invaded my flour! If they soil the grain, my entire fortune is lost!'

Kasim rushed into the street in his nightshirt, shouting:
'Help! Porters, neighbors! My granary is overrun by ravenous rats! I will sell every sack of flour for half-price right now to anyone who carries it away before morning!'

Bilal, waiting in the lane with fifty townspeople and porters, cheered:
'We are ready, Master Baker!'
The townsfolk carried out every single sack of flour, paying Kasim half-price in cash. When the bins were emptied, they found not a single rat, only twenty harmless chirping crickets!

Kasim realized he had been completely outwitted, but with his sacks sold and the cash in hand, he could not retract the sale.
The bread was baked, the prices returned to normal, and the children of Damascus were fed, proving that compassionate wit can defeat cold-hearted avarice.
moral: Hoarding food during famine to artificially inflate prices is a grave sin that invites swift, poetic retribution. [TE]

title: Story of a Sultan of Al-Hind and His Son Mohammed (తెలుగు)
summary: In a magnificent coastal kingdom of India ruled Sultan Shams al-Din, whose only son, Prince Mohammed, grew up surrounded by velvet cushio... [TE]
keywords: story of a sultan of al-hind and his son mohammed
full_text:
In a magnificent coastal kingdom of India ruled Sultan Shams al-Din, whose only son, Prince Mohammed, grew up surrounded by velvet cushions, golden fans, and fawning courtiers. The young prince believed that bread grew on silver trays and that common laborers were born merely to serve kings.

Seeing his son's dangerous detachment, the Sultan summoned his guards one midnight, placed the sleeping prince on an ordinary merchant dhow sailing for the port of Surat, and commanded the captain:
'Leave him on the docks with nothing but a rough wool vest and five copper coins. Tell him the Sultan has disowned him until he returns with a purse filled with gold earned by his own sweat.'

Prince Mohammed awoke on the windy stone wharves of Surat, surrounded by shouting porters and smelling of salted fish. When he proclaimed his royal birth, the sailors laughed uproariously:
'A prince? Then carry this sack of peppercorns to the warehouse, Your Majesty, and earn two coppers for breakfast!'

Hunger soon conquered pride. His royal tunic tore, his soft hands blistered, and he spent his first night sleeping on a pile of jute sacks.
The next morning, he apprenticed himself to an elderly carpenter named Master Dawood. Dawood taught him to plane cedar timber, handle the saw, and carve mortise-and-tenon joints.

For three years, Mohammed lived among working men. He learned the value of a hard-earned loaf of bread, the sorrow of an artisan whose child falls sick without medicine, and the quiet dignity of a community that shares its crusts.
His body grew strong, his mind alert, and his heart filled with deep empathy for the toiling multitudes. With his savings, he carved beautiful wooden ship-fittings that merchants bought with eager praise.

At last, with a leather purse filled with gold dinars earned by his carpentry, Mohammed returned to his father's palace.
He knelt before the throne, not in silk, but in his carpenter's apron, presenting the purse:
'Father, I return not as an idle prince, but as a man who knows how bread is won and how a kingdom's true wealth resides in the hands of its craftsmen.'

Tears of profound joy streamed down Sultan Shams al-Din's cheeks. He embraced his son:
'Now, Mohammed, thou art worthy to wear the crown. For he who has never bent his back to work cannot know how to lift the burdens of his people.'

Mohammed succeeded his father, ruling India with legendary justice, lowering taxes on working artisans, and building schools for the children of laborers.
moral: A ruler's son must learn the dignity of manual labor and honest hardship before he is fit to wear a crown. [TE]

title: Tale of the Fisherman and His Son (తెలుగు)
summary: On the rocky coast of the Persian Gulf lived an elderly fisherman named Jabir and his bright young son, Tariq. For forty years Jabir had ... [TE]
keywords: tale of the fisherman and his son
full_text:
On the rocky coast of the Persian Gulf lived an elderly fisherman named Jabir and his bright young son, Tariq. For forty years Jabir had cast his solitary net into the sea, catching only enough sardines and mullet to stave off starvation.

One evening, seeing his father's weary shoulders and trembling fingers, Tariq said:
'Father, the sea is vast, yet thou fishest only in the shallow breakers where other boats have already disturbed the schools. Let us study the flight of the sea-gulls and the currents of the deep shoals.'

Tariq observed that every afternoon, flocks of white gulls gathered around a submerged coral reef two miles offshore, diving into the blue water.
The boy constructed a small, light outrigger from driftwood, fitted it with a woven reed sail, and persuaded his father to sail to the reef before dawn.

Casting their nets above the deep reef waters, they hauled up nets teeming with magnificent red snapper and kingfish, which fetched ten times the price of shore sardines in the harbor market!

With their first earnings, Tariq did not buy luxuries. He bought strong hemp ropes and cedar planks to build a seaworthy fishing smack, and invited five elderly, impoverished fishermen of their village to join their crew as equal partners.

Within two years, their small cooperative fleet provided fresh fish to the entire provincial capital. When a severe winter storm threatened to destroy the harbor boats, Tariq's knowledge of the coastal reefs enabled him to guide all twenty village vessels safely into a sheltered tidal lagoon.

The Governor of the province appointed Tariq Chief Warden of the Fisheries. Jabir sat upon the harbor terrace in warm wool robes, watching his son manage the port with wisdom and benevolence, thanking heaven for a son whose clever mind and loving heart brought prosperity to an entire coast.
moral: Wisdom shared across generations transforms modest toil into enduring security and honor. [TE]

title: Tale of the Third Larrikin Concerning Himself (తెలుగు)
summary: In the city of Rayy lived a greedy village alderman named Mu'in, who took a plump roasted goose prepared by a poor widow for her orphaned... [TE]
keywords: tale of the third larrikin concerning himself
full_text:
In the city of Rayy lived a greedy village alderman named Mu'in, who took a plump roasted goose prepared by a poor widow for her orphaned children, claiming it was his 'inspection tribute'.

A quick-witted student named Salim, lodging in the widow's attic, vowed to restore justice with a laugh.
He went to the alderman's banquet hall where Mu'in sat with four pompous friends, boasting of his feast.

Salim entered with an air of urgent gravity, carrying an open parchment:
'Your Honor! A grave grammatical and theological dispute has arisen among the scholars of the academy, and only an alderman of your vast intellect can settle it! The dispute concerns the ancient fable of the Goose that Divided the World.'

Mu'in, flattered beyond measure, puffed up his chest: 'Speak, scholar! I shall divide the goose according to cosmic wisdom!'

Salim carved the roast goose and presented the pieces:
'To you, O Alderman, as the head of the municipality, belongs the head of the goose, that your mind may remain elevated above mundane affairs!
To your two senior counselors belong the two wings, that you may fly together into the clouds of administrative glory!
To your two junior clerks belong the two drumsticks, that they may run swiftly to execute your decrees!
And to me, a poor, humble student representing the hungry orphan children of this district, belongs the humble torso and breast of the goose!'

Before the stunned alderman could comprehend the division, Salim wrapped the roasted bird's body in a clean linen cloth, bowed with profound reverence, and slipped out of the garden gate!

He carried the warm roast goose straight to the widow and her hungry children, who feasted with joyous laughter.
When the alderman realized he was left with only a goose head on his plate, his guests burst into unstoppable laughter at how cleanly his greed had been rebuked by witty justice.
moral: Humorous wit that exposes hypocrisy and restores stolen goods brings joy to the community. [TE]

title: History of Abu Niyyah and Abu Niyyatayn (తెలుగు)
summary: Two traveling companions journeyed across the desert of Nejd: Abu Niyyah (He of Good Faith), whose heart was simple, honest, and trusting... [TE]
keywords: history of abu niyyah and abu niyyatayn
full_text:
Two traveling companions journeyed across the desert of Nejd: Abu Niyyah (He of Good Faith), whose heart was simple, honest, and trusting, and Abu Niyyatayn (He of Two Intentions), who was scheming, jealous, and deceitful.

As their water ran dry beneath the blazing sun, Abu Niyyah shared his remaining drops with his companion. But when Abu Niyyah's canteen was empty, Abu Niyyatayn refused to share a single sip of his water unless Abu Niyyah surrendered all his gold and even his woolen cloak!
Having taken everything, the treacherous Abu Niyyatayn abandoned his companion half-dead beside a desolate dry well, riding away on the camel.

Abu Niyyah dragged himself into the shade of the well's stone wall, whispering prayers of patience and forgiveness.
As night fell, two desert spirits alighted upon the rim of the well. Believing themselves alone, one spirit said to the other:
'Dost thou know that the King of Damascus suffers from an incurable blindness, which no royal physician can heal? Yet the cure is simple: three drops of dew from the leaves of the wild jujube bush growing behind this well, dropped into his eyes at sunrise, will restore his sight instantly!'
The second spirit added: 'And dost thou know that beneath the dry foundation of this very well lies a buried chest containing the lost emerald signet of King Solomon, alongside an abundant spring of sweet water that would turn this entire wilderness into a blossoming garden?'

When dawn broke, Abu Niyyah gathered the dew from the jujube leaves, drank from the moisture, and dug beneath the well stone. Instantly, sweet water gushed forth, accompanied by the ancient signet ring!

Abu Niyyah traveled to Damascus, requested an audience with the blind King, and applied the jujube dew to the monarch's eyes.
Instantly, the King's blindness was dissolved! Overjoyed, the King made Abu Niyyah his Grand Vizier and gave him the royal princess in marriage.

Years later, a ragged, miserable beggar was brought to the vizier's diwan: it was Abu Niyyatayn, who had lost his ill-gotten wealth to bandits and lived in squalor.
Instead of taking revenge, the noble Abu Niyyah embraced him, fed him, and gave him a purse of gold, saying:
'Brother, I harbor no malice. Good faith has brought me honor, while two intentions brought thee misery.'

Envious to the core, Abu Niyyatayn asked how Abu Niyyah had gained his fortune. Abu Niyyah honestly recounted the story of the desert well and the spirits.
Greedy Abu Niyyatayn immediately rode to the same well, hid beneath the stone wall, and waited for the spirits to arrive, hoping to overhear more secrets.

At midnight, the spirits returned, furious:
'Someone has revealed our secrets! The King's sight is healed, the water flows, and the emerald signet is gone! A spy must be lurking near!'
Searching the shadows, the spirits found Abu Niyyatayn cowering behind the stones and hurled him into the bottomless pit, where his treachery was buried forever.

Abu Niyyah governed Damascus with righteousness and peace, proving that sincere goodness is an impenetrable fortress against evil.
moral: A pure intention brings divine protection and eventual glory, while malice and double-minded deceit destroy their own author. [TE]

title: The History of the King's Son of Sind and the Lady Fatimah (తెలుగు)
summary: Prince Mansur, heir to the kingdom of Sind, was renowned for his learning and valor. During a diplomatic voyage across the Indian Ocean, ... [TE]
keywords: the history of the king's son of sind and the lady fatimah
full_text:
Prince Mansur, heir to the kingdom of Sind, was renowned for his learning and valor. During a diplomatic voyage across the Indian Ocean, his vessel was caught in a fierce typhoon and shattered upon the coast of Oman.

Mansur was washed ashore unconscious, where he was discovered by the Lady Fatimah, daughter of the local Omani governor. Moved by the stranger's noble countenance and plight, Fatimah sheltered him in her family's garden pavilion, tending his injuries with soothing balsams.

As Mansur recovered his health, a pure and noble love blossomed between them, founded on mutual respect, shared poetry, and moral devotion. Mansur declared his royal lineage and asked for Fatimah's hand in marriage. Her father, the Governor, gladly consented to the union.

However, before the wedding could be celebrated, an aggressive corsair fleet raided the port, abducting Lady Fatimah along with other captives while Mansur was hunting in the hills.

Devastated but resolute, Prince Mansur disguised himself as an itinerant lute player and set sail across the seas, following every rumor of the pirate fleet. For two years he searched the maritime ports from Aden to Zanzibar, playing songs of longing that carried Fatimah's name in encoded verses.

At last, in the fortified island citadel of the corsair captain, Mansur's melody was heard through a high, barred window. A voice sang back the answering verse of the poem they had composed together!

That night, Mansur scaled the sea-cliff walls, overpowered the guards using his swordsmanship, and rescued Fatimah from her tower.
Together, they slipped into the harbor, commandeered the captain's swiftest galley, and sailed for Sind.

When they arrived at the capital of Sind, the aged King wept with joy at his son's safe return. The city celebrated their wedding with magnificent festivities lasting forty days.
Prince Mansur and Princess Fatimah ruled Sind with harmony and justice, remembered in chronicles as two souls whose unwavering fidelity conquered storms, distance, and chains.
moral: Chastity, reciprocal honor, and patient fortitude unite noble souls across oceans and trials. [TE]

title: History of the Lovers of Syria (తెలుగు)
summary: In Damascus lived two noble families, the Banu Asad and the Banu Hilal, between whom an ancient rivalry had smoldered for generations ove... [TE]
keywords: history of the lovers of syria
full_text:
In Damascus lived two noble families, the Banu Asad and the Banu Hilal, between whom an ancient rivalry had smoldered for generations over land boundaries and ancestral pride.

Yet fate decreed that young Walid of Banu Asad and gentle Salma of Banu Hilal should meet during a festival at the Great Umayyad Mosque. Their hearts recognized each other immediately: their love was pure, devoid of malice, and guided by deep virtue.

Knowing their fathers' entrenched enmity, Walid refused to enter into deceitful elopement. He said to Salma:
'Our love must heal our families, not tear them apart. I will win thy father's blessing through honor, or perish in the attempt.'

Soon after, a devastating desert locust swarm attacked the fertile Ghouta orchards of Damascus, followed by a band of desert raiders seeking to pillage the distressed farms.
The estate of Salma's father, Sheikh Hilal, was surrounded by raiders in the dead of night.

Walid, hearing the alarm bells, did not hesitate. Gathering his brothers and loyal kinsmen of Banu Asad, he rode into the fray, fighting courageously to break the siege. During the fierce combat, Walid threw himself before a falling blade meant for Sheikh Hilal, taking a severe wound to his shoulder to shield his father's rival.

The raiders were driven off. As Sheikh Hilal held the bleeding young hero in his arms, tears of shame and gratitude fell upon his beard.
'Young man,' cried the elder, 'thou hast shed thy blood to protect the man who hated thy father! Such nobility shames all ancient grudges!'

Walid's father, Sheikh Asad, arrived at dawn. Seeing his wounded son and his former rival embracing in mutual tears, the two patriarchs clasped hands over Walid's sickbed, renouncing their feud forever.

When Walid recovered, the entire city of Damascus attended the wedding of Walid and Salma. Their union united the two houses in perpetual peace, proving that true love has the power to extinguish ancient fires of hatred and plant gardens of lasting reconciliation.
moral: Sincere love accompanied by self-sacrifice and honor elevates human life above petty factional disputes. [TE]

title: History of Al-Hajjaj Bin Yusuf and the Young Sayyid (తెలుగు)
summary: The formidable and stern governor Al-Hajjaj bin Yusuf sat in his audience hall in Kufa, surrounded by armored guards with drawn scimitars... [TE]
keywords: history of al-hajjaj bin yusuf and the young sayyid
full_text:
The formidable and stern governor Al-Hajjaj bin Yusuf sat in his audience hall in Kufa, surrounded by armored guards with drawn scimitars. A young descendant of the Prophet's house, a youth of sixteen named Sayyid Yahya, was brought before him in chains, accused of speaking publicly against the governor's harsh taxes.

Al-Hajjaj fixed him with a piercing gaze and said:
'Boy, dost thou not know that my word commands death and life in this province? What madness drove thee to speak against my authority?'

Sayyid Yahya stood erect, his chains clinking softly, but his eyes were clear, steady, and devoid of fear:
'O Governor, life and death are held solely in the hands of the Almighty, who created thee from dust and will return thee to dust. Thy authority is a temporary trust; if thou usest it to crush the weak and extract sweat from the poor, thy power is not majesty, but a heavy debt thou must pay on the Day of Reckoning.'

The courtiers gasped at the youth's boldness, expecting the executioner's blade to fall.
Al-Hajjaj's brow darkened with thunder:
'Art thou not afraid of this sword?'

Yahya replied with serene eloquence:
'Why should I fear the sword that can only sever a mortal neck, while neglecting to fear the Lord who can punish an unjust soul for eternity?
A ruler who listens only to flattery is like a sick man who drinks honey mixed with poison. The truest loyalty a subject can show his governor is to remind him of justice when wrath blinds his judgment.'

Al-Hajjaj sat in silence for a long time. The fierce governor, known for unyielding ruthlessness, was struck to the heart by the boy's moral courage, eloquence, and unshakeable faith.

Slowly, Al-Hajjaj raised his hand:
'Strike off his chains! By Allah, I have heard ten thousand courtiers sing my praises, but none possessed the courage of this youth. A kingdom that silences voices like his is already doomed.'

Al-Hajjaj rewarded the young Sayyid with gifts, revoked the oppressive tax on the district, and allowed Yahya to depart with highest honors, demonstrating that unyielding truth spoken without fear has power to soften iron hearts.
moral: Truth spoken with fearless eloquence and spiritual dignity disarms the fiercest tyrants. [TE]

title: Night Adventure of Harun al-Rashid and the Youth Manjab (తెలుగు)
summary: Caliph Harun al-Rashid, walking through the quiet lanes of Baghdad with Vizier Ja'afar, heard sweet strains of a lute and a youth's voice... [TE]
keywords: night adventure of harun al-rashid and the youth manjab
full_text:
Caliph Harun al-Rashid, walking through the quiet lanes of Baghdad with Vizier Ja'afar, heard sweet strains of a lute and a youth's voice singing verses of poignant beauty from a modest rooftop:
'The night is dark, the stars shine clear,
Yet sorrow holds my spirit dear;
Not for gold do I pine or sigh,
But for an honest roof beneath the sky.'

Intrigued, the Caliph climbed the exterior stairs and greeted the singer, who introduced himself as Manjab, a poor calligrapher from Basra.
Manjab welcomed the disguised strangers with warm hospitality, offering his only meal: a small dish of dates and a pitcher of cold well-water.

'Young man,' asked Harun al-Rashid, 'thy voice bears rare beauty, and thy calligraphy on yonder table is of imperial quality. Why dost thou live in such frugal poverty?'

Manjab smiled gently:
'Noble traveler, my father died burdened with debts. For five years I have labored eighteen hours each day copying manuscripts to repay every copper he owed to the merchants of Basra. Yesterday, I paid the final dinar. I have nothing left in my pocket, but tonight my heart sings with pure joy, for my father's memory is clean before God and man.'

The Caliph was deeply moved by the youth's extraordinary filial piety and unyielding integrity.
Before departing, Harun al-Rashid slipped a gold signet ring beneath Manjab's ink-stand, saying:
'Tomorrow at noon, bring this ring to the gate of the Grand Palace, and inquire for the merchant Harun.'

The next day, Manjab arrived at the palace gates, showed the ring to the captain, and was escorted into the magnificent imperial diwan.
Beholding the guest of the previous night seated upon the throne of the Caliphate, Manjab trembled and prostrated himself.

Harun al-Rashid descended from his throne, raised the young man with his own hands, and said:
'Manjab, thou hast honored thy father through honest sweat and selfless devotion. Today, the Caliphate honors thee.'

The Caliph appointed Manjab Chief Master of the Imperial Scriptoria, endowed him with an estate by the Tigris, and provided dowries for his sisters, showing that heaven never forgets those who uphold filial duty and righteous conduct.
moral: Generosity exercised in secret brings heavenly rewards; kings find true joy in elevating the humble. [TE]

title: The Loves of the Lovers of Bassorah (తెలుగు)
summary: In the port city of Bassorah lived a young merchant named Utbah, who fell into sudden poverty through shipwreck and was forced to sell hi... [TE]
keywords: the loves of the lovers of bassorah
full_text:
In the port city of Bassorah lived a young merchant named Utbah, who fell into sudden poverty through shipwreck and was forced to sell his cherished estate. The greatest sorrow of his heart was parting with his beloved betrothed, Rayya, whose impoverished guardian arranged her marriage to a wealthy emir of Damascus.

Utbah, unable to bear the separation, traveled on foot behind the caravan to Damascus, subsisting on wild roots and sleeping under city walls merely to breathe the air of the city where Rayya resided.

Wandering near the palace of the Governor of Damascus, Utbah recited verses of mournful longing that caught the ear of the Governor, Emir Khalid.
The Governor summoned the ragged youth and asked:
'Who art thou, and what sorrow inspires such sublime poetry?'

Utbah confessed his entire history with complete honesty:
'My lord, I seek no charity or gold. I seek only to know that Rayya is treated with the gentle honor she deserves. If she is happy, my soul can endure any exile.'

Emir Khalid was astonished by love so utterly devoid of selfishness.
He immediately sent for Rayya's wealthy betrothed and presented the case with great dignity. The wealthy merchant, hearing of Utbah's profound fidelity and seeing the true devotion between the lovers, declared:
'By Allah, I will not be the barrier between two hearts joined by heaven. I release her betrothal willingly.'

Governor Khalid then did what only the most magnanimous of rulers could do: he gave Utbah an estate in Damascus, provided a lavish dowry of ten thousand dinars, and presided over the wedding of Utbah and Rayya with full civic honors.

The citizens of Damascus celebrated the event as the Triumph of Pure Hearts, proving that sincere love and royal generosity can transform hopeless tragedy into everlasting joy.
moral: Selfless love that seeks the welfare of the beloved above all desires inspires noble hearts to supreme generosity. [TE]

title: Story of the Darwaysh and the Barber's Boy and the Greedy Sultan (తెలుగు)
summary: In Samarkand lived an elderly dervish named Baba Qutb, who owned a simple wooden comb. Whenever he combed the hair of a poor, honest pers... [TE]
keywords: story of the darwaysh and the barber's boy and the greedy sultan
full_text:
In Samarkand lived an elderly dervish named Baba Qutb, who owned a simple wooden comb. Whenever he combed the hair of a poor, honest person, their mind was filled with serene wisdom and freedom from worry.

A humble orphan boy, apprenticed to a harsh barber, often brought warm water to the dervish without asking for pay. In gratitude, the dervish combed the boy's unruly curls. Instantly, the boy's face shone with radiant peace, and he became renowned for his gentle manners and razor-sharp intellect.

Rumors of the 'miraculous comb' reached the ears of the greedy Sultan of Samarkand.
Believing the comb could transmute hair into solid gold or reveal buried treasures, the Sultan sent his guards to arrest the dervish and confiscate the wooden comb.

Seated upon his throne, the Sultan demanded: 'Comb my beard with this talisman, that I may double my imperial treasury!'
The dervish replied calmly:
'O King, this comb cannot create gold. It untangles the knots of anger and washes away the dirt of covetousness from hearts that are ready for peace. Upon an arrogant head, it works no magic.'

The Sultan, scoffing at the warning, snatched the comb and dragged it violently through his perfumed beard.
Immediately, the brittle wooden teeth snapped against his coarse whiskers, and a swarm of angry wasps that had nested in the hollow comb flew out, stinging the Sultan's nose and forehead!

Howling in pain, the Sultan dropped the broken comb, while his courtiers ran in confusion.
The dervish picked up the pieces, bowed courteously, and walked out of the palace gates unhindered.

Outside, he gave the remaining fragments to the barber's apprentice, saying:
'Keep these scraps, my boy. For the true comb of wisdom is a clean conscience and an honest heart, which no tyrant can ever steal or break.'

The Sultan spent a week nursing swollen cheeks, learning that sacred gifts cannot be conquered by royal greed.
moral: Spiritual treasure cannot be seized by royal decree; greed turns blessings into ashes. [TE]

title: The Loves of Al-Hayfa and Yusuf (తెలుగు)
summary: In the desert lands of the Banu Hilal lived Princess Al-Hayfa, celebrated throughout Arabia not only for her radiant beauty, but for her ... [TE]

full_text:
In the desert lands of the Banu Hilal lived Princess Al-Hayfa, celebrated throughout Arabia not only for her radiant beauty, but for her peerless mastery of poetry, astronomy, and statecraft. Many proud tribal chieftains sought her hand, but she declared:
'I will marry only a man whose mind matches my own in wisdom, whose heart knows justice, and whose sword defends the helpless.'

From the neighboring tribe came Prince Yusuf, a youth famed for his noble character, modesty, and poetic brilliance.
When Yusuf entered the council of Al-Hayfa's tribe, the two engaged in a famous poetic dialogue, matching rhymed verses on philosophy, virtue, and cosmic law. In each exchange, Yusuf answered with such profound depth and graceful courtesy that Al-Hayfa's heart recognized him as her true equal.

However, a jealous rival chieftain from the north, seeking to prevent their alliance, launched a surprise raid with five hundred lances against Yusuf's encampment.

Instead of waiting for rescue, Princess Al-Hayfa donned a suit of silver chain mail, rallied her tribe's horsemen, and rode alongside Yusuf into battle!
Side by side, their lances moving with coordinated precision, they broke the enemy ranks and captured the aggressor chieftain, sparing his life on condition of perpetual peace.

The two tribes united under their joint rule. Al-Hayfa and Yusuf governed as equal partners in wisdom and justice, building libraries and oases across the desert, remembered for centuries as the model of true union where love and intellect shine together.
moral: Intellectual partnership and shared moral principles form the unbreakable foundation of true love. [TE]

title: The Three Princes of China (తెలుగు)
summary: The Emperor of China, reaching his eightieth year, gathered his three sons to determine the succession. He handed them a sacred ancestral... [TE]
full_text:
The Emperor of China, reaching his eightieth year, gathered his three sons to determine the succession.
He handed them a sacred ancestral heirloom, the Jade Mirror of Truth, saying:
'Travel through the four corners of our empire for one year. Whosoever performs the deed that reflects the purest radiance in this mirror shall be crowned Emperor.'

The eldest prince, Prince Kang, led a great legion to the northern frontiers, defeated a fierce horde of barbarians, built a fortress of stone, and returned proud of his military glory.
When he held the Jade Mirror, the surface remained dull and clouded with the smoke of burning villages.

The second prince, Prince Bao, journeyed to the southern ports, established vast maritime trading routes, brought back shiploads of pearls and silk, and filled the imperial vaults with gold.
When he looked into the mirror, it reflected only cold metal and the shadows of weary miners.

The youngest prince, Prince Ming, traveled alone on foot through the central provinces, which had been devastated by a catastrophic flood of the Yellow River.
Finding thousands of displaced peasant families starving, Ming did not build fortresses or hoard gold. He rolled up his silk sleeves, helped the villagers drain flooded fields, rebuilt dikes with his own hands, distributed imperial grain stores, and taught farmers to plant fast-growing rice.
For a whole year he lived on boiled millet, sleeping in thatch huts among the villagers.

When Prince Ming returned to the palace in his stained linen tunic, he held the Jade Mirror before his father.
Instantly, the jade burst into a blinding, celestial luminescence that filled the imperial diwan with golden light! In the mirror shone the smiling faces of ten thousand children who had been saved from starvation.

The Emperor stood up with tears of reverence:
'My son, conquests destroy and gold tarnishes, but relieving the suffering of the innocent is the eternal light of Heaven. Thou art our true Emperor.'

Ming was crowned Emperor of China, ruling with deep compassion and ushering in an era of peace and abundance remembered as the Golden Age.
moral: The true measure of a ruler is not military conquest or wealth, but the capacity to alleviate human suffering. [TE]

title: The Righteous Wazir Wrongfully Gaoled (తెలుగు)
summary: In the Persian city of Shiraz served a righteous Grand Vizier named Nizam al-Mulk, who was beloved by the people for his incorruptible ju... [TE]
full_text:
In the Persian city of Shiraz served a righteous Grand Vizier named Nizam al-Mulk, who was beloved by the people for his incorruptible justice.
Corrupt courtiers, unable to bribe him, forged letters implying that the Vizier was plotting with foreign powers. Deceived by these forged scrolls, the young Sultan stripped Nizam of his offices and cast him into the darkest subterranean dungeon of the citadel.

Months passed. The dungeon warden, expecting to find the former Vizier weeping in misery or offering bribes for release, was amazed to find Nizam sitting calmly on his stone bench, carving chess pieces from fallen limestone and composing verses of spiritual contentment.

The warden asked: 'Master, how canst thou remain serene in this damp darkness after ruling an empire?'
Nizam replied with a calm smile:
'I possess four medicines that cure all despair:
First: The certainty that nothing occurs without divine decree.
Second: The knowledge that impatience only multiplies suffering.
Third: The awareness that whatever happens could have been worse.
Fourth: The clear conscience that I never wronged an innocent soul or took a dishonest copper.
Stone walls can bind my limbs, but they cannot imprison an innocent heart.'

Meanwhile, without Nizam's wise guidance, the kingdom fell into chaos: tax collectors embezzled revenues, banditry flourished on trade routes, and the treasury emptied.
The Sultan, realizing something was deeply wrong, re-examined the forged documents and discovered the watermark of the corrupt chamberlain!

Overcome with remorse, the Sultan rushed down to the dungeon in person, fell to his knees before Nizam, and wept:
'O wise father, forgive my reckless blindness! Return to the diwan and govern our realm!'

Nizam gently raised the young king, harbored no resentment, and returned to his duties. The corrupt chamberlain was banished, and the Sultan learned never again to condemn a faithful servant without indisputable proof.
moral: Patience, clear conscience, and unwavering integrity endure through prison walls until truth prevails. [TE]

title: The Cairene Youth the Barber and the Captain (తెలుగు)
summary: In the vibrant Khan al-Khalili bazaar of Cairo, a high-spirited young student named Karim was getting his head shaved in Master Salim's b... [TE]
keywords: the cairene youth the barber and the captain
full_text:
In the vibrant Khan al-Khalili bazaar of Cairo, a high-spirited young student named Karim was getting his head shaved in Master Salim's barbershop. The barber was notorious for talking incessantly and gesticulating wildly with his razor in hand.

As Master Salim leaned out the shop window to shout a comment to a passing donkey driver, his razor accidentally caught the feather plume of a passing Captain of the Janissaries, cleanly slicing the magnificent ostrich feather in two!

The fierce Captain whirled around with eyes blazing, drawing his broad yatagan sword:
'Insolent dog! Thou hast insulted the imperial guard! Prepare to die!'

Master Salim dropped his razor and fainted onto the floor tiles.
Karim, sitting in the barber's chair with his head half-lathered in white soap foam, leaped up, grabbed a towel, bowed with exaggerated courtly elegance, and cried:

'Hold, noble Captain of the Citadel! Do not sheath thy blade in ordinary flesh! My barber is a certified imperial stylist trained in the palaces of Constantinople! He saw that thy magnificent plume was four inches too long according to the latest decree of the Grand Vizier! He performed the delicate imperial cut to ensure thy helmet meets the highest standard of palace fashion!'

The Captain paused, bewildered, looking from his sliced feather to Karim's completely solemn face and lathered scalp.
'Palace fashion?' muttered the Captain.
'Indeed!' affirmed Karim. 'Look how aerodynamic and martial thy helmet appears now! Even the Sultan's chief falconer wears his plume at that exact angle!'

The Captain looked into the barber's bronze mirror, admired his new silhouette, and sheathed his sword with a broad grin:
'By Allah, youth, thou art right! It looks far more ferocious!'
He tossed a silver coin to the trembling barber, patted Karim on the shoulder, and marched proudly down the street.

When he was gone, Master Salim sat up, gasping:
'Karim, my son, thy quick tongue saved my throat!'
Karim washed the soap from his brow and laughed:
'A handful of wit and a courteous tongue are better than a thousand shields when dealing with angry soldiers!'
moral: Presence of mind and good humor defuse volatile misunderstandings into moments of shared laughter. [TE]

title: The Goodwife of Cairo and Her Four Gallants (తెలుగు)
summary: In Cairo lived a virtuous and beautiful woman named Sitt al-Husn, whose husband, a noble merchant, was unjustly detained abroad on a comm... [TE]
keywords: the goodwife of cairo and her four gallants
full_text:
In Cairo lived a virtuous and beautiful woman named Sitt al-Husn, whose husband, a noble merchant, was unjustly detained abroad on a commercial dispute.
During his absence, four influential men of the city—the Chief Kazi, the Grand Vizier's secretary, the Captain of the Watch, and a wealthy grain merchant—shamelessly pestered her with unwanted advances, each abusing his authority to demand her favor.

Sitt al-Husn, determined to protect her honor and punish their insolence, devised a masterstroke of comedic justice.

She sent secret, identical invitations to each of the four suitors, inviting each to visit her house that evening at staggered intervals of half an hour.
She then hired an expert carpenter to build a massive cedar wardrobe with four separate, deep interior compartments, each fitted with a spring bolt that locked from the outside.

At dusk, the Chief Kazi arrived in his velvet judicial robes, eager and boasting. Before he could speak three words, Sitt al-Husn cried: 'Heavens! My husband's fierce brother has returned! Quick, hide in this cabinet!'
The Kazi scrambled into the first compartment, and she snapped the lock shut!

Half an hour later, the Grand Vizier's secretary arrived, perfume wafting from his silk sleeves. A sudden knock sounded at the door. 'Woe is me!' she cried. 'The watchmen have surrounded the house! Conceal thyself in this wardrobe!' The secretary leaped into the second compartment, which locked behind him!

Next arrived the Captain of the Watch, who in turn was terrified by a pretended alarm and shoved into the third compartment!
Finally, the wealthy grain merchant arrived, only to be pushed into the fourth compartment!

With all four pompous suitors securely locked in separate compartments, Sitt al-Husn sent a messenger to the Governor of Cairo:
'Your Excellency, I have in my possession a rare antique wardrobe containing four extraordinary curiosities of the city, which I wish to present to the municipal council.'

The Governor and his retinue assembled in her courtyard.
With a radiant smile, Sitt al-Husn turned the keys:
Out tumbled the Chief Kazi in rumpled robes, the Secretary covered in cedar dust, the Captain of the Watch trembling with humiliation, and the Grain Merchant clutching his knees!

The Governor stared in shock, then burst into roaring laughter along with the entire assembly.
Sitt al-Husn addressed the court:
'Behold, your Excellency! These are the guardians of law, security, and commerce in Cairo, who use their titles to harass an unprotected wife while her husband travels!'

The Governor, admiring her brilliant wit and courage, dismissed the corrupt officials, appointed honorable replacements, and sent an armed escort to bring her husband safely home with royal indemnity.
The tale became celebrated as Cairo's greatest victory of female intellect over arrogant folly.
moral: Virtuous wit and ingenious resourcefulness protect honor while teaching foolish suitors an unforgettable lesson. [TE]

title: The Tailor and the Lady and the Captain (తెలుగు)
summary: In Cairo lived an industrious tailor named Marwan and his devoted wife, Dalal. Marwan was celebrated for his impeccable sewing, crafting ... [TE]
keywords: the tailor and the lady and the captain
full_text:
In Cairo lived an industrious tailor named Marwan and his devoted wife, Dalal. Marwan was celebrated for his impeccable sewing, crafting robes for noblemen and commoners alike.

An arrogant captain of the Citadel guard, strutting past the tailor's shop window, took a fancy to Dalal and resolved to displace the humble tailor.
He strode into the workshop, threw down three bolts of heavy gold-threaded damask, and demanded haughtily:
'Tailor, sew me five ceremonial coats from this cloth by tomorrow noon. If a single seam is crooked, or if thou art late by one minute, I shall have thy shop closed and confiscate thy goods!'

Marwan worked through the night, but realizing the impossible timeline, grew exhausted.
Dalal stepped forward: 'Husband, let me cut and baste the linings while thou sewest the outer seams.'

Working in harmony with swift, practiced fingers, the husband and wife completed all five coats before dawn, stitching them with absolute perfection.
However, Dalal noticed that inside each collar, the arrogant captain had requested an embroidered phrase praising his own valor.

Dalal cleverly altered the embroidery with minute gold stitches. Instead of 'The Invincible Captain', the delicate letters read: 'Patience and Modesty are the Crown of the Brave.'

When the Captain arrived at noon, expecting to find the tailor exhausted and behind schedule, he was astonished to see five magnificent coats laid out in flawless order.
When he inspected the collar and read the subtle moral reminder, his face flushed.
The Captain looked at the united, dignified couple standing quietly before him with clear eyes and honest hands.

His arrogance melted into respect.
'Tailor,' he admitted, 'thou and thy wife have outworked my haste and outwitted my pride. The work is worthy of an emperor.'
He paid Marwan double the agreed price, apologized for his roughness, and became a lifelong patron and protector of the workshop, proving that collaborative diligence and moral dignity command genuine respect.
moral: Honest industry and fidelity safeguard a home against intrusive pride. [TE]

title: The Syrian and the Three Women of Cairo (తెలుగు)
summary: A wealthy merchant from Aleppo named Firas arrived in Cairo, boasting loudly in the caravanserais: 'The people of Cairo are simple folk! ... [TE]
keywords: the syrian and the three women of cairo
full_text:
A wealthy merchant from Aleppo named Firas arrived in Cairo, boasting loudly in the caravanserais:
'The people of Cairo are simple folk! No Cairene can outwit a Syrian who has traded in the grand souks of Aleppo and Damascus!'

Three clever Cairene sisters, Amina, Safiya, and Maryam, who managed an inherited pottery shop, overheard his boasting and resolved to puncture his vanity.

The next morning, Amina approached Firas in the spice market, asking with a bewildered expression:
'O noble Syrian merchant, canst thou help me? I have a pouch of dried mountain herbs which my grandmother swore can turn common river mud into fragrant incense. Does Aleppo possess such miracles?'
Firas, eager to claim the secret, bought the pouch of ordinary dried mint for ten silver dirhams!

An hour later, Safiya met him near the Nile bridge, weeping:
'Alas! I dropped my copper bracelet into the river! An astrologer told me that if a Syrian merchant of pure heart throws an onion into the current, the river spirits will bring the bracelet to the surface!'
Firas, wanting to prove his purity, bought an expensive onion from a vegetable boat, tossed it with great ceremony into the Nile, and waited on the bank for two hours while local boatmen laughed at his vigil!

Finally, Maryam approached him, holding an ordinary clay jar:
'Kind merchant, this jar holds the captured North Wind, which brings rain to thirsty crops. I cannot open it, lest it blow away my rooftop.'
Firas, determined to possess such a marvel, offered fifty dinars for the sealed jar.
When he broke the wax seal in his lodgings, nothing came out but a faint smell of vinegar!

The next day, Firas found the three sisters sitting together in their pottery shop, smiling warmly.
Amina handed him back his sixty silver dirhams:
'Take back thy money, merchant of Aleppo. We took thy coins not out of greed, but to teach thee a lesson. Never boast that one city is wiser than another, nor judge the intellect of strangers by thy own vanity.'

Firas blushed crimson, took back his silver, and bowed with genuine humility. He spent the rest of his trading season in Cairo conducting business with quiet respect, learning that boasting is the surest bait for clever laughter.
moral: Boasting of superior cunning in a foreign city leads to comedic defeat; modesty is the safest traveler's guide. [TE]

title: The Lady With Two Coyntes (తెలుగు)
summary: In a turbulent border town of Mesopotamia lived a noble and virtuous matron named Sitt Nur. One afternoon, while her family was working i... [TE]
full_text:
In a turbulent border town of Mesopotamia lived a noble and virtuous matron named Sitt Nur. One afternoon, while her family was working in the olive groves, two armed ruffians broke into her walled garden, seeking to loot the house and intimidate its mistress.

Instead of screaming or showing terror, Sitt Nur stood calmly upon her terrace, greeted them with serene courtesy, and said:
'Welcome, brothers. You enter with drawn daggers, yet you come to a house of peace. If it is gold you seek, sit upon this bench; I shall bring you refreshing mint water and the keys to our grain chest.'

Her absolute composure unnerved the two men. They sat down, glancing at one another in confusion.
Sitt Nur brought them two bowls of water and placed a heavy iron balance upon the table.

'Before you take our grain,' she said with a warm smile, 'resolve a riddle that has divided our village elders. A traveler has two bags: one filled with heavy iron daggers, and the other filled with light silver coins. If he enters a peaceful town, which bag will buy him friends, and which will bring him the gallows?'

The first bandit muttered: 'The silver coins buy friends, of course.'
Sitt Nur replied:
'Then why carry iron daggers when you can earn silver through honest labor?
Look at you: two strong young men, capable of building houses or harvesting dates, choosing to hide in shadows like hunted jackals.
Take these twenty silver dirhams from my household coffer. Go, buy tools, return to your villages with honor, and let no man call you thieves.'

Her profound dignity, gentle reasoning, and moral authority pierced through the crust of their hardened hearts.
The two bandits dropped their heads in shame, sheathed their weapons, and refused to accept the money.
'By Allah, noble lady,' the elder said, 'thy words have slain our wicked intentions more surely than any sword. We came as robbers, but we leave as men who remember our mothers.'

They bowed with deep reverence and departed. They left the border town to find honest labor, proving that moral courage and graceful speech can disarm violence where weapons only breed bloodshed.
moral: Quick intelligence and composed dignity protect the innocent from violence without spilling blood. [TE]

title: The Whorish Wife Who Vaunted Her Virtue (తెలుగు)
summary: In the city of Basra lived a wealthy woman named Samira, who spent her days lecturing all the women of the neighborhood on the superiorit... [TE]
keywords: the whorish wife who vaunted her virtue
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived a wealthy woman named Samira, who spent her days lecturing all the women of the neighborhood on the superiority of her morals, her absolute purity, and her flawless character.
'None among you,' she would boast at every gathering, 'possesses my devotion, my discipline, and my spotless reputation. I am the very crown of virtue in Basra!'

Her husband, an honest merchant named Tariq, grew weary of her endless boasting, which alienated their neighbors and filled their home with cold vanity.
He resolved to test whether her supposed virtue was genuine or merely an empty cloak of pride.

One evening, Tariq arranged with an elderly, trustworthy kinswoman to visit their home disguised as a distressed widow seeking a night's shelter.
The old woman knocked at the door in threadbare clothes, shivering in the cold rain:
'I pray you, good folk, grant me a dry corner near your hearth for one night.'

Instead of showing the compassion she so loudly preached, Samira pushed the beggar away, scolding:
'Away from my gate! I do not allow ragged strangers near my clean rugs! It would tarnish the dignity of my household!'

Tariq intervened, brought the old woman inside, gave her warm broth, and let her rest in the guest chamber.
The next morning, the disguised kinswoman revealed her true identity before a gathering of the neighborhood elders.

Tariq spoke gently to his wife:
'Samira, thou hast spent years boasting of thy spotless virtue to the four winds. Yet when a cold, hungry traveler stood at thy door, thy virtue turned to stone.
True virtue does not consist in proclaiming oneself pure while despising the unfortunate; it lives in quiet kindness, humble service, and a heart open to those in need.'

Samira stood silent, her face burning with deep shame before her neighbors.
The lesson humbled her spirit: she ceased her self-righteous lecturing, opened her home to charitable works, and learned that the purest virtue is that which seeks no applause.
moral: True virtue is silent, modest, and proven by steady conduct, whereas loud boasting often conceals glaring flaws. [TE]

title: Coelebs the Droll and His Wife and Her Four Lovers (తెలుగు)
summary: In the Syrian city of Hama lived a clever court jester named Juha, celebrated for his merry jokes, and his devoted wife, Marjana. Four we... [TE]

full_text:
In the Syrian city of Hama lived a clever court jester named Juha, celebrated for his merry jokes, and his devoted wife, Marjana.
Four wealthy boasters of the neighborhood—a vain perfume merchant, a pompous scribe, an arrogant bailiff, and a boastful apothecary—made a foolish bet at the public bathhouse that they could outwit Juha and woo Marjana with expensive gifts.

Marjana, indignant at their presumption, informed Juha immediately.
Juha chuckled: 'Let us prepare a comedy that will cure them of bragging forever!'

Marjana sent word to each boaster separately, telling him to come to their courtyard garden at nightfall to receive a 'token of admiration'—on condition that he wear an absurd costume to prove his devotion.
To the perfume merchant, she prescribed wearing a bear-fur rug; to the scribe, a necklace of dried eggplants; to the bailiff, an inverted copper cooking kettle on his head; and to the apothecary, a garland of garlic and leeks.

At nightfall, the four arrived one by one, each creeping through the garden gate in his ridiculous attire, believing himself the sole favorite.
Juha, perched on the roof with a large bronze gong and a bucket of river water, waited until all four had gathered beneath the trellis.

Suddenly, Juha banged the gong with deafening fury, shouting:
'Help! Robbers! Monsters have broken into my garden! One looks like a bear, one has a kettle for a head, and two are demons draped in onions!'

Juha dumped the bucket of cold water over them, while the neighborhood watchmen, alerted by the gong, rushed into the courtyard with torches.
The torches illuminated the four respected citizens in their ridiculous getups: the kettle slipped over the bailiff's eyes, the scribe was tangled in eggplant strings, and the perfume merchant was slipping on wet bear-fur!

The entire neighborhood, along with the Governor of Hama, gathered to witness the spectacle.
Juha laughed from the terrace:
'Behold, citizens! These four gentlemen came seeking to outwit an honest home. Here are their true colors!'

The four boasters paid a heavy fine for nocturnal trespassing, slinking away in utter disgrace.
Juha and Marjana celebrated their victory with tea and sweet cakes, showing that fidelity combined with good humor turns arrogance into a city-wide laughingstock.
moral: Vanity and deceit expose themselves to public mockery, while sharp wit preserves marital tranquility. [TE]

title: The Gatekeeper of Cairo and the Cunning She-Thief (తెలుగు)
summary: At the fortified Bab al-Futuh gate of Cairo stood an old gatekeeper named Uncle Mansur, famous for never letting an unauthorized traveler... [TE]
keywords: the gatekeeper of cairo and the cunning she-thief
full_text:
At the fortified Bab al-Futuh gate of Cairo stood an old gatekeeper named Uncle Mansur, famous for never letting an unauthorized traveler or smuggler pass through his portal. He boasted: 'No fly can enter Cairo without my seal!'

One morning, an intelligent young woman named Layla, whose father had been unjustly imprisoned on false charges of tax evasion, resolved to reach the Grand Vizier's diwan inside the citadel. The guards at the gates had been ordered by a corrupt prefect to turn away any petitioners from her village.

Layla approached the gate carrying a large, heavy wicker basket covered with cabbage leaves.
Uncle Mansur barred her way with his spear: 'Halt, girl! What is in the basket?'
Layla replied innocently: 'Only cabbages for the soup kitchens, master.'
Mansur, proud of his thoroughness, thrust his spear into the basket—and out hopped a frightened live hare, which darted between his legs and raced into the busy street!

Mansur and his three guards abandoned their posts, shouting and chasing the hare across the marketplace.
While the guards were scrambling after the animal, Layla calmly walked through the open gate, carrying her second basket containing the legal petitions and accounts proving her father's innocence!

She reached the Grand Vizier, presented the audited books, and secured her father's immediate release.

Returning to the Bab al-Futuh gate that evening, she found Uncle Mansur still breathless, holding the captured hare.
She bowed politely:
'Here are five silver dirhams for thy trouble, Uncle Mansur. The hare was quick, but truth is swifter.'

Uncle Mansur stared, realized how cleanly he had been outmaneuvered, and laughed heartily:
'By Allah, maiden! Thy wit is sharper than my spear. Henceforth, I will inspect what matters to human justice, rather than chasing hares!'
The old gatekeeper became Layla's lifelong friend and defender, learning that wisdom surpasses stubborn brute force.

title: Tale of Mohsin and Musa (తెలుగు)
summary: In Baghdad lived two cousins: Mohsin (The Benevolent) and Musa (The Schemer). Their father left them an equal inheritance of five thousan... [TE]
full_text:
In Baghdad lived two cousins: Mohsin (The Benevolent) and Musa (The Schemer). Their father left them an equal inheritance of five thousand gold dinars each.

Mohsin invested his share in honest trade, established a bakery that provided free bread to widows and orphans, and treated his apprentices with fatherly affection.
Musa, on the other hand, hoarded his gold in iron chests, lent money at extortionate interest, and sneered at Mohsin's charity:
'Thou art a fool, Mohsin! Bread given away is gold drowned in the river. Wealth is meant to be hoarded, not scattered!'

Years passed. A terrible fire broke out in the merchant quarter of Baghdad. Musa's fortified warehouse, locked with triple bolts, trapped its own heat, and all his silks, tapestries, and ledgers burned to fine ash! Musa was left penniless, weeping in the street.

Hearing of his cousin's ruin, Mohsin did not utter a single word of reproach.
He went immediately to Musa, embraced him warmly, took him to his own home, clothed him in fine wool robes, and divided his remaining trading stock equally with him, saying:
'Brother, wealth is a loan from heaven. When thine is lost, mine is thine. Take half of my business, and let us rebuild together.'

Musa wept bitter tears of remorse. His heart of stone broke under the warmth of Mohsin's unconditional generosity.
'O Mohsin,' he sobbed, 'for twenty years I mocked thy charity, believing myself wise. Today I see that the gold I hoarded burned in an hour, but the kindness thou didst scatter among the people built a fortress of love that no fire can touch.'

Musa reformed his ways completely, becoming Mohsin's faithful partner in both commerce and philanthropy. Their business flourished tenfold, proving that generous charity is the only investment that never fails.
moral: Selfless generosity and trust in divine providence outlast envious schemes, yielding enduring honor. [TE]

title: Mohammed the Shalabi and His Mistress and His Wife (తెలుగు)
summary: Mohammed the Shalabi (The Fashionable Youth) was the darling of Cairo's elite salons. Wealthy, handsome, and foolishly vain, he spent his... [TE]
keywords: mohammed the shalabi and his mistress and his wife
full_text:
Mohammed the Shalabi (The Fashionable Youth) was the darling of Cairo's elite salons. Wealthy, handsome, and foolishly vain, he spent his patrimony hosting lavish feasts for shallow acquaintances and shower gifts on glamorous flatterers, while neglecting his prudent, modest wife, Fatima, who kept their ancestral home in quiet order.

One day, his wise father-in-law, Sheikh Hasan, resolved to open Mohammed's eyes to the superficiality of his companions.
Sheikh Hasan instructed Mohammed to test his companions:
'Kill a sheep from the flock, sew it inside a blood-stained linen shroud, carry it to the doors of thy fashionable friends at midnight, and tell them thou hast killed a man in an accidental brawl and need a secret garden to bury the corpse.'

Mohammed laughed, confident in his friends' devotion.
At midnight, he dragged the blood-stained bundle to the mansion of his closest dining companion, Emir Basim.
When Basim heard the plea, he slammed the door shut from the inside, whispering: 'Madman! Dost thou wish to hang me with thee? Away from my gate!'
He went to the second friend, a poet who had composed twenty odes to their eternal friendship. The poet threatened to call the night watch if Mohammed did not vanish immediately!
A third fashionable companion refused even to unlatch his shutters.

Shattered and exhausted, Mohammed returned to his own home at dawn, dragging the heavy sack.
Fatima met him at the courtyard gate. Seeing the blood-stained sack and Mohammed's trembling hands, she did not scold, panic, or ask questions.
She locked the outer gate, brought a shovel from the garden shed, and said with quiet tears:
'Husband, whatever misfortune has befallen thee, thy life is my life. Let us bury it beneath the fig tree, and if the watch comes, I will stand beside thee to the end.'

Mohammed dropped the sack, unstitched the linen, and revealed the sheep's carcass!
He fell to his knees before Fatima, weeping in profound shame:
'My noble wife! I squandered fortunes on wolves who fled at the first shadow of danger, while ignoring the angel who stood ready to share my grave!'

Mohammed renounced his frivolous lifestyle forever. He dedicated his life to Fatima and their family, living in honor and mutual devotion, having learned that true loyalty is found not in festive laughter, but in the steadfast courage of love.
moral: Flattery and fair-weather friends vanish in the hour of trial; genuine fidelity is proven by quiet sacrifice. [TE]

title: The Fellah and His Wicked Wife (తెలుగు)
summary: In a quiet village along the Nile lived an honest, hardworking fellah (farmer) named Mas'ud. While plowing his master's field one morning... [TE]
keywords: the fellah and his wicked wife
full_text:
In a quiet village along the Nile lived an honest, hardworking fellah (farmer) named Mas'ud. While plowing his master's field one morning, his plowshare struck a buried earthenware pot filled with ancient Roman gold coins.

Being a man of absolute integrity, Mas'ud did not steal the gold. He carried it straight to the village headman, saying:
'This gold was found in the field of our neighbor, Sheikh Omar; it belongs to him according to law.'

However, Mas'ud's wife, a greedy and discontented woman named Bahija, was furious with him:
'Fool! Thou hadst enough gold to buy ten houses, and thou gavest it away to a rich sheikh! I will have my share, or I will ruin thee!'

That night, Bahija slipped into the headman's granary, stole the pot of gold, hid it in a dry well behind their barn, and substituted a pot filled with dead hornets.
The next morning, she went before the village magistrate, falsely accusing her husband of hiding the real treasure:
'My husband is a liar! He gave you hornets and kept the gold for himself!'

The magistrate, accompanied by the village elders, went to the granary and opened the pot. To Bahija's horror, when the lid was removed, a swarm of stinging hornets flew out, attacking only Bahija, stinging her face and arms until she shrieked and leaped into the irrigation ditch!

Meanwhile, sheep dogs digging near the dry well unearthed the stolen pot of gold.
The magistrate examined the evidence: Mas'ud's honest hands, Bahija's deceit, and the recovered coins.
Sheikh Omar, touched by Mas'ud's steadfast integrity throughout the ordeal, rewarded the honest fellah with half the treasure, a permanent title to five acres of fertile land, and cattle.

Bahija, disgraced by her own malicious deceit, was banished from the village councils, while Mas'ud lived in prosperous peace, celebrated by all the peasants as a shining example of unbending honesty.
moral: Contentment and honesty preserve a home, while deceitful greed brings ruin upon the treacherous. [TE]

title: The Woman Who Humoured Her Lover At Her Husband's Expense (తెలుగు)
summary: In the market town of Tripoli lived a merchant named Khalid, known for his gentle demeanor and quiet habits. An idle young aristocrat of ... [TE]

full_text:
In the market town of Tripoli lived a merchant named Khalid, known for his gentle demeanor and quiet habits. An idle young aristocrat of the town, foolishly assuming Khalid was simple-minded, tried to ingratiate himself with Khalid's household through extravagant flatteries and secret messages.

Khalid, whose quiet exterior concealed a mind like a polished razor, intercepted the youth's letters.
Instead of flying into a useless rage, Khalid decided to teach the interloper an unforgettable lesson in public embarrassment.

Khalid composed a reply in an anonymous hand, inviting the young gallant to climb the orchard wall at midnight to receive 'the golden chest of the family heirlooms'.
The youth, dressed in his finest embroidered silk coat and perfumed with musk, scaled the garden wall with an empty velvet sack, dreaming of easy riches.

As he dropped onto the orchard grass, he found himself surrounded not by treasure, but by three large, wooden bee-hives that Khalid had strategically arranged beneath the trellis!
Before the youth could move, Khalid, standing safely behind a protective mesh on the terrace, lightly shook the hives with a cord.

A cloud of angry midnight bees swarmed out!
The terrified young aristocrat ran blindly through the briars, shedding his silk coat, losing his slippers, and jumping straight into the muddy irrigation ditch, where he croaked like a bullfrog among the reeds!

The next morning, Khalid brought the muddy silk coat and slippers to the town market square, offering them to the highest bidder as 'the lost attire of a midnight gardener'.
The entire town recognized the youth's coat, and the young boaster was so thoroughly laughed at that he fled Tripoli for a year.

Khalid returned home to his garden, demonstrating that quiet prudence and clever defensive wit are more than enough to protect domestic honor from foolish arrogance.
moral: Underestimating the quiet wisdom of a faithful partner leads to the swift exposure of duplicity. [TE]

title: The Kazi Schooled By His Wife (తెలుగు)
summary: In Cairo presided a venerable Kazi named Abu Tahir, who was an absolute master of legal texts, statutes, and ancient commentaries. Yet in... [TE]
keywords: the kazi schooled by his wife
full_text:
In Cairo presided a venerable Kazi named Abu Tahir, who was an absolute master of legal texts, statutes, and ancient commentaries. Yet in his judgments, he was excessively rigid, ignoring human circumstances and imposing mechanical fines on the poorest litigants.

His wife, Lady Sitt al-Qudat, was a woman of extraordinary intelligence and practical insight.
One evening at dinner, Abu Tahir boasted:
'No jurist in Egypt understands the science of law better than I. My verdicts are infallible!'

Lady Sitt al-Qudat smiled quietly. The next morning, she disguised herself in the heavy veil of a poor widow, went to her husband's public court, and presented a complaint:
'O Chief Kazi! I have a neighbor who owns a magnificent, fertile grapevine. The vines have grown over the wall into my modest courtyard. Every autumn, ripe clusters fall upon my paving stones. My neighbor claims that because the roots are in his soil, the fallen fruit belongs to him, and demands I pay him twenty silver dirhams for the grapes my hungry children ate. What is your judgment?'

Abu Tahir stroked his beard, opened his heavy law books, and pronounced sternly:
'The law is clear! The tree follows the root! The fallen fruit belongs to the owner of the trunk. Thou must pay twenty dirhams or go to debtors' prison!'

The veiled woman bowed, walked out, and returned home.
That evening, when Abu Tahir sat down to his lavish dinner, he found his plate containing only dry bread crusts and a cup of cold water.
He frowned: 'Where is the roasted chicken? Where is the saffron rice with pine nuts?'

Sitt al-Qudat sat opposite him, smiling calmly:
'Husband, the money I had for the market was paid to the neighbor whose grape cluster fell into our courtyard! For according to the Chief Kazi's brilliant verdict this morning, we owe him twenty dirhams!'

Abu Tahir stared at his wife, recognizing her voice and her eyes beneath the veil.
She looked at him with profound gentleness:
'Abu Tahir, thou art wise in books, but blind in life. When a tree overhangs another's wall, its shade and fruit are heaven's gift of neighborly love, not a cause for prison. If law does not serve mercy and common sense, it is only a blunt instrument that starves the innocent.'

Abu Tahir blushed, dropped his head in profound humility, and embraced his wife.
From that day forward, the Kazi never issued a verdict without considering human compassion, becoming celebrated throughout Egypt as the most humane and beloved judge of his generation.
moral: Theoretical knowledge of law is useless without practical justice and empathy for the human heart. [TE]
